title: ENH: Native IEEE 754 infinity handling in Cython rolling aggregations
body:
Closes #57549

The current behavior drops inf values during timedelta rolling windows because of a legacy block in _prep_values that forcefully converted inf -> nan. Removing this block locally exposed that the underlying Cython engine (pandas/_libs/window/aggregations.pyx) was not equipped to handle raw infinities, specifically causing Welford's algorithm to permanently poison state variables (mean_x, ssqdm_x) with NaN during window exits. This is what triggered the ASAN/UBSAN failures in previous attempts to fix this issue.

Changes in this PR:

 1.   Removed the inf -> nan conversion in _prep_values to allow raw float propagation.

 2.   Patched roll_var in the Cython backend. The engine now actively tracks infinities within the active window. If an inf is present, it safely bypasses the Welford update, returns NPY_NAN for that specific window, and correctly resets state to prevent poisoning subsequent windows.

title: BUG: parallel read_csv (GH-64347) diverges from the serial path in several cases
body:
Adversarial testing of the parallel `read_csv` path added in GH-64347 turned up several cases where the parallel result diverges from the serial (`mode.max_threads=1`) result on the *same* file. Reporting them together since most share a root cause. All reproduce on `main` through the default path on a non-Windows machine (files must exceed the 50 MB parallel threshold).

### Root cause for most of these: the parallel path ignores `low_memory=False`

`_can_parallelize_csv` never consults `low_memory`, so `read_csv(big_file, low_memory=False)` is still split into `n_workers` byte-range chunks. That reintroduces exactly the per-chunk type/NA-inference divergences that `low_memory=False` exists to prevent: a "lean" chunk sees a different value distribution than the whole file and infers differently. Bug 2 and Bug 3 below are both instances of this.

---

### 🔴 Bug 1 — `EmptyDataError` on a valid headerless file with a blank first line

`header=None` (without `names`) on a file whose first physical line is blank or whitespace-only raises, where the serial path reads it fine (it skips the blank line).

```python
import os, pandas as pd

with open("f1.csv", "wb") as fh:
    fh.write(b"\n")  # leading blank line
    fh.write(b"".join(f"{i},{i*2},x{i}\n".encode() for i in range(2_600_000)))  # ~59 MB

pd.read_csv("f1.csv", header=None)
# -> EmptyDataError: No columns to parse from file

with pd.option_context("mode.max_threads", 1):
    pd.read_csv("f1.csv", header=None)   # OK, (2600000, 3)
```

**Cause:** in `_read_csv_parallel`, column-name inference builds `name_buf = preamble + first_line`; when `first_line` is blank, `TextFileReader(name_buf, ...)` raises `EmptyDataError`. That is not a `ParserError` subclass, so the `except (ParserError, UnicodeDecodeError)` fallback in `_read` doesn't catch it. Also fires when `skiprows` lands `data_start` on a blank line with `header=None`. (The `names=[...]` form falls back cleanly via the `n_first_rows != 1` guard — only bare `header=None` crashes.)

**Fix:** catch `EmptyDataError` around the name-inference `TextFileReader` and `return None` (fall back). Falling back is always safe: if the serial path would also raise, we reproduce it. Validated locally, 78 tests in `test_parallel_read.py` still pass.

---

### 🔴 Bug 2 — `dtype_backend="pyarrow"` raises on large ints where serial succeeds

A chunk that sees only large integers (> 2⁵³) attempts a numeric/pyarrow conversion and raises, while the whole-file serial read keeps the column as `double`/string.

```python
import pandas as pd

BIG = "9223372036854775807"
with open("f2.csv", "w") as fh:
    fh.write("c0\n")
    fh.write("\n".join("1.5" if i == 2_000_000 else BIG for i in range(4_000_000)))  # ~76 MB
    fh.write("\n")

pd.read_csv("f2.csv", dtype_backend="pyarrow", low_memory=False)
# -> pyarrow.lib.ArrowInvalid: Integer value 9223372036854775807 not in range ...

with pd.option_context("mode.max_threads", 1):
    pd.read_csv("f2.csv", dtype_backend="pyarrow", low_memory=False)   # OK, dtype double[pyarrow]
```

The guard treats `int`-kind + `float`-kind chunks as safe to `concat`, which holds for numpy/`numpy_nullable` but not pyarrow (its `concat` does a checked int→double cast that fails above 2⁵³). Depending on magnitude the parallel path raises `ArrowInvalid` (int in `[2⁵³, 2⁶⁴)`) or `OverflowError` (`> 2⁶⁴`). This is **pyarrow-specific** — `numpy` and `numpy_nullable` match serial in all cases tested. Note that with the default `low_memory=True`, a large file makes the serial path chunk internally too, so *both* raise; the clean parallel-only regression is under `low_memory=False`.

---

### 🔴 Bug 3 — Silent NA-mask divergence (wrong data, no error)

This is the most concerning: no exception, wrong values. NA tokens are kept as literal strings instead of NA when a chunk contains only `{NA-token} + {int in [2⁶³, 2⁶⁴-1]}`.

```python
import pandas as pd

OVER = "9223372036854775808"  # 2**63
with open("f3.csv", "w") as fh:
    fh.write("c0\nabc\n")
    fh.write("\n".join("nan" if i % 5 == 0 else OVER for i in range(4_000_000)))  # ~64 MB
    fh.write("\n")

par = pd.read_csv("f3.csv", low_memory=False)
with pd.option_context("mode.max_threads", 1):
    ser = pd.read_csv("f3.csv", low_memory=False)

ser["c0"].isna().sum()   # 800000  (all "nan" -> NA)
par["c0"].isna().sum()   # 200000  (600000 "nan" kept as the literal string "nan")
```

Both columns have dtype `str`, so the per-column dtype reconciliation (`_read_csv_parallel`, which compares only `dtype.kind`) sees `str == str` and concatenates without falling back.

**Mechanism.** A chunk of only `{NA-token, uint64-range int}` overflows int64 → retries uint64 → hits `uint64_conflict` (`seen_uint && seen_null`) → routed to the "leave AS IS" branch in `_convert_tokens`, which calls `_string_convert(..., na_filter=0, ...)` (`parsers.pyx` ~L1139 / ~L1147) and emits NA tokens literally. The whole-file serial read also contains `abc`, so it takes the object branch with the real `na_filter` and masks NA. This affects default NA tokens **and** custom `na_values` (list and dict), under object/`str`/pyarrow/`numpy_nullable`. It does **not** affect empty strings, bool+NA, values that overflow uint64, or `keep_default_na=False`.

**Note on the fix:** the `na_filter=0` "AS IS" emission is intentional and tested (`test_na_values_uint64`, GH-14983 asserts uint64-conflict columns are kept literal), so this can't be fixed by simply passing `na_filter` through — that reverts GH-14983. The parallel-specific regression should instead be addressed by respecting `low_memory=False` (see below). The default `low_memory=True` case can't be made byte-identical to a whole-file read without giving up parallelism, since serial `low_memory` already gives context-dependent NA here — probably a doc note.

---

### Lower-severity

- **Bug 4 — inconsistent error *type* for incompatible explicit `dtype`.** `dtype={"c": "Int64"}` on a column of mixed float/overflow-int can raise `OverflowError` from the parallel path vs `TypeError` from serial. Both fail; only the message differs. It is deterministic (the first chunk's error propagates via ordered `future.result()`), not a thread race.
- **Bug 5 — duplicated warnings from worker threads.** A converter+dtype `ParserWarning` fires once per chunk from the `ThreadPoolExecutor` workers (serial: 1, parallel: N), with a racy `stacklevel`.
- **Bug 6 — mmap unmap deferred on the error path.** When a worker raises anything other than `ParserError`/`UnicodeDecodeError`, its traceback pins the memoryview, so `mm.close()` raises `BufferError` and is suppressed; the mapping is unmapped only when the traceback is GC'd (transient address-space/FD hold). Bug 1 and Bug 2 both exercise this path.

---

### Suggested fixes

1. **Bug 1** — catch `EmptyDataError` in name inference → `return None`.
2. **`low_memory=False` gate** — `if kwds.get("low_memory") is False: return False` in `_can_parallelize_csv`. This removes the parallel-specific part of both **Bug 2** and **Bug 3** for callers who opted out of chunked inference. (Validated: they fall back and match, 78 tests pass.)
3. **Bug 2** under default `low_memory` — additionally gate `dtype_backend="pyarrow"` or fall back when a pyarrow int chunk exceeds 2⁵³.
4. **Bug 5 / Bug 6** — polish; Bug 6 is roughly a one-liner.

### Verified solid (no divergence found)

Thread/memory safety under a 250×-repeat concurrency stress (byte-identical every run; the SIMD tokenizer scan never over-reads past the mmap end); quoted embedded newlines (a boundary inside a quote always leaves a chunk mid-quote → `EOF inside string` → fallback, incl. a 50k-embedded-newline field spanning 16 chunks); the byte-offset/chunk-boundary math (1-row × 16-worker, multibyte headers, giant lines, huge preambles); `dtype="category"`, `encoding_errors`, BOM/CRLF/no-trailing-newline, thousands/decimal, uint64+NA precision, and wide/multi-column reads.

Not tested here (would need a different environment): free-threaded (no-GIL) builds, Windows/Linux specifics.

title: BUG: bdate_range/date_range business-day fast path lost periods and boundaries (GH#64648)
body:
The vectorized business-day range fast path (GH-64648) resolved the range endpoints from a fixed calendar-day buffer, which diverged from correct results in two ways:

- A `CustomBusinessDay` whose holidays blank out whole weeks could leave the `needed * 7 + 6` day buffer holding fewer than `periods` on-offset days, so `date_range`/`bdate_range` **silently returned a short (or empty) result**. For example, `date_range("2024-01-01", periods=6, freq=CDay(holidays=<all of Jan-Feb>))` returned an empty index instead of the first 6 business days in March.
- The path never applied the GH-35342 / GH-64790 time-of-day boundary fix, so an `end` whose time-of-day was earlier than `start`'s dropped the last on-offset date. For example, `date_range("2024-01-01 09:00", "2024-01-05 08:00", freq="B")` returned 4 dates instead of 5.

The endpoints are now resolved with offset arithmetic instead of a calendar-day guess, so the on-offset count is exact regardless of holidays/weekmasks. The arithmetic is done on normalized dates with the time-of-day re-attached afterwards, so an offset's `normalize=True` still does not strip the time-of-day from the output (GH-44025). The `end + periods` roll-back semantics (GH-64834) and the vectorized enumeration that provides the speedup are preserved.

title: BUG: merge(sort=False) silently corrupts matches for extreme integer keys (GH#64148)

labels.name: Indexing
labels.description: Related to indexing on series/frames, not to indexes themselves

body:
Investigating a regression from GH-64148: the range-like fast path in `merge(sort=False)` promotes one side's key to a `RangeIndex` and looks the other side up via `RangeIndex.get_indexer`. For extreme integer keys this overflowed/wrapped and silently dropped matches or returned out-of-bounds (garbage) ones, in both `how="left"` and `how="right"`.

Four variants:
- uint64 keys above `INT64_MAX` → silent match-drop (all-NaN)
- targets near `INT64_MIN` → false match / out-of-bounds take
- a two-element key whose implied step overflows int64 → silent match-drop
- keys whose range span exceeds `INT64_MAX` while step and stop each fit int64 → silent match-drop (e.g. keys `[-2**62 - 1, -1, 2**62 - 1]`: the member `2**62 - 1` sits at offset `2**63`, which wraps negative in int64)

Root causes are two pre-existing utilities the fast path newly relies on: `RangeIndex._get_indexer` (`target - start` overflow) and `maybe_sequence_to_range` (uint64→int64 wrap and step/stop overflow). Both are fixed here: `_get_indexer` establishes membership with exact comparisons, then computes offsets with uint64 modular arithmetic — exact for any in-window target, since the true offset always lies in `[0, 2**64)`. The `RangeIndex.get_indexer` overflow is itself a released bug (e.g. `RangeIndex(10, 13).get_indexer([INT64_MIN])` returned a spurious match, and genuine members of wide-span ranges failed to match), so it gets a whatsnew entry; the merge fast path itself is unreleased.

title: BUG: tz_localize/tz_convert wrong for non-nanosecond resolution before 1677
body:
Non-nanosecond ``Localizer.__cinit__`` scales the timezone transition/offset arrays from nanoseconds down to the target resolution with floordiv. The first transition is the ``NPY_NAT + 1`` ("beginning of time") sentinel, and floor-dividing it turns it into a real value around 1677 — essentially the nanosecond floor, which is why nanosecond resolution never hit this.

For ``s``/``ms``/``us`` resolutions, any tz-aware value before ~1677 then sorts *before* the corrupted sentinel, so ``bisect_right(...) - 1`` yields ``pos == -1`` and ``deltas[-1]`` is read out of bounds (wraparound is disabled), giving non-deterministic garbage. The same ``Localizer`` drives both directions, so ``tz_convert`` returned garbage wall times and ``tz_localize`` raised spurious "nonexistent time" errors.

Repro:

```python
pd.Series(np.array(["1600-01-01"], "M8[s]")).dt.tz_localize("UTC").dt.tz_convert("Asia/Kolkata")
```

Fix: preserve the ``NPY_NAT + 1`` sentinel exactly through the scaling (a real transition can never equal ``INT64_MIN + 1``). Verified that non-nanosecond results now match nanosecond ground truth and stdlib ``zoneinfo`` across a range of timezones and dates spanning 1678–2262.

Pre-existing since GH-47299 (non-nanosecond support). No standalone issue was filed; opening as a draft.

title: BUG: setitem-with-expansion casting regressions from GH#62523

labels.name: Indexing
labels.description: Related to indexing on series/frames, not to indexes themselves

body:
Follow-up to GH-62523, fixing two live defects it left behind. Both only affect the unreleased 3.1.0 development line, so no whatsnew entry is added.

**1. Naive `datetime64`/`timedelta64` setitem-with-expansion crashed.** `ser.loc[new_label] = value` on a naive datetimelike Series raised `AttributeError: 'numpy.ndarray' object has no attribute '_ndarray'` for any value. `infer_and_maybe_downcast` returns a raw M8/m8 ndarray for these dtypes, which `concat_compat` then mixed with the `DatetimeArray`/`TimedeltaArray` `_values` in its homogeneity-assuming fastpath. Fixed by wrapping the result with `ensure_wrapped_if_datetimelike` before the concat. (tz-aware and `Period` were unaffected because their `ExtensionDtype` avoids that fastpath.)

**2. Arrow `_cast_pointwise_result` raised `ArrowInvalid` on cross-resolution results.** The `timestamp`/`time`/`decimal` branches cast the inferred result back to the original type with no guard, so a finer-resolution/precision result that could not be cast down (e.g. `timestamp[us]` into a `timestamp[s]` column, or a rescaled `decimal`) raised instead of retaining the finer type. This affected both setitem-with-expansion and `map`/`agg`. Fixed by catching `ArrowInvalid` and keeping the inferred type, matching the existing `integer`/`floating` branches. (The `date` branch is safe — dates are whole days.)

Regression tests added in `test_loc.py` (setitem-with-expansion) and `test_arrow.py` (map path).

title: BUG: idxmax/idxmin wrong row for nullable UInt64 with NA, and when all values tie the NA sentinel fill (GH#64478)
body:
Fixes a regression introduced in GH-64478, plus the family of argmin/argmax sentinel-tie bugs it surfaced.

**Precision regression (GH-64478):** that PR changed the `+/-inf` sentinel fill in `nanops._get_fill_value` from a Python `int` to `np.int64(...)`. For `uint64` masked arrays this promotes the array to `float64` in `np.where` under NEP 50 (no common integer type for `uint64` + `int64`), silently losing precision for values above `2**53` — so `DataFrame.idxmax`/`idxmin` on a nullable `UInt64` column with missing values returned the wrong row. Fixed by returning `uint64` sentinels for unsigned dtypes (`u8max` for the min-fill, `0` for the max-fill), which keeps the array unsigned and also brackets the full `uint64` range (previously real values above `i8max` made the NA-fill the "minimum").

**Sentinel ties:** the NA fill values equal the dtype extremes, so real values can tie the fill, and `argmin`/`argmax` then return an NA position that precedes them. The `uint64` max-fill of `0` makes this common (e.g. an all-zero column with a leading NA). Fixed in `nanargmin`/`nanargmax`: a winner landing on a masked position means every unmasked value ties the fill, so the first unmasked position is returned instead. This also fixes the pre-existing analogues on main:

- `idxmax` on a float column containing only `-inf` and NaN returned the NaN row (`idxmin` with `+inf` likewise; both `Series` and `DataFrame`)
- `DataFrame.idxmax`/`idxmin` on nullable integer columns whose values all equal the dtype extreme (`i8min`/`i8max`/`u8max`) returned the NA row

title: BUG: PeriodArray._from_sequence integer interpretation flipped by NA (GH#64227)
body:
Follow-up to GH-64231, which added integer support to `PeriodArray._from_sequence` but left two inconsistencies:

- **Integer interpretation flipped by NA.** The object path (`_extract_ordinal`) read integers as *raw ordinals* while the int-array path (`from_calendar_ordinals`) reads them as *calendar years*. Since an NA forces object dtype, adding a `None` silently flipped the interpretation:

  ```python
  pd.Series([2000, 2001], dtype="period[D]")  # -> 2000-01-01, 2001-01-01
  pd.Series([2000, None], dtype="period[D]")  # was -> 1975-06-24, NaT
  ```

  Year-like is canonical (matches scalar `Period(2000, freq="D")` and the examples in GH-64227), so object-path integers are now routed through `Period(item, freq)`, preserving the `NaT` sentinel.

- **Masked/arrow integer arrays with NA.** `PeriodArray._from_sequence(pd.array([2000, None], dtype="Int64"), dtype="period[D]")` raised a misleading `TypeError: PeriodArray does not allow floating point in construction`, because `np.asarray` casts integers-with-NA to float. These are now routed through object dtype so the integers survive; genuine float EAs are still rejected.

title: BUG: PeriodIndex silently truncated out-of-bounds integer input (GH#64158)
body:
Regression from GH-64158. `PeriodIndex(integer_array, freq=freq)` interprets each integer as a year and feeds it into `period_ordinal`'s 32-bit `int` year parameter. Values outside the int32 range were silently wrapped into that field, so e.g. `PeriodIndex([2**32 + 1985], freq="Y")` returned year `1985` instead of raising — while the scalar `Period(2**32 + 1985, freq="Y")` path raises `OutOfBoundsDatetime`.

Validate the range and raise `OutOfBoundsDatetime` to match the scalar path, mirroring the guard `period_ordinals_from_fields` already applies to its year field.

title: BUG: Timedelta/to_timedelta raise bare OverflowError for inf/overflowing floats (GH#63275)
body:
closes #63275

Non-finite float input (``inf``/``-inf``) to :class:`Timedelta` and :func:`to_timedelta` was routed through ``int(item)``, raising a bare ``OverflowError``. Since that isn't a ``ValueError``, ``errors="coerce"`` couldn't catch it either, so it also broke coercion to ``NaT``. Pandas 2.3.x gave ``NaT``/``OutOfBoundsTimedelta``.

- Both the object-array path (``array_to_timedelta64``) and the scalar ``Timedelta.__new__`` float branch now gate on ``item.is_integer()`` instead of ``int(item) == item`` (mirroring the existing pattern in ``tslib.pyx``). ``float("inf").is_integer()`` is ``False``, so non-finite floats fall through to ``_numeric_to_td64ns`` → ``OutOfBoundsTimedelta`` (a ``ValueError``, so ``coerce`` gives ``NaT``). NaN never reaches this branch — it's caught earlier by ``checknull_with_nat_and_na``.
- Folded in a related pre-existing quirk the round-float change routed floats into: an overflowing round float / integer with a coarse unit (e.g. ``Timedelta(1e19, unit="s")`` and ``Timedelta(10**19, unit="s")``) went through ``np.timedelta64(value, unit)``, which raises a bare ``OverflowError``. That call is now wrapped to re-raise ``OutOfBoundsTimedelta``.

The float64-dtype (non-object) array path goes through ``cast_from_unit_vectorized`` and is unaffected — its handling of out-of-bounds values under ``coerce`` is pre-existing and out of scope here.

title: BUG: date_range with end off-offset and periods dropped a period for anchored offsets (GH#64834)
body:
Addresses the still-live part of GH-64834. #65356 (the main-targeted redo of #64880) kept the tests and whatsnew but dropped the actual fix, on the assumption GH-64648 covered it. That's only true for `B`/`bh`, which use the vectorized daily-offset-mask path; anchored offsets fall through to `_generate_range` and stayed broken.

On main (silently returns fewer than `periods` dates):

```python
>>> len(pd.date_range(end="2020-01-15", periods=3, freq="W-SUN"))
2   # expected 3
>>> len(pd.date_range(end="2020-01-15", periods=2, freq="ME"))
1   # expected 2
```

`_generate_range` rolls `start` onto the offset but never `end`, so when `start` is derived from `(end, periods)` an off-offset `end` yields a `start` one step short. Fix rolls `end` onto the offset first (rollback for `n>=0`, rollforward for `n<0`), mirroring the existing start-rolling logic.

Verified byte-identical to pandas 2.2.3 across a 360-case `freq × end × periods` grid (incl. time-of-day, `bh`, `B`). Note GH-64834 is already closed, so no `closes` line here.

title: BUG: to_timedelta Day offset mixed with sub-second element (GH#64306)
body:
The list-like path of :func:`to_timedelta` computed a ``Day`` offset as a raw seconds value (``item.n * 86400``) but never rescaled it to the array's inferred resolution. When a ``Day`` was mixed with any finer-resolution element, the resolution-inference second pass ran at the finer unit while the seconds value was stored verbatim, silently producing a wrong ``Day`` value:

```python
>>> to_timedelta([to_offset("D"), Timedelta(1, "ns")])
TimedeltaIndex(['0 days 00:00:00.000086400', '0 days 00:00:00.000000001'], dtype='timedelta64[ns]', freq=None)  # before
TimedeltaIndex(['1 days 00:00:00', '0 days 00:00:00.000000001'], dtype='timedelta64[ns]', freq=None)  # after
```

All-``Day`` lists stayed at seconds resolution, so the test added with the original feature (GH-64240, PR GH-64306) never exercised this path.

The ``Day`` branch now rescales through ``convert_reso``, mirroring the ``timedelta64`` branch, and raises ``OutOfBoundsTimedelta`` on overflow instead of silently wrapping.

No whatsnew entry: the Day-offset feature (GH-64240) is unreleased, so this defect never shipped.

title: BUG: loc/iloc split-path 2D setitem with a list of 1-D arrays silently transposed (GH#64230)

labels.name: Indexing
labels.description: Related to indexing on series/frames, not to indexes themselves

body:
A list of equal-length 1-D arrays is a 2D value — a list of rows — just like a list of lists or a 2D ndarray. On the split (mixed-dtype) path, `_is_2d_value` only treated a `list` as 2D when its first element was a `list`/`tuple`, missing `ndarray`. As a result:

```python
df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [0.0, 0.0], "b": [0, 0], "c": [0.0, 0.0]})
df.loc[:, ["a", "c"]] = [np.array([1, 2]), np.array([3, 4])]
# a=[1, 2], c=[3, 4]  -- silently transposed
```

The equivalent `np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])` value, and the uniform-dtype (single-block) path, both correctly give `a=[1, 3], c=[2, 4]`. A non-square value (e.g. 3×2) wrongly raised `ValueError`.

This is a regression from GH-64230, which replaced `np.ndim(value) == 2` with the `_is_2d_value` fast path (`np.ndim` had treated a list of equal-length 1-D arrays as 2D). Fix by recognizing `ndarray` as a valid row type, restoring the prior behavior while keeping the fast path's avoidance of `np.asarray` on plain lists.

GH-64230 is unreleased (in the `3.1.0.dev0` whatsnew), so no whatsnew entry is added.

title: BUG: rolling cov/corr NaN poisoning after empty window (GH#65739)

labels.name: Missing-data
labels.description: np.nan, pd.NaT, pd.NA, dropna, isnull, interpolate

body:
Follow-up to GH-65739. The numerical-stability rewrite of rolling `cov`/`corr` introduced a regression: `remove_cov`/`remove_corr` divide by `nobs` without the `nobs==0` guard that `remove_var` already has. When a rolling window's valid-pair count drops to 0, the running mean becomes `0/0 -> NaN`, which then poisons every subsequent overlapping window (the instability-recompute check `fabs(old)*tol > fabs(NaN)` is `False`, so it never clears).

```python
x = pd.Series([1.0, 10.0, 20.0, 30.0])
y = pd.Series([1.0, np.nan, 20.0, 30.0])
x.rolling(2).cov(y)   # was all-NaN incl. i=3 (expected 50.0)
x.rolling(2).corr(y)  # was all-NaN incl. i=3 (expected 1.0)
```

Guarded `if nobs[0]:` around the Welford downdate in both helpers, mirroring `remove_var` exactly — when `nobs` hits 0, reset the running mean/co-moment accumulators to 0 and clear the instability flag instead of dividing by zero.

Verified against a brute-force per-window reference over 2000 randomized trials (random windows / `min_periods` with NaN gaps): 0 mismatches.

title: BUG: bare DateOffset(n) a no-op on vectorized path near DST (GH#61870)
body:
Follow-up to GH-61870 / GH-61862, which aligned scalar `Timestamp + DateOffset(n)` with `DateOffset(days=n)` near DST but left the vectorized path broken.

Adding a keyword-less `DateOffset(n)` (integer `n`, no temporal kwds) to a `DatetimeIndex`/`Series` was a **complete no-op**, while scalar `Timestamp + DateOffset(n)` correctly added `n` days:

```python
ts = pd.Timestamp("2021-11-06 12:00", tz="US/Pacific")
ts + pd.DateOffset(1)                       # 2021-11-07 12:00 -08:00  (correct)
pd.DatetimeIndex([ts]) + pd.DateOffset(1)   # 2021-11-06 12:00 -07:00  (unchanged — bug)
pd.Series([ts]) + pd.DateOffset(1)          # unchanged — bug
```

`.shift(freq=DateOffset(n))` was likewise a silent no-op.

`RelativeDeltaOffset._pd_timedelta` builds its delta from `kwds` only. A bare `DateOffset` has empty `kwds` (with `_offset=relativedelta(days=1)`, `_use_relativedelta=True`), so `td_kwds` came out empty and the delta fell through to `Timedelta(0)` — the array path then added zero. The scalar path sidesteps this via its own `other + timedelta(self._n)` branch, hence the divergence.

Default the empty-kwds case to `n` days, so the vectorized path matches both the scalar path and `DateOffset(days=n)` (the years/months-only case still yields `Timedelta(0)`, since months are applied separately via `shift_months`). Since a bare `DateOffset` has `_use_relativedelta=True`, the array path runs on wall-clock values, keeping the result DST-consistent.

No whatsnew entry: GH-61870 is unreleased (3.1.0 dev), so this is a within-cycle regression; the existing `:issue:`61862`` note is now fully accurate.

title: DEPR: deprecate default openpyxl read_excel engine for xlsx/xlsm (GH#56542)
body:
Follows up GH-56542 (the xlrd/pyxlsb deprecation): steers the remaining common formats toward calamine.

Warns when ``read_excel`` reads an ``.xlsx``/``.xlsm`` file, no ``engine`` is passed (and ``io.excel.<ext>.reader`` is left at ``auto``), and ``python-calamine`` is installed — i.e. the case where the default would flip from ``openpyxl`` to ``calamine`` in a future version. The warning is self-triaging: output is unchanged for nearly all files, so it tells users that and points to the release notes for the rare differences (error cells under ``keep_default_na=False``; a date-formatted cell holding an out-of-range serial). Passing ``engine=`` or setting the option silences it.

Scope notes:
- ``ods`` intentionally stays on ``odf`` — calamine cannot read some ODS files and mishandles error/time cells there.
- ``Pandas4Warning`` (a ``DeprecationWarning``), so it is hidden outside ``__main__``/pytest by default.
- Incidental default-engine reads in the writer/openpyxl/fsspec/gcs/common test modules are filtered; a new test asserts the warning fires on the default path and is silenced by an explicit engine or the config option.

No user-facing behavior change yet — warning only.

title: PERF: direct fast_float path for float parsing in read_csv C engine
body:
For the default float converter with default settings (no thousands separator, ``'e'``/``'E'`` exponent), call fast_float directly via ``pd_fast_double`` instead of routing through ``precise_xstrtod_wrapper`` → ``precise_xstrtod_with_end``. It succeeds only when a numeric-looking token parses cleanly and consumes exactly ``[start, end)``; leading/trailing spaces, ``inf``/``nan`` spellings, and junk return nonzero so the caller retries through the full converter with its legacy semantics (verified: decimal-comma, custom scientific char, and inf/nan inputs still take the old path).

Removing the wrapper indirection for the common case speeds up float-column reads. Benchmarks (M3 Pro, warm cache, serial reads, best-of-4 over 9 interleaved rounds, 2.5M-row single-column files):

| case | base | this PR | speedup |
|---|---|---|---|
| floats, positive | 296 ms | 277 ms | **1.07x** |
| floats, ~50% negative | 357 ms | 333 ms | **1.07x** |
| floats, scientific notation | 326 ms | 310 ms | **1.05x** |

Values verified identical to the Python engine, including ``inf``/``nan``/``±0.0`` and full precision.

**Stacked on GH-65767.** The only net change here is the single ``pd_fast_double`` commit — it needs the ``word_end`` / token-length threading from that PR. The rest of the diff belongs to GH-65767 and will disappear once it merges, at which point I'll rebase this onto ``main``. Marked draft until then.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

title: PERF: use fast_float for integer parsing in read_csv C engine
body:
Moves `str_to_int64`/`str_to_uint64` from `tokenizer.c` into `pd_strtoi.cpp` (C++ with C linkage) and parses integers through the public `fast_float::from_chars_advanced` API — locale-independent, errno-free, and 8 digits at a time. Bumps the vendored fast_float to 8.2.10, whose reworked overflow check correctly rejects 20-digit values that wrap mod 2^64 (regression test added). The historical error-code contract (`NO_DIGITS`/`INVALID_CHARS`/`OVERFLOW`, `seen_sint`/`seen_uint`, GH-64631 trailing-junk detection) is documented at the top of the file and preserved; no heap allocation on any path.

Earlier revisions of this PR used a hand-rolled SWAR fast path; per review it was dropped in favor of the public fast_float API. Benchmarks below compare both against the same `main` baseline (M3 Pro, 1M-row files, `engine="c"`, best-of-7 reads per round, interleaved rounds across matched local builds, per-case medians; speedup vs `main` in parens):

| case | main | SWAR (earlier revision) | this PR |
|---|---|---|---|
| int64, 3 mixed-magnitude cols | 127.2 ms | 102.0 ms (1.25x) | 108.9 ms (1.17x) |
| small ints (1–2 digits) | 26.2 ms | 22.9 ms (1.14x) | 25.1 ms (1.04x) |
| 19-digit ints | 47.8 ms | 36.0 ms (1.33x) | 37.0 ms (1.29x) |
| uint64 (> int64 max) | 55.7 ms | 56.4 ms (0.99x) | 45.1 ms (1.24x) |
| thousands="," | 46.1 ms | 47.5 ms (0.97x) | 44.2 ms (1.04x) |

The fast_float version gives back some of the SWAR win on short/mixed ints but gains on uint64, which the SWAR fast path never covered (it was `str_to_int64`-only). The thousands-separator path initially measured ~3% slower than `main`; fusing the tsep-strip into a single bounded pass (per review) recovered it to 1.04x. All integer paths are 1.04–1.29x vs `main`.

Builds on the integer-parsing work in GH-65347 and GH-65350.

title: BUG: merge key dtype differs between symmetric how='left'/how='right' calls
body:
- [x] closes #56454
- [x] [Tests added and passed](https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/dev/development/contributing_codebase.html#writing-tests) if fixing a bug or adding a new feature
- [x] All [code checks passed](https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/dev/development/contributing_codebase.html#pre-commit).
- [x] Added [type annotations](https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/dev/development/contributing_codebase.html#type-hints) to new arguments/methods/functions.
- [x] Added an entry in the latest `doc/source/whatsnew/vX.X.X.rst` file if fixing a bug or adding a new feature.
- [x] I have reviewed and followed all the [contribution guidelines](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/development/contributing.html)
- [x] If I used AI to develop this pull request, I prompted it to follow `AGENTS.md`.

`a.merge(b, on="key", how="left")` and `b.merge(a, on="key", how="right")` describe the same logical join, but the shared key column's dtype depended on which frame `.merge()` was called on, not on `how`. `_get_merge_keys` always drops the shared join-key column from `self.right` and keeps it from `self.left`, regardless of `how`. `_maybe_add_join_keys` normally reconciles this via `find_common_type` when there are missing/unmatched rows to fill, but when every row already lines up 1:1 (both `left_indexer` and `right_indexer` are `None`), that reconciliation step is skipped entirely, so the output silently kept `self.left`'s dtype even for a right join.

This adds a narrowly-scoped case: only when `how == "right"` and no reindexing is needed on either side, use the right frame's original key array/dtype (mirroring how a left join already keeps the left frame's dtype in that same situation). `how="right"` merges that do need reindexing/filling are untouched and continue to go through the existing `find_common_type` reconciliation path unchanged.

One existing test (`test_merge_ea_and_non_ea`) asserted the old (buggy) behavior for `how="right"` and has been updated to reflect the corrected, symmetric dtype.

AI disclosure: I used an AI coding assistant (Claude) to investigate the root cause, implement this fix, and write the tests/whatsnew entry. I reviewed, tested, and take responsibility for the change.

body:

### Summary
A `CHANGELOG.md` file would help users understand what changed between versions and make upgrade decisions easier.

title: DEPR: warn for non-standard listlikes in numpy-dtype Series/Index arithmetic (GH#62423)
body:
xref GH-62423

Follow-up to GH-62560, which deprecated arithmetic/comparison between pandas objects and non-standard list-likes (``tuple``, ``range``, ``deque`` → scalar-like in a future version) but did not fire for the most common spelling: numpy-dtype ``Series``/``Index`` **dunder** ops (``ser + tup``, ``ser == tup``, ``idx + range(...)`` were all silent).

Adds the warning via a shared ``ops.maybe_warn_listlike`` helper at the four uninstrumented sites: ``IndexOpsMixin._arith_method``, ``Series._cmp_method``, ``Index._cmp_method``, and ``Categorical._cat_compare_op``.

Deliberately left unwarned because the current behavior is *already* scalar-like (so nothing changes in the future):
- object-dtype comparison (routes a tuple through ``comp_method_OBJECT_ARRAY`` → ``scalar_compare``)
- ``MultiIndex`` comparison (a tuple is a single entry)
- hashable list-likes on ``Categorical`` (only the positional/non-hashable branch warns)

``range`` in arithmetic is caught before it is converted to an ndarray for the EA path, so it warns once (no double-warning for EA-backed values, which warn downstream).

title: BUG: MultiIndex.get_locs wrong rows for list-like partial-string keys

labels.name: Indexing
labels.description: Related to indexing on series/frames, not to indexes themselves

body:
Regression from GH-64807: the vectorized list-like path in `MultiIndex.get_locs` used the level's exact-match `get_indexer`, so a list-like of partial-string keys on a Datetime/Period level silently matched only the exact-coerced timestamp (or raised `KeyError`) instead of the full partial-date range that the equivalent scalar key matches.

```python
mi = pd.MultiIndex.from_product([pd.date_range("2020-01-01", "2020-03-31"), ["a", "b"]])
mi.get_locs(["2020-02"])      # 58 rows
mi.get_locs([["2020-02"]])    # was 2 rows, now 58
```

Gate the fast `get_indexer` + `isin` path on `_supports_partial_string_indexing`: partial-indexing levels (Datetime/Period) fall back to per-element `_get_level_indexer` resolution; all other levels keep the fast path. The introducing PR is unreleased, so no whatsnew entry.

title: BUG: Period.to_timestamp wrong unit for normalized freq (GH#63760)
body:
GH-63760 changed ``Period.to_timestamp`` / ``PeriodIndex.to_timestamp`` to default to microsecond unit, but computed the result ``unit`` from the *raw, pre-normalization* ``freq`` argument (``freq == "ns"`` / ``self.freq.base == "ns"``). The actual dt64 resolution is decided by the *normalized target base*: ``period_ordinal_to_dt64`` / ``periodarr_to_dt64arr`` give nanoseconds only when the base is nanosecond, and microseconds otherwise. The two disagree in two cases:

- A target freq that normalizes to nanoseconds but isn't literally ``"ns"`` (e.g. ``"1ns"``, ``Nano()``): ``Period("2020", "D").to_timestamp("1ns")`` returned ``Timestamp("51969-08-29")`` (a nanosecond ordinal reinterpreted as microseconds).
- A nanosecond ``Period`` converted to a coarser target: ``Period("2020-01-01", "ns").to_timestamp("D")`` returned 1970 garbage with ``unit="ns"`` (a microsecond value reinterpreted as nanoseconds).
- The ``PeriodIndex`` array path raised a bare ``AssertionError`` (``assert dta.unit == unit``) on the same inputs.

Fix: derive ``unit`` from the normalized target ``base`` after freq normalization. The array-path assertion is now redundant (the produced data already carries the correct resolution) and is removed. For the ``how="E"`` branch — where the value ignores ``freq`` and routes through a ``how="start"`` recursion — the end-adjustment now takes its unit from the recursively computed timestamp's ``.unit``, removing the pre-normalization gate entirely.

title: BUG: PeriodIndex.from_fields silent corruption on mismatched lengths / NaN (GH#65921)
body:
Follow-up to GH-65921, which vectorized `PeriodIndex.from_fields` and dropped two guardrails the old scalar loop had: `zip(strict=True)` length validation and the scalar `Period` constructor's NaN rejection. The regression is unreleased (same 3.1 dev cycle), so there is no issue to close.

Two silent-corruption paths resulted:

- **Length mismatch / OOB read.** A tuple field isn't recognized as list-like by `_make_field_arrays`, so it's `np.repeat`-expanded rather than length-checked. `period_ordinals_from_fields` then loops over `len(years)` with `boundscheck(False)` and reads past the shorter field arrays:
  ```python
  PeriodIndex.from_fields(year=(2020, 2021), month=[1, 2], freq="M")
  # -> [2020-01, 2020-02, 2020-12, 2020-12]  (garbage OOB read)
  ```
- **NaN silently cast.** `.astype(np.int64)` turned `NaN` into a garbage ordinal:
  ```python
  PeriodIndex.from_fields(year=[np.nan, 2020], month=[1, 2], freq="M")
  # -> [Period('0-01'), Period('2020-02')]
  ```

Both now raise a clean `ValueError`, matching pre-GH-65921 behavior. The fix adds an O(1) equal-length check at the top of the Cython kernel and rejects NaN before the int64 cast in both the quarter and non-quarter paths.

title: BUG: DataFrame.sum on overflowing timedelta64 silently saturates (GH#43178)
body:
closes #43178

Follow-up to GH-65926, which added the timedelta-overflow guard only to the scalar branch of `nanops._wrap_results`. As a result `Series.sum` raised `OutOfBoundsTimedelta`, but `DataFrame.sum` (both `axis=0` and `axis=1`) silently returned an `int64`-max-saturated result with only a `RuntimeWarning`.

This guards the ndarray branch as well. A naive guard would regress `skipna=False`: the `NaT` sentinels (`iNaT`) are summed into the float result *before* `_mask_datetimelike_result` overwrites those positions with `NaT`, so two or more `NaT` accumulate past `int64` bounds and trip a false overflow. The same latent bug already affected the scalar branch (`Series([NaT, NaT]).sum(skipna=False)` wrongly raised).

The fix makes the guard mask-aware via a `masked` parameter on `_wrap_results`: positions destined to become `NaT` are exempt from both the raise and the `m8` cast. This makes `Series.sum` and `DataFrame.sum` consistent for genuine overflow and fixes the `skipna=False` all-`NaT` false-raise for both.

Note: `groupby.sum` / `resample.sum` on overflowing `timedelta64` still saturate silently — that is a separate Cython `group_sum` int64-accumulation path with no float intermediate for `_wrap_results` to guard, and is left for a follow-up.

title: BUG: to_json segfault on datetime/timedelta subclass without _creso (GH#65904)
body:
closes #65904

Follow-up to GH-65956, which hardened the first `getattr` in `get_long_attr` but left the second one — for `_creso` — unguarded. When an object passes `PyDate_Check`/`PyDelta_Check` and carries a `_value` attribute but no `_creso` (e.g. an object-dtype `datetime.date`/`datetime.timedelta` subclass), `PyObject_GetAttrString(o, "_creso")` returns `NULL` and `PyLong_Check(NULL)` dereferences NULL, segfaulting straight from public `to_json`.

NULL-check `reso` and return `-1`, matching the convention the first getattr and both call sites already use so the `AttributeError` propagates instead of crashing.

title: BUG: read_hdf did not round-trip missing values in a string Index (GH#9604)

labels.name: Missing-data
labels.description: np.nan, pd.NaT, pd.NA, dropna, isnull, interpolate

body:
closes #9604

A string `Index` serialized a missing value and the literal string `"nan"` to the same bytes, so neither could reliably survive a round-trip: a real `NaN` was read back as the string `"nan"`, and a literal `"nan"` was read back as `NaN`. (The latter was fixed in GH-65603 by skipping NaN substitution for indices, which in turn regressed the former — this restores both.)

The fix encodes missing values with a per-index NaN sentinel chosen to avoid colliding with any real value, persists it alongside the index, and substitutes it back on read, so both a genuine `NaN` and a literal `"nan"` round-trip in the `fixed` and `table` formats. Files written by older pandas lack the sentinel attribute and read back exactly as before.

title: DOC: make andrews_curves/parallel_coordinates plot examples self-contained
body:
The `.. plot::` examples for `pandas.plotting.andrews_curves` and `pandas.plotting.parallel_coordinates` fetched `iris.csv` from `raw.githubusercontent.com`. Sphinx *executes* `.. plot::` directives to render the image (the `# doctest: +SKIP` only suppresses the doctest runner), so every docbuild made two live network calls to GitHub. When GitHub rate-limited the CI runner, the build failed with `HTTPError: HTTP Error 429: Too Many Requests` — and since docs are built with `--warnings-are-errors`, that intermittently broke the Doc Build CI across unrelated PRs.

These were the only two docstrings in pandas that fetched data over the network in a plot directive. The other 66 `.. plot::` examples in `pandas/plotting/_core.py` build data inline, and the sibling `radviz` example in the same file already does. This brings the two anomalies in line: inline the iris data so the plots render offline and the docbuild no longer depends on the network.

title: BUG: warn when to_hdf complib is passed without complevel (GH#29310)
body:
closes #29310

Passing `complib` to `DataFrame.to_hdf`/`HDFStore` without `complevel` silently produced an **uncompressed** store, because `complevel` defaults to `0` (which disables compression). This was surprising enough that it was originally spotted while updating the io.rst performance-comparison table, where the "compressed" HDF files came out byte-for-byte identical to the uncompressed ones.

Rather than change the compression behavior (the demand signal is modest, and `complevel=0`/`None` disabling compression is documented and intentional), this emits a `UserWarning` from the `HDFStore` constructor when `complib` is given without `complevel`, so the ignored option is no longer silent. Explicitly passing `complevel=0` stays silent, since that is a deliberate request for no compression.

Notes:
- The silent-ignore only affected the store-constructor path (what `to_hdf` uses). The `put`/`append` path already handled `complib`-without-`complevel` (table format defaults to level 9; fixed format raises), so the warning is scoped to the constructor.
- Docs updated: the `complib` docstrings (`to_hdf` and `HDFStore`), the io.rst compression section, and the io.rst performance-comparison examples (now pass `complevel=9` so they actually compress).
- `_check_roundtrip`/`_check_roundtrip_table` in the tests set `complib` without `complevel`, so `test_frame[True]` had been silently round-tripping uncompressed data; they now pass `complevel` too.

title: BUG: plotting BDay data with subplots or mixed frequencies (GH-64311)
body:
Fixes three regressions from GH-64311 (avoid Period[B] in plotting), which replaced the `PeriodIndex[B]` plotting index with a plain int64 business-day-ordinal index. That int64 index carries no `freq` and no `asfreq`, breaking:

- `subplots=True, sharex=False` raised `AttributeError` — only the first axis received the business-day frequency, so sibling axes had none.
- Overlaying a higher-frequency series onto a business-day axis raised `AttributeError` from `asfreq` on the int64 ordinal index.
- Overlaying business-day data onto an existing lower-frequency (e.g. monthly) axis silently clobbered `ax.freq` to `"B"` before resampling, leaving the existing line at its original ordinals so the two lines ended up on incompatible scales.

`_get_freq` now derives `"B"` directly from an integer index, the per-axis frequency crutch in `LinePlot`/`ScatterPlot._make_plot` is removed, and a shared `_asfreq_plotting` helper re-expresses `PeriodIndex` ↔ int64 business-day ordinals in both directions without ever creating a `Period[B]`. Plotted x-ordinals are byte-identical to the pre-GH-64311 behavior across mixed-frequency overlays; three regression tests added.

The regression is unreleased (GH-64311 is 3.1.0-dev only), so no whatsnew entry.

title: BUG: Series.str.normalize NFC/NFKC returned decomposed output for ArrowDtype (GH#64359)

labels.name: Strings
labels.description: String extension data type and string data

body:
GH-64359 switched `ArrowExtensionArray._str_normalize` from an elementwise `unicodedata.normalize` to `pc.utf8_normalize`. On the shipped pyarrow wheels (verified on both 23.0.1 and 24.0.0), `pc.utf8_normalize` only *decomposes* for the composing forms `NFC`/`NFKC` — it skips the canonical composition step — so `ArrowDtype`-backed strings came back decomposed:

```python
>>> ser = pd.Series(["café"], dtype=pd.ArrowDtype(pa.string()))
>>> list(ser.str.normalize("NFC")[0])   # before: ['c', 'a', 'f', 'e', '́']  (decomposed)
>>> list(ser.str.normalize("NFC")[0])   # after:  ['c', 'a', 'f', 'é']       (composed, matches unicodedata)
```

This contradicts the method's contract (`normalize` returns the Unicode normal form, and the docstring documents `NFC != NFD`). Only `pd.ArrowDtype(pa.string())` was affected — `string[pyarrow]`/`str` route through the unicodedata path and were always correct. The decomposition forms `NFD`/`NFKD` are correct (and faster) via `pc.utf8_normalize`, so those are kept.

Fix: fall back to `unicodedata.normalize` for `NFC`/`NFKC`, keep `pc.utf8_normalize` for `NFD`/`NFKD`. The existing test only exercised ASCII (no character to compose), which is why the regression slipped through; it's extended here to cover all four forms with composing inputs against the `unicodedata` oracle.

The underlying defect is arguably upstream — the Arrow C++ kernel source correctly requests `UTF8PROC_COMPOSE`, yet the shipped wheels return decomposed output, pointing at the bundled/linked utf8proc (build-dependent). Worth reporting to Arrow separately; regardless, pandas shouldn't depend on which utf8proc a wheel bundled.

No whatsnew entry: the regression was introduced and fixed within the unreleased 3.1.0 dev cycle, so no released version was affected.

title: DEPR: read_feather and DataFrame.to_feather (GH#66177)
body:
closes #66177

Deprecates `read_feather` and `DataFrame.to_feather` (emitting `Pandas4Warning`, to be enforced in 4.0), directing users to `read_parquet` / `DataFrame.to_parquet`. This spun out of the review of GH-66169, where pyarrow ≥24 deprecated the `pyarrow.feather.read_table` / `write_feather` wrappers that back pandas' feather I/O.

## Why deprecate

- Feather is largely redundant with Parquet for pandas users, which is already the recommended columnar storage format.
- The underlying `pyarrow.feather` Python API is itself deprecated as of pyarrow 24.

pyarrow's own feather deprecation warnings (suppressed inside pandas per GH-66169) stay suppressed, so users see a single, clean pandas deprecation rather than pyarrow's internal-API noise on top.

## Alternative considered: migrate to `pyarrow.ipc` instead of deprecating

Recording this since the CI trigger in GH-66169 does **not** actually force removal. Feather V2 *is* the Arrow IPC file format (`ARROW1` magic, byte-identical), and pyarrow 24 deprecated only the `pyarrow.feather` wrappers — not the format. So we could instead migrate the implementation onto `pyarrow.ipc` and keep the public API:

- **Read** — ~a one-line swap: `pa.ipc.open_file(handle).read_all()` + column `.select()`. Loses only the `use_threads` read hint.
- **Write** — ~15 lines re-deriving feather's V2 defaults (LZ4 default compression, `"uncompressed"` → `None`, `compression_level` → `pa.Codec`, `chunksize` → `max_chunksize`); pandas would then own that kwarg contract.
- **Feather V1** (`FEA1`, opt-in `version=1`) is dropped either way — `pyarrow.ipc` can neither read nor write it. Preserving V1 *reads* would require magic-byte sniffing plus pyarrow's private `_feather` API.

We chose deprecation over migration: Feather is redundant with Parquet, and migrating means pandas taking on wrapper code and a V1 break to maintain a low-value format.

title: BUG: incorrect tz offsets for distant dates with negative-DST zoneinfo timezones (GH#65712)
body:
Follow-up to GH-65733, which added a zoneinfo Python-API fallback for distant-date DST offsets but only engaged it for dates beyond ~2100. That left a **2088–2099 hole** for negative-DST zones — `Africa/Casablanca` and `Africa/El_Aaiun` (the only zones with `_tz_after.dst_diff < 0`).

These zones' Ramadan-based POSIX rule keeps "DST" in effect for nearly the whole year, so `_get_zoneinfo_trans_and_deltas` computes per-year `(start, end)` transition intervals that overlap across calendar years. Flattening them into a single sorted transition list invents spurious offset stretches, inverting std/dst — so `tz_convert`/`tz_localize` returned offsets that were off by an hour and internally inconsistent (e.g. Casablanca UTC-noon 2099 → `14:00+01:00` where the underlying value is 12:00 UTC, vs stdlib `13:00+01:00`). Dates >2099 were already rescued by the fallback; dates ≤2087 use real historical transitions; only the 2088–2099 extrapolated window was wrong.

Fix: for negative-DST zones (`dst_offset < std_offset`), skip generating the unreliable extrapolated transitions while keeping `has_tz_rule=True`, so the already-wired per-value zoneinfo fallback (used by both `tz_convert` and `tz_localize`) handles all dates beyond the last historical transition (~2087). Negligible perf cost, since dates that far out are rare.

xref GH-65712

title: BUG: Arrow as_unit truncated toward zero and silenced overflow
body:
Regression from GH-63573, which switched `ArrowExtensionArray._dt_as_unit` to `pc.cast(..., safe=False)`. That truncates toward zero and silently wraps on int64 overflow, whereas numpy/pandas `as_unit` floors toward -inf and raises on out-of-bounds.

Consequences before this PR:
- Negative durations rounded the wrong way, e.g. `-93784567890123ns -> s` gave `-93784s` instead of `-93785s`.
- Pre-epoch timestamps crossed the epoch, e.g. `1969-12-31 23:59:59.123456789ns -> s` gave `1970-01-01 00:00:00` instead of `1969-12-31 23:59:59`.
- Out-of-bounds upcasts (e.g. year-2600 `timestamp[s] -> ns`) silently returned int64-wrapped garbage instead of raising.

The `safe=False` path was only exercised by tests using positive, in-range values, where truncation and floor happen to coincide.

Fix keeps the Arrow-native fast path but makes it direction-aware: downcasts floor toward -inf via int64 arithmetic, and same/finer-resolution casts use `safe=True` so overflow raises `OutOfBoundsDatetime`/`OutOfBoundsTimedelta`, matching the numpy-backed behavior. Adds regression tests covering negative durations, pre-epoch timestamps, and overflow.

title: BUG: HDFStore min_itemsize={'index': N} rejected with MultiIndex columns (GH#12154)
body:
The MultiIndex-columns `min_itemsize` guard added in GH-65602 (for GH-12154) rejected *every* non-`'values'` key, including the reserved row-index key `'index'`. But `'index'` is not a per-column data request — it sizes the row-index string column (via `IndexCol.maybe_set_size`). So `append(min_itemsize={'index': 50})` on a MultiIndex-columns frame raised `ValueError`, and the suggested `{'values': N}` workaround can't size the index, so the capability was lost and a later append with longer index labels would overflow.

Fix: thread the reserved index cname into `validate_data_columns` and exempt it alongside `'values'`. Genuine per-column keys (e.g. `{1: N}`, `{(1, 'a'): N}`) still raise the clear error.

Confirmed the index is always keyed by `'index'` in table format (never its actual name, before or after this change), so `new_index.cname` is the exact exemption. Regression only exists in the unreleased 3.1.0.dev, so no whatsnew entry.

title: BUG: read_hdf left store open on errors other than ValueError/TypeError/LookupError (GH#28430)
body:
closes #28430

`read_hdf` only closed a store it had opened when `store.select` raised `ValueError`, `TypeError`, or `LookupError`. Any other error — e.g. an `AssertionError` — left the file handle open, so a later attempt to reopen the file for writing raised `the file ... is already opened. Please close it before reopening in write mode`.

Close the store on any failed read via a `try/finally` gated on a success sentinel, while leaving it open on success so iterator/`chunksize` results (which need the store to stay open) still work.

title: DEPR: allowing non-(ndarray, ExtensionArray, Index, Series) in is_array_like usages (GH#52834)

labels.name: Indexing
labels.description: Related to indexing on series/frames, not to indexes themselves

body:
xref GH-52834

`is_array_like` is just `is_list_like(obj) and hasattr(obj, "dtype")`, so internal call sites that use it also accept any duck-typed array (a list-like with a `dtype` attribute) — e.g. arrays from other libraries. In most of these spots we really want `isinstance(obj, (np.ndarray, ExtensionArray, Index, Series))`.

This is the first step toward that. It adds a transitional helper `is_array_like_deprecate_non_pandas` and swaps it in at the internal `is_array_like` call sites (indexing/setitem, `MultiIndex.set_levels`, `ExtensionArray.fillna`, string/arrow array setitem and comparisons). Runtime behavior is unchanged; a `Pandas4Warning` is now emitted when the object is array-like only by duck-typing. Wrapping the input in `np.asarray`, `pd.array`, or `pd.Index` retains the current behavior.

This does **not** fully resolve GH-52834: the public `pd.api.types.is_array_like` is intentionally left unchanged here, and the call sites are not yet flipped to `isinstance`. Those are follow-ups once this deprecation has baked.

Note for the follow-up isinstance replacement: the check must use the concrete `ExtensionArray` class (equivalently, both `ABCExtensionArray` and `ABCNumpyExtensionArray`) — `ABCExtensionArray` alone excludes `NumpyExtensionArray` (`_typ="npy_extension"`), which is what `pd.array(x, dtype=<numpy dtype>)` produces.

title: CI: Cap hypothesis <6.156 on 32-bit build (missing i686 wheel needs Rust)
body:
The `Linux-32-bit` job started failing on `main` at dependency install (not in pandas code). hypothesis 6.156.1 (2026-07-03) began shipping a compiled extension with platform wheels but **no i686 wheel**. On 32-bit Linux pip falls back to building the sdist, which needs a Rust target that rustup doesn't support:

```
Target triple not supported by rustup: i386-unknown-linux-gnu
Rust not found, installing into a temporary directory
```

Cap hypothesis to `<6.156` for the 32-bit job only. The Musl (x86_64), Python-dev (x86_64), and Pyodide (wasm32) jobs all have prebuilt 6.156.x wheels and are unaffected, so they're left unpinned. The cap can be lifted once hypothesis publishes an i686 wheel or makes the compiled extension optional.

title: BUG: Fix resampling with CustomBusinessDay/BusinessDay and closed='right'
body:
Resampling with end-of-period offsets like `CustomBusinessDay` ("C") and `BusinessDay` ("B") was not correctly aligned when `closed="right"`.

In `pandas/core/resample.py` line 2701 (inside `_adjust_bin_edges`), the function only checked for specific end-of-period offsets like `"BME"`, `"ME"`, `"W"`, etc., but did not include `"B"` (BusinessDay) or `"C"` (CustomBusinessDay). When `closed="right"`, these offsets also need their bin edges rolled forward to the last moment of the day, otherwise data on the last day overflows into a new/extra bin containing `NaN` at the end and casts integer columns to `float64`.

This PR:
1. Updates `_adjust_bin_edges` to check for `"B"` and `"C"` as end-of-period offsets.
2. Adds a regression unit test `test_resample_custom_business_day` to verify correct binning and dtype preservation for `CustomBusinessDay` resampling.

title: PERF: Pure Python loops when calculating validity masks and offset arrays in Interchange Protocol
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the main branch of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

### Problem Description
Currently, when exporting string columns via the DataFrame Interchange Protocol (`pandas/core/interchange/column.py`), pandas processes the validity mask and offset buffers using slow element-wise Python loops:

```python
# Validity Mask loop
mask = np.zeros(shape=(len(buf),), dtype=np.bool_)
for i, obj in enumerate(buf):
    mask[i] = valid if isinstance(obj, str) else invalid

# Offsets loop
for i, v in enumerate(values):
    if isinstance(v, str):
        b = v.encode(encoding="utf-8")
        ptr += len(b)
    offsets[i + 1] = ptr
```

These manual loops incur significant overhead on larger string arrays.

#### Proposed Optimization
We can vectorize these buffer constructions using Python list comprehensions and NumPy functions:

1. Construct the boolean validity mask via `[isinstance(obj, str) for obj in buf] `and direct array casting.
2. Accumulate string byte-lengths into a list and execute a single vectorized cumulative sum call (`np.cumsum`) to generate the offsets array.

#### Performance Benchmarks
Benchmarked on a string column with 100k rows (with 5% missing values):
| Operation | Old (Master) | New (Optimized) | Speedup |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Validity Mask** | 0.188 seconds | 0.102 seconds | **1.84x** |
| **Offsets Buffer** | 0.421 seconds | 0.267 seconds | **1.57x** |

title: PERF: High overhead in stack frame warning inspections (find_stack_level)

labels.name: Needs Triage
labels.description: Issue that has not been reviewed by a pandas team member

body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the main branch of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

### Problem Description
Whenever pandas raises a warning, it invokes `find_stack_level()` to trace the call stack and identify the calling context outside of pandas. Currently, this function walks the stack frames and calls `inspect.getfile(frame)` inside a loop:

```python
while frame:
    filename = inspect.getfile(frame)
    if filename.startswith(pkg_dir) and not filename.startswith(test_dir):
        frame = frame.f_back
        n += 1
```

For workloads that emit multiple warnings (or libraries relying heavily on pandas warnings), this function is highly inefficient because:
1. `inspect.getfile(frame)` is slow as it does lookup caching, module parsing, and absolute path validation inside the interpreter loop.
2. It repeatedly imports `pandas` and resolves `pkg_dir` and `test_dir` paths on *every* warning invocation.

### Proposed Optimization
1. Cache the `pkg_dir` and `test_dir` paths globally at the module level.
2. Retrieve the filename directly via `frame.f_code.co_filename` instead of calling `inspect.getfile(frame)`.

### Performance Benchmarks
We benchmarked 500,000 runs of the original stack inspection vs. the optimized caching and `co_filename` check on a local environment:

| Implementation | 500,000 runs | Overhead per call |
|---|---|---|
| **Original (`master`)** | 3.67 seconds | ~7.33 microseconds |
| **Optimized** | 0.19 seconds | ~0.38 microseconds |

This yields a **~19x speedup** (95% reduction in call overhead).

- [x] Added an entry in the latest `doc/source/whatsnew/vX.Y.Z.rst` file if fixing a bug or adding a new feature.

## Summary

When `read_csv` is called with a `thousands` separator, float parsing falls back to `precise_xstrtod`. That path caps significant digits at 17, but previously counted **leading zeros** against that budget. For an 18-character zero-padded value like `"000000000010084566"`, the final significant digit was pushed into the exponent instead of the mantissa, so the value became `10084560.0` instead of `10084566.0`.

The standard (no-thousands) path uses `fast_float` and was already correct; only the fallback path was affected.

## Fix

Skip leading zeros when accumulating the integer mantissa so they do not consume the digit budget. A `seen_digit` flag keeps all-zero inputs like `"000"` valid.

```python
>>> from io import StringIO
>>> import pandas as pd
>>> data = "val\n000000000010084566.0\n"
>>> # before: 10084560.0
>>> pd.read_csv(StringIO(data), thousands=",")["val"][0]
10084566.0
```

title: fix: handle np.uint64 wrapping in Series.to_json()
body:
Closes #66142

When np.uint64 scalars are stored in an object-dtype Series, the ujson C encoder casts them to NPY_INT64, causing values >= 2^63 to wrap to negative numbers.

title: PERF: String column serialization in Interchange protocol is slow

labels.name: Needs Triage
labels.description: Issue that has not been reviewed by a pandas team member

body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the main branch of pandas.


### Reproducible Example


### Problem Description
Currently, when serializing string columns to a byte buffer in the DataFrame Interchange Protocol (`pandas/core/interchange/column.py`), pandas uses a slow element-wise Python loop:

```python
for obj in buf:
    if isinstance(obj, str):
        b.extend(obj.encode(encoding="utf-8"))
```

For large DataFrames ($100k+$ or $1M+$ rows), this loop is highly inefficient because:
1. It calls `.encode("utf-8")` once for every single string element inside the Python interpreter.
2. It uses `bytearray.extend()` iteratively, introducing overhead.
3. The check `isinstance(obj, str)` is run iteratively in Python.

### Proposed Optimization
We can leverage NumPy to filter nulls/invalid elements in C-space and then perform a single C-optimized join and a single vectorized `.encode()` call:

```python
# Drop null values to avoid joining None/NaN
b = "".join(buf[pd.notna(buf)]).encode(encoding="utf-8")
```

### Performance Benchmarks
We benchmarked the original loop logic vs. the optimized NumPy mask & join approach on array sizes with 5% missing values:

| Size (Strings) | Original Loop | Optimized Python | Speedup Factor |
|---|---|---|---|
| **10,000** | 0.00530s | 0.00227s | **2.34x** |
| **100,000** | 0.06940s | 0.02344s | **2.96x** |
| **1,000,000** | 0.22295s | 0.10143s | **2.20x** |

title: CI: Scope forkserver launch method to ASV CI task (GH#66193)
body:
closes #66193

asv 0.6.6 (pulled in by GH-66147) changed the default benchmark launch method from `forkserver` to `spawn` on all platforms. Under `spawn` every benchmark runs in a fresh interpreter that re-imports pandas, so the `asv run --quick --dry-run` smoke test in the ASV Benchmarks CI job ballooned from minutes to ~4 hours (pandas has ~940 benchmark functions, most parameterized).

This passes `--launch-method=forkserver` in the `ci-asv` Pixi task, restoring the pre-0.6.6 behavior for the CI job: pandas is imported once in a fork server and each benchmark is a cheap `fork()`.

Scoping the flag to the (Linux) CI task — rather than setting `launch_method` in `asv.conf.json` — leaves asv's default untouched for everyone else, so local `asv run` keeps working on Windows, where `forkserver` is unavailable. Also bumps the asv floor to `>=0.6.6`.

## Description
Fixes a regression where str.match with a compiled regex could raise a false conflicting flags ValueError when flags were not explicitly provided.

## Root cause
Conflict checking compared compiled-pattern flags against default flags, even when the caller did not pass flags.

## Fix
- Use no_default semantics for case and flags
- Preserve compiled pattern flags when flags is omitted
- Infer case from compiled pattern when case is omitted
- Keep explicit conflict checks for truly conflicting inputs

## Tests
- Updated compiled-regex match coverage
- Added regression test for default compiled-flag behavior

Closes #66138

title: BUG: cast_from_unit_vectorized near-bounds float overflow (GH#57366)
body:
Follow-up to GH-57366 / #64438, which fixed most of the near-bounds float overflow in `cast_from_unit_vectorized` but left an exact-boundary gap.

The overflow check compared the analytic `result_f = base*m + frac*m` against the exactly-representable ±2\*\*63 boundary. But `result_f` is itself a rounded float, so a value whose exact ns result is within half a ULP of the boundary lands on the wrong side of the comparison:

- **Silent data corruption:** a negative float whose exact ns value is just past `INT64_MIN` rounds *to* `-2**63`, escapes the check, and the integer `base*m + int64(frac*m)` then wraps modulo 2\*\*64 to a large **positive** timestamp; `errors="coerce"` returned garbage instead of `NaT`. Affects units us/s/m/h/W.
- **Spurious raise:** an in-bounds float just shy of `INT64_MAX` rounds *up* to `2**63` and raised `OutOfBoundsDatetime`, diverging from the scalar `cast_from_unit` path. Affects units D/W.

Now the int64 wrap is detected directly — a valid result agrees with its float64 estimate to within a few ULP, while a wrap shifts it by ~2\*\*64. The vectorized path again matches the exact scalar cast (verified against it over 85k boundary-adjacent values). No perf impact (net-neutral: the added int64→float64 cast offsets the removed float comparisons).

No whatsnew entry: both directions were introduced by #64438 within the same unreleased 3.1.0 cycle, and the existing GH-57366 entry already describes the intended behavior.

title: DOC: fix incorrect HDFStore.put/append parameter docs (GH#60920)
body:
Addresses part of GH-60920.

The `complib` and `axes` parameters of `HDFStore.append`, and `complib` of `HDFStore.put`, were documented as "This parameter is currently not accepted" — placeholder text added by earlier numpydoc-enforcement PRs (GH-58305, GH-58384) purely to satisfy validation. All three are in fact accepted and functional:

- `complib` compresses table-format writes (verified: 3.6 MB → 93 KB).
- `axes` selects which axis becomes the table's indexed/appendable axis (`[0]` vs `[1]` produce structurally different tables).

This also documents the real downstream defaults that were previously omitted: `nan_rep` (`'nan'`) and `chunksize` (`100000`).

Docstring-only; no behavior change. Numpydoc validation passes for both methods. The remaining API-design questions in GH-60920 (e.g. `min_itemsize` → `max_itemsize`, the dead `columns` parameter) are left for discussion, so the issue stays open.

title: BUG: groupby quantile with non-null NaN and all-NaT groups (GH#64330)

labels.name: Missing-data
labels.description: np.nan, pd.NaT, pd.NA, dropna, isnull, interpolate

body:
Follow-up fixing two defects in :meth:`GroupBy.quantile`, both surfaced by the quickselect rewrite in GH-64330.

- A float ``NaN`` that is *not* flagged by the null mask (a non-null ``NaN`` in a pyarrow or masked float array) was copied into the quickselect buffer, where it corrupts ``kth_smallest_c``'s ordering comparisons and produces non-monotonic garbage. It is now skipped like any other NA, matching the non-grouped ``Series.quantile`` result.
- An all-``NaT`` datetime-like group came back as ``NaN`` and was cast to ``i8``. That cast is platform dependent — ``INT64_MIN`` (== ``NaT``) on x86 but ``0`` (the Unix epoch) on arm64 — so all-``NaT`` groups silently became ``1970-01-01`` on Apple Silicon / Graviton. Those positions are now mapped to ``iNaT`` explicitly (also silencing an "invalid value encountered in cast" warning).

Verified no measurable perf impact (best-of-7): the added ``val != val`` check is compile-time removed for integer/datetime-like dtypes and is lost in the noise for float dtypes.

title: BUG: repr with 0-d ndarray in object column raises (GH#64638)
body:
`repr`/`to_string` of a Series/DataFrame/Index holding a 0-d ndarray in an object-dtype column raised `TypeError: iteration over a 0-d array`.

The `isinstance` allowlist added to `pprint_thing` in GH-64638 matches `np.ndarray` without an `ndim == 0` guard, so a 0-d array (which is not iterable) reached `_pprint_seq` and raised on `iter()`. The prior `is_sequence` check excluded 0-d arrays because `iter()` raises, letting them fall through to `str()`. This restores that behavior with an explicit guard.

The regression is unreleased (introduced in 3.1.0 dev by GH-64638), so no whatsnew entry.

title: BUG: Timedelta(np.str_) raising TypeError (GH#48974)
body:
GH-48974 was only partially fixed by GH-64754: the array path (`array_to_timedelta64`) cast `np.str_` to `str` before the Cython typed-str parse helpers, but the scalar `Timedelta.__new__` str branch did not. As a result:

```python
>>> pd.Timedelta(np.str_("1 day"))
TypeError: Expected str, got numpy.str_
>>> pd.to_timedelta(np.str_("1 day"))   # scalar path
TypeError: Expected str, got numpy.str_
```

`np.str_` arises naturally from e.g. `np.array(["1 day"])[0]`. This adds the same cast at the top of the scalar str branch, extends the regression test to cover scalars (regular + ISO), and updates the whatsnew entry (which already claimed `to_timedelta` was fixed) to also name the `Timedelta` constructor.

title: BUG: Series/DataFrame constructor to honor unit of timedelta64 dtype for all numeric input (GH#63499)
body:
Follow-up to GH-63499, which made the timedelta constructor honor the dtype's unit only for integer input. Float input — and mixed int/float input — was excluded, so it fell through to being treated as nanoseconds and then cast down to the coarser resolution, silently truncating to zero:

```python
pd.Series([1.5, 2.5, 90.0], dtype="timedelta64[s]")  # -> all 0 days (90s lost!)
pd.Series([1, 2.5, 90],     dtype="timedelta64[s]")  # -> all 0 days
pd.Series([1, 2, 3],        dtype="timedelta64[s]")  # -> 1s/2s/3s (correct)
```

Now all numeric input (including with missing values: None/NaN/NaT/`pd.NA`) is interpreted in the dtype's unit, matching `to_timedelta(..., unit=...)`. Applies to `Series`, `DataFrame`, and `pd.array`.

Implementation: rather than growing the `lib.infer_dtype` string check, `_from_sequence` materializes the input via `ensure_arraylike_for_datetimelike` and dispatches on the resulting dtype; object-dtype input is classified by `lib.is_integer_float_array` over its non-null values (promoted `cdef` → `cpdef` with a stub line).

Known corners (pre-existing, left for follow-ups):
- Large non-round floats raise `OutOfBoundsTimedelta` via the int64-ns intermediate even when the value fits the target unit (e.g. `pd.Series([1e10 + 0.5], dtype="timedelta64[s]")`); round floats take the integer path and work. Same limitation as `to_timedelta(..., unit="s")` — previously this returned a silently-wrong value (~10 seconds).
- Object input mixing Timedelta-likes with numerics keeps the `"ns"` default for the numeric values (`[Timedelta("1s"), 2.0]` -> `[1s, 0s]`), where `to_timedelta(..., unit=...)` applies the unit.

title: BUG: IntervalArray hashing nondeterministic across processes (GH#64605)
body:
Follow-up to GH-64605. `IntervalArray._hash_pandas_object` salted the hash with `np.uint64(hash(self.closed) % (2**63))`. The builtin `str` hash is randomized per process (`PYTHONHASHSEED`), so `hash_array` on interval data produced different values in different processes — breaking any cross-process consumer of the hash (e.g. dask shuffles on interval data).

Replace the salt with a fixed mapping over the four `VALID_CLOSED` values. The value is still siphashed through `hash_array`, so the four `closed` variants remain distinct and well-distributed.

Categorical-of-`Interval` hashing was unaffected: `Categorical._hash_pandas_object` goes through `np.asarray` → object array of `Interval` scalars, which stringifies deterministically and never reaches `IntervalArray._hash_pandas_object`.

No whatsnew entry: GH-64605 is unreleased (3.1.0.dev), so this bug never shipped.
