title: BUG: date_range with end + periods and off-offset end returns invalid result (GH#65011)
body:
Follow-up to GH-65011, which added a ``periods=1`` short-circuit to ``_generate_range`` but left the ``end``-anchored path unable to handle an off-offset ``end``.

When only ``end`` and ``periods`` are given, ``_generate_range`` never rolled an off-offset ``end`` onto the offset grid the way it rolls ``start``. So:

- ``date_range(end="2020-01-15", periods=1, freq="MS")`` returned ``DatetimeIndex(["2020-01-15"], freq="MS")`` — an off-grid value with ``freq`` still pinned, i.e. an internally-invalid index (constructing ``DatetimeIndex(["2020-01-15"], freq="MS")`` directly raises).
- ``date_range(end="2020-01-15", periods=3, freq="MS")`` returned only 2 elements.

The fix restores the end-anchor roll (mirror of the existing start-rolling) that shipped in v3.0.3/v3.0.4 via GH-64880 (for GH-64834) but was never forward-ported to ``main`` after a refactor dropped it. The latest release (v3.0.4) already behaves correctly, so this is an unreleased regression on ``main`` — no whatsnew entry.

Verified against v3.0.4 across ``MS``/``QS``/``ME``/``W``/``LastWeekOfMonth``/``FY5253`` and negative offsets; added a parametrized regression test.

title: BUG: SparseArray.astype to int silently dropped NaT fill via Series.astype (GH#49631)
body:
closes #49631

The GH-49631 fix in GH-64955 was gated on whether the `astype` argument was a string (e.g. `"Sparse[int64]"`) vs an explicit `SparseDtype` object. But `NDFrame.astype` resolves the string to a `SparseDtype` object *before* dispatching to `SparseArray.astype`, so the `NaT -> iNaT` fill-value conversion was skipped on the `Series`/`DataFrame` path — silently turning the `NaT` fill into `0` (real dense data corruption when the fill position isn't stored explicitly). It was also broken via an explicit `SparseDtype("int64")` object.

That same gating additionally raised `IntCastingNaNError` when casting a *fully dense* float `SparseArray` (whose `NaN` fill is never used) to an integer subtype — a regression introduced by GH-64955.

Fix: key the fill conversion on NA-fill semantics rather than the argument's syntactic form. Convert the fill only for a datetimelike source with an NA (`NaT`) fill going to a non-NA subtype (where the integer cast is a view, matching the dense `.astype`), and skip when the array is fully dense. A `float` `NaN` fill going to `int` still relabels to the target fill without raising, as before.

Regression tests cover the `Series.astype` path (string and object forms) and the fully-dense float→int case.

title: BUG: DatetimeIndex/TimedeltaIndex constructor pins a non-conforming freq (GH#65012)
body:
Follow-up to GH-65012, which fixed GH-61086 (accepting equivalent-but-not-equal freqs such as `QS-FEB` vs `QS-MAY`). That change validated a passed `freq` against only the first step (`self[0] + freq == self[1]`), fully validating only holiday/FY5253 offsets. But a fixed-step (`Tick`/`Day`) or business/custom offset can match the first gap by coincidence yet diverge on a later step, so a non-conforming `freq` was silently pinned:

- `DatetimeIndex(<MS data>, freq="31D")` pinned `<31 * Days>` (Jan 2000 happens to have 31 days). `shift(1)` then returned wrong values and dropped an element (len 3 -> 2).
- `DatetimeIndex(<ME data>, freq="BME")` pinned `<BusinessMonthEnd>` even when a later month-end (e.g. 2000-04-30, a Sunday) is not on the BME offset.

Now validate every step via `_validate_frequency` for `len >= 2`, keeping the `len == 0` and `len == 1` (`is_on_offset`) fast paths. Equivalent freqs (GH-61086) are still accepted.

No whatsnew: the offending shortcut was introduced during the 3.1.0 dev cycle (GH-65266) and never shipped in a release.

title: BUG: DataFrame.agg with list of funcs mishandles non-reduction methods (GH#65031)
body:
Follow-up to GH-65031, which added a DataFrame-level reductions fast path for `DataFrame.agg` with a list of string functions. That path treated **any** Series-returning DataFrame method as a column-wise reduction, so methods whose result isn't indexed by the columns silently misbehaved:

- `df.agg(["value_counts"])` and `df.agg(["duplicated"])` returned an all-NaN 1-row frame
- `df.agg(["memory_usage"])` returned wrong values (24 vs 156), or raised `ValueError: cannot reindex on an axis with duplicate labels` on mixed dtypes

Gate the fast path on `row.index.equals(sub.columns)` so only genuine column-wise reductions (`sum`, `mean`, `count`, `nunique`, …) use it; anything else falls back to the existing per-column path, restoring the pre-GH-65031 result.

title: BUG: unstack placed values under wrong labels for unsorted-codes MultiIndex (GH#65107)
body:
Follow-up to GH-65107, which introduced an identity-indexer fast path in `_Unstacker`.

`_indexer_is_identity` short-circuited on `index.is_monotonic_increasing`, which reflects the tuple *values*, but the reordering it skips (`take_nd`) is driven by the *codes*. A `MultiIndex` whose values are monotonic while its codes are unsorted (e.g. non-lexsorted levels like `levels=[["b","a"], [1, 2]]`) then skipped the take and placed values under the wrong row labels:

```python
mi = pd.MultiIndex(levels=[["b", "a"], [1, 2]], codes=[[1, 1, 0, 0], [0, 1, 0, 1]])
pd.Series([10, 20, 30, 40], index=mi).unstack()
# ("a", 1) -> 10 ended up under row "b"
```

Fix: test the codes-based sort indexer via `lib.is_range_indexer` instead of the value-based monotonicity check. `_indexer_and_to_sort` is already computed during `__init__` (via `_make_selectors`), so the check stays free and the `take_nd`-skipping perf win of GH-65107 is preserved.

The regression only ever existed on the unreleased 3.1.0 dev branch, so no whatsnew entry is added.

title: BUG: union(sort=False) retained freq on non-monotonic datetimelike result (GH#65191)

labels.name: Index
labels.description: Related to the Index class or subclasses

body:
The `sort=False` branch of `DatetimeTimedeltaMixin._fast_union` unconditionally pinned `result._freq = self.freq`. That branch is only reached when `self[0] > other[0]`, so it prepends `other`'s earlier values *after* `self`'s values — the result is **always non-monotonic**. A non-monotonic index carrying a freq is invalid: `.shift(1)` then feeds `start > end` into `_generate_range` and **silently returns an empty index**.

This regressed in GH-65191, which moved freq handling from the array to the index level and dropped the array-level `_concat_same_type` conformance check that previously withheld freq on non-conforming concatenations. This restores that behavior for the `sort=False` path by not pinning a freq — `_simple_new` yields `freq=None`, and `shift` now raises a clear `NullFrequencyError` instead of silently emptying.

Affects all 7 freqs tested for `DatetimeIndex` and `TimedeltaIndex`. The existing `test_union_sort_false` used a bare `assert_index_equal` (which does not check `freq`), so the regression went uncaught; that test is strengthened and a focused `DatetimeIndex` regression test is added.

title: CI: Fix pyarrow-nightly job (stale nightly wheel + feather deprecations)
body:
Fixes the failing `Pyarrow Nightly` job on `main`. Two parts:

**1. Stale nightly wheel (the actual break).**
`pixi.lock` pinned `pyarrow==25.0.0.dev186`, which has been garbage-collected from the [scientific-python-nightly-wheels](https://pypi.anaconda.org/scientific-python-nightly-wheels/simple/pyarrow/) index (it retains only ~6 recent dev builds), so the environment 404'd on install before any test ran. This bumps **only** the `pyarrow-nightly` environment to `dev235` (currently the freshest build), via:

```
pixi update --environment pyarrow-nightly pyarrow
```

No other environment is relocked, so this deliberately avoids the unrelated dependency churn a full `pixi update` pulls in — the auto-generated refresh in GH-66147 additionally reds Type Checking (an `optype` bump using PEP 695 syntax vs the 3.11 mypy target) and Downstream Compat (numpy 2.5 `.shape` deprecation via scikit-learn). Those are separate issues; this PR keeps them out of the critical path.

**2. Feather deprecations.**
pyarrow ≥24 deprecates `pyarrow.feather.read_table` / `write_feather` (still used by `pandas/io/feather_format.py`) in favor of `pyarrow.ipc`. Under the suite's `-W error` those `FutureWarning`s fail `test_read_fspath_all[read_feather-pyarrow-path4]` and `test_write_fspath_all[to_feather-writer_kwargs2-pyarrow]`. Ignore them alongside the existing pyarrow deprecation filters.

**Not a permanent fix.** The `dev235` pin will itself age out of the nightly index — this is a bridge to get CI green now. Migrating feather I/O off the deprecated API (`pyarrow.ipc`, with a Feather V1 story) and rethinking the nightly-lock/canary CI setup are separate follow-ups.

title: TST: pivot_table margins with distinct parameterized EA dtypes (GH#55484)
body:
Adds a regression guard for the `pivot_table` margins path when two `values` columns share an :class:`ExtensionDtype` kind but differ in parameters (interval subtypes, disjoint :class:`CategoricalDtype`s).

This was originally opened as a fix for a margin-cast bug in `_add_margins` (follow-up to GH-65301 / GH-55484): `result.select_dtypes([dtype])` over-matched parameterized EA dtypes and could `astype` a margin cell to a *different* column's dtype, silently corrupting the value. That over-match has since been fixed upstream by the `select_dtypes` exact-instance matching work (GH-40234, GH-66119), so the code change is no longer necessary.

Reduced to the regression test, which guards the `pivot_table` margins path specifically — a path the `select_dtypes` PRs don't exercise directly.

No whatsnew: test-only.

title: BUG: DataFrame.loc setitem-with-expansion writes dict keys instead of aligned values (GH#42099)

labels.name: Indexing
labels.description: Related to indexing on series/frames, not to indexes themselves

body:
When adding a new column via label-list `.loc` expansion, a dict value was sanitized positionally into its *keys* instead of being aligned by key:

```python
df = DataFrame({"a": [10, 20, 30, 40]})
df.loc[[0, 1, 2], "data"] = {0: "x", 1: "y", 2: "z"}
# before: column [0.0, 1.0, 2.0, NaN]  (float64 — the keys!)
# after:  column ['x', 'y', 'z', NaN]  (values aligned by key)
```

This regressed in GH-65418: its new list-like branch added a `return` that skipped the `_setitem_with_indexer` alignment a dict used to fall through to. The existing-column and `df.loc[:, "new"]` null-slice paths were unaffected, leaving the behavior inconsistent. Normalizing a dict to a Series routes it back through the dtype-preserving, key-aligning path, matching those paths and the sibling handling in `_setitem_with_indexer_split_path` / `_setitem_single_block`.

The regression was contained entirely in unreleased 3.1.0 (released 3.0.x aligns dicts correctly), so no whatsnew entry.

title: BUG: read_hdf fails to round-trip CategoricalIndex edge cases (GH#65576)
body:
closes #65576

For `format="table"`, `IndexCol.convert` did not mirror `DataCol.convert`'s NaN-category handling, leaving two live bugs in the recently-added `CategoricalIndex` round-trip (GH-33909, GH-16118):

- A `CategoricalIndex` with a category equal to the `nan_rep` string (e.g. the default `"nan"`) wrote fine but **every** subsequent `read_hdf` raised `ValueError: Categorical categories cannot be null`, permanently bricking the key. The categories metadata `Series` decodes the `"nan"` category back to `NaN` on read; `convert` now drops NaN categories and remaps the codes, matching how a categorical *column* already behaves (GH-21741).
- An all-`NaN` `CategoricalIndex` (zero categories) read back as a plain integer `Index` of raw codes, because empty categories cannot be stored as metadata and `IndexCol` only inferred `meta="category"` from a present metadata node. `meta` is now persisted as an explicit attribute so the index round-trips as categorical.

Both behaviors now match a categorical data column across read, all-NaN round-trip, and append. No whatsnew entry — GH-65576 is unreleased (`3.1.0.dev0`), so this is a regression against unreleased work; the existing feature entry already documents the round-trip.

title: BUG: date_range/bdate_range with periods drops entries for sparse CustomBusinessDay (GH#65604)
body:
Follow-up to GH-64648 / GH-65604, addressing a further regression in the same fast path.

`generate_daily_offset_range` (the fast "daily range + filter" path for `freq="B"`/`"C"`) sized its internal calendar-day buffer as `needed_on_offset * 7 + 6`, assuming on-offset dates are at most 7 calendar days apart. A sparse weekmask combined with holidays landing on on-offset days pushes consecutive on-offset dates arbitrarily far apart, so the buffer under-filled and `date_range`/`bdate_range` **silently** returned fewer than `periods` entries — no exception, so the iterative fallback never triggered:

```python
>>> pd.bdate_range(start="2026-03-02", periods=4, freq="C",
...                weekmask="Mon", holidays=["2026-03-09", "2026-03-16"])
# before: 3 dates  ['2026-03-02', '2026-03-23', '2026-03-30']
# after:  4 dates  ['2026-03-02', '2026-03-23', '2026-03-30', '2026-04-06']
```

The fix grows the buffer until enough on-offset dates are produced. It terminates because the buffer eventually overflows the datetime bounds, raising into the caller's existing iterative fallback (which already handles near-bounds cases). The common holiday-free path succeeds on the first iteration, so there's no perf cost there.

This regression only exists on `main` — 3.0.x predates GH-64648 and uses the old `_generate_range` path. No 3.1.0 has been released, so no whatsnew entry.

## Test plan

- [x] New regression test covering `start`- and `end`-anchored cases across all resolution units (fails on pre-fix source, passes on the fix)
- [x] Cross-checked the fast path against a brute-force iterative reference over many weekmask/holiday configs, `n=1,2,3`, various `periods`, both anchors — 0 mismatches
- [x] Full `pandas/tests/indexes/datetimes/` + business-day offset tests pass
- [x] mypy, pyright, and pre-commit clean

title: BUG: unstack CoW-aliasing untracked for tz-aware/period columns (GH#65748)
body:
Follow-up to GH-65748, which fixed `unstack` silently corrupting the source `DataFrame` via an untracked zero-copy view — but only for numpy blocks.

`Block._unstack` gates reference-tracking on `np.may_share_memory(new_values, self.values)`. When `self.values` is an NDArrayBacked EA (tz-aware `DatetimeArray`, `PeriodArray`), `np.asarray` boxes it into a fresh object array of scalars, so the check is **always** `False`. The zero-copy view from GH-65107 stays untracked, `refs=None`, and mutating the unstacked result writes through to the source:

```python
idx = pd.MultiIndex.from_product([["a", "b"], [1, 2]])
col = pd.to_datetime(["2000", "2001", "2002", "2003"]).tz_localize("UTC")
df = pd.DataFrame({"f": [1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0], "t": col}, index=idx)
res = df.unstack()
res.iloc[0, 2] = pd.Timestamp("2099", tz="UTC")
df["t"][0]  # 2099 -- source corrupted (also period[D])
```

This only surfaces for multi-block frames (a single datetimelike column has `_can_fast_transpose=True` and routes to `_Unstacker.get_result`, which tracks refs correctly). tz-naive datetime/timedelta escaped it because `np.asarray` returns their underlying view.

Fix: compare the backing `._ndarray` for EA values, mirroring the `add_references` logic in `get_result`. The zero-copy view is preserved; CoW now triggers a copy before either object is mutated.

No whatsnew entry: GH-65107 and GH-65748 both landed in the unreleased 3.1.0 dev cycle, so this regression was never in a released pandas.

title: BUG: HDFStore.remove with combined large "in" filter and condition deleted wrong rows (GH#17567)
body:
closes #17567

A `where` clause that combines a large "in" selector (more than 31 values, e.g. `"index in [...]"`, too many for numexpr so it is realized as a post-read **filter**) with a numexpr **condition** (e.g. `"index in [...] and A >= 1"`) deleted the wrong rows.

`Selection.select_coords` returned early in the `condition is not None` branch, applying only the numexpr condition and dropping the filter. `HDFStore.remove` (via `AppendableTable.delete`) then deleted the rows matching *only* the condition, and `select_as_coordinates` returned those wrong coordinates. The `remove` data loss has shipped since v3.0.x; the `select_as_coordinates` half was a regression from GH-65782, which moved filter application into `select_coords` only for the condition-less path and removed the compensating post-filter loop in `read_coordinates`.

This applies the filter on top of `get_where_list`'s result, so the condition path and the full-range path share one filter loop and both return the correct intersection.

Extends the GH-65782 regression test with a combined filter+condition case, parametrized over a small (≤ 31, numexpr-condition) and large (> 31, filter) selector; it fails on the large case without the fix.

title: BUG: HDFStore.select drops data-column filter with iterator/chunksize (GH#12953)
body:
Follow-up to GH-65785, which added the iterator/chunksize gate but not the underlying coordinate fix.

When a ``where`` combines a numexpr row condition with an ``==``/``!=`` filter on a data column of more than 31 values (the numexpr ``_max_selectors`` cutoff), the term splits into a numexpr condition plus a post-read filter. The chunked/iterator path reads by row coordinates, and ``Selection.select_coords`` returned ``get_where_list(condition)`` while silently dropping ``self.filter`` — so extra rows that fail the filter leaked through (a plain non-iterator read applies the filter and returns fewer rows).

The ``_where_selects_columns`` gate added in GH-65785 deliberately waves data-column filters through to this coordinate path, so the drop was reachable via ``iterator=True``/``chunksize`` (and directly via ``select_as_coordinates``). This applies the post-read filter to the coordinates in the condition branch too, matching a plain read. Long-standing (predates GH-65785), so a whatsnew entry is included.

title: BUG: array_equivalent raising/wrong on float16 and byte-swapped dtypes

labels.name: Missing-data
labels.description: np.nan, pd.NaT, pd.NA, dropna, isnull, interpolate

body:
Fixes a regression introduced by GH-65192, whose short-circuit fastpath
routed all float/complex dtypes through `lib.array_equivalent_float` (a
Cython helper whose `floating` fused type only accepts native
float32/float64). This broke `Series.equals`/`DataFrame.equals` and
`array_equivalent` on supported dtypes:

- `float16` -> `TypeError: No matching signature found`
- byte-swapped `>f8`/`>f4` -> `ValueError: Big-endian buffer not supported`
- non-native complex `>c16`/`>c8` -> **silently wrong**: `np.finfo(dtype).dtype`
  returns a native float, so the `.view()` reinterpreted the byte-swapped
  bytes and distinct values could compare equal.

The fastpath is now gated on native byte order and a supported itemsize
(keeping native float32/64 and complex64/128), falling back to the numpy
expression otherwise.

title: DOC: note HDF5 pandas_version removal breaks reads by older pandas (GH#62792)
body:
Follow-up to GH-65606, which stopped writing the ``pandas_version`` attribute in ``to_hdf`` (GH-62792).

The v3.1.0 whatsnew entry described only the internal detail that was dropped ("used internally to detect files written by pandas versions older than 0.10.1"), which doesn't tell users anything actionable. Docs-only; no behavior change.

title: PERF: default read_csv parallel workers to available physical cores
body:
**Draft, sequenced after GH-66275** (that PR's commits are merged into this branch, so the diff includes them until it lands; only the `_cpu.py` detection module, the `_default_n_workers` policy and their docs/tests are new here).

Replaces the fixed default worker count for parallel `read_csv` with detection: the machine's **physical core count** (SMT siblings excluded), clamped to the CPUs actually available to the process — CPU affinity (`taskset`, SLURM cpusets) and cgroup CFS quotas (Docker `--cpus`, Kubernetes limits) — and to an absolute cap of 16. This keeps a default read from oversubscribing a shared many-core server or a CPU-limited container, which plain `os.cpu_count()` (the GH-66275 default) would. `mode.max_threads` still overrides everything.

An earlier revision of this PR counted only *performance* cores, based on measurements of the pre-rework parallel path where efficiency cores regressed throughput. On the GH-66275 worker-queue structure that inverted — a slow core now just pulls fewer chunks from the queue instead of straggling the gather — so efficiency cores are included. Measured on a 6P+6E M3 Pro (1M-row × 10-col fixtures, best-of-5 medians, this branch):

| fixture | 6 workers (P-cores only) | 12 workers (all physical) |
|---|---|---|
| float | 129.6 ms | 116.0 ms (−10%) |
| int | 96.3 ms | 89.3 ms (−7%) |
| mixed | 106.8 ms | 95.5 ms (−11%) |
| str | 74.9 ms | 76.6 ms (0%) |

SMT siblings stay excluded (a hyperthread adds no memory bandwidth to the bandwidth-bound parse its sibling is running); Windows stays serial by default per the GH-64347 findings.

title: BUG: `pivot_table` with `margins=True` raises KeyError when dict aggfunc doesn't cover every aggregated column
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/development/contributing_environment.html) of pandas.

### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "random1": [1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0],
        "random2": [10, 20, 30, 40],
        "type": ["a", "a", "b", "b"],
    }
)

# aggfunc only covers "random1"; "random2" is picked up implicitly via `values`
df.pivot_table(index="type", aggfunc={"random1": "mean"}, margins=True)
```

### Issue Description

Raises:

```
KeyError: 'random2'
```

Without `margins=True`, the exact same call works fine and silently excludes `random2` from the result (since it isn't a key in the `aggfunc` dict):

```python
>>> df.pivot_table(index="type", aggfunc={"random1": "mean"})
      random1
type
a         1.5
b         3.5
```

This also reproduces when `values` is passed explicitly and includes a column not covered by the dict:

```python
df.pivot_table(index="type", values=["random1", "random2"], aggfunc={"random1": "mean"}, margins=True)
```

The root cause seems to be in `_compute_grand_margin` in `pandas/core/reshape/pivot.py`: it iterates over every column in `data[values]` and looks up `aggfunc[k]` for each one. When `aggfunc` is a dict that doesn't have a key for `k`, this will raise a `KeyError`, which propagates uncaught (only `TypeError` is currently swallowed there). I guess the fix is to skip columns not present in the dict, consistent with the non-margins aggregation path's existing (if implicit) behavior of silently dropping such columns.

I found as an incidental, separate issue while investigating and trying to fix #12210 on my own (dict `aggfunc` containing a list of functions per column + `margins=True`). However, this is a distinct root cause/code path and reproduces independently of list-vs-scalar functions.

### Expected Behavior

`margins=True` should produce the same set of columns as `margins=False` (i.e. silently drop columns the `aggfunc` dict doesn't cover), rather than raising `KeyError`.

### Installed Versions

main branch (post `84d7518bdc`)

title: BUG: `to_json` wraps large `np.uint64` object-dtype scalars as negative ints (#66142)
body:
**Summary**
`Series.to_json()` / `DataFrame.to_json()` could silently corrupt large unsigned 64-bit integers when they were stored as **numpy scalars in an object-dtype column**.

For example:
```python
>>> pd.Series([np.uint64(2**63)], dtype=object).to_json()
# before: '{"0":-9223372036854775808}'   # wrong (signed wrap)
# after:  '{"0":9223372036854775808}'    # correct
```
This only affected the **object-dtype + `np.uint64` scalar** path. These cases already worked:
- plain Python `int` values (e.g. `2**63`) in object dtype
- a real `uint64` Series/array (not object dtype)

**Why it happened:** the ujson encoder treated every numpy integer scalar as a signed 64-bit value (`int64`). Values from `2**63` through `2**64 - 1` do not fit in signed `int64`, so they wrapped to negative numbers.
**Fix:** detect `np.uint64` scalars explicitly. If the value still fits in signed `int64`, keep the fast integer path; if it is larger, encode it via the existing big-integer (`JT_BIGNUM`) path, same as oversized Python ints. That preserves the exact decimal digits in JSON.

**Files changed**
- `pandas/_libs/src/vendored/ujson/python/objToJSON.c`: special-case `NPY_UINT64` in the numpy integer-scalar branch; route values `> INT64_MAX` through `JT_BIGNUM`
- `pandas/tests/io/json/test_pandas.py`: regression tests for object-dtype Series/DataFrame with large `np.uint64` scalars
- `pandas/tests/io/json/test_ujson.py`: stop capping `uint64` at `int64` max in the scalar max round-trip test
- `doc/source/whatsnew/v3.1.0.rst`: release note under Bug fixes / I/O

**Fixes**
- [x] closes #66142

title: BUG: Series.to_json() wraps np.uint64 values ≥ 2**63 in object dtype (GH#66142)
body:
Fixes #66142

`np.uint64` scalars ≥ `2**63` stored in `object` dtype Series were
serialized through the signed `int64` path in `objToJSON.c`, causing
values to wrap to negative numbers.

The fix checks specifically for `UInt64` scalars before the generic
integer cast, converts to a Python `int` via
`PyLong_FromUnsignedLongLong`, then reuses the existing `PyLong`
overflow path (`JT_BIGNUM`) for values that don't fit in signed int64.

Also updated `test_int_max` to remove the workaround that avoided
testing `uint64` max, since the unsigned path now handles it correctly.

title: DEPR: deprecate convert_dates and keep_default_dates in read_json (GH#59161)
body:
closes #59161

Deprecate the `convert_dates` and `keep_default_dates` keywords in `read_json`. A `Pandas4Warning` is raised only when either keyword is explicitly passed; behavior is otherwise unchanged.

The name-based date-conversion heuristic these keywords drive can silently override an explicit `dtype`, and is the main behavioral divergence between the `ujson` and `pyarrow` engines. Removing it in a future major version narrows that gap.

Because a dict `dtype` currently *loses* to that heuristic, the warning recommends migrations that work today: `dtype=False` to disable type conversion, or `to_datetime` after reading. Whether a per-column `dtype` entry should override date inference (so `dtype` alone can express per-column opt-out) is left as a design question for the enforcement stage.

Interop with GH-66144: the pyarrow-engine option validator accepts the new not-passed sentinel, so a plain `read_json(..., engine="pyarrow")` keeps working; explicitly-passed unsupported values still raise before the deprecation warning fires.

title: BUG: read_json(engine="pyarrow") now raises for silently-ignored options
body:
The ``"pyarrow"`` engine for :func:`read_json` (added in GH-48893) passes its input straight to ``pyarrow.json.read_json``, so any argument pandas would otherwise apply itself was silently ignored -- producing a wrong result rather than an error. For example ``typ="series"`` returned a DataFrame, ``convert_dates=False`` had no effect, and a non-UTF-8 ``encoding`` crashed with a raw ``UnicodeDecodeError``.

These now raise ``ValueError`` for ``engine="pyarrow"`` (matching the ``read_csv`` pyarrow-engine precedent): ``typ="series"``, an explicit ``convert_axes``, ``convert_dates`` other than ``True``, ``keep_default_dates=False``, ``date_unit``, ``precise_float=True``, a non-UTF-8 ``encoding``, ``encoding_errors`` other than ``"strict"``, ``storage_options``, an explicit ``compression``, and a scalar or non-``ArrowDtype`` ``dtype``. Building on GH-59516, a ``dtype`` mapping is still supported, but every value must resolve to an ``ArrowDtype`` (previously non-Arrow entries were silently dropped). The default ``ujson`` engine is unaffected, and passing the supported defaults explicitly still works.

Notes:

- **compression**: pyarrow infers compression from the file extension itself and ignores pandas' ``compression`` argument, so the default ``"infer"`` still reads ``.gz``/``.zst`` files, but any explicit value (method string or dict) now raises since pandas cannot guarantee it is honored.
- **Out of scope** (pre-existing, noted only): a ``dtype`` mapping with an ``ArrowDtype`` for a column absent from the data still adds a phantom null column and reorders columns (pyarrow ``explicit_schema`` semantics); text-mode file objects such as ``StringIO`` still fail with pyarrow's raw ``TypeError``.

title: feat(NaN): add limit_behavior option to interpolate to skip large gaps
body:
Closes #64588.

## Summary

This PR introduces a new `limit_behavior` keyword for `Series.interpolate` and `DataFrame.interpolate` to control how interpolation behaves when a missing-value gap exceeds the specified `limit`.

Currently, `limit` restricts only the number of consecutive values that are filled. If a gap is larger than the limit, pandas partially fills the gap and leaves the remaining values as missing.

This PR adds an alternative behavior:

* `limit_behavior="fill"` (default): preserves the existing behavior by filling up to `limit` consecutive missing values.
* `limit_behavior="skip"`: if a contiguous missing-value gap is larger than `limit`, the entire gap is left unchanged and no interpolation is performed for that gap.

This provides a convenient way to avoid interpolating across large missing regions without requiring users to manually detect and mask oversized gaps after interpolation.

### Example

```python
ser = pd.Series([1.0, np.nan, np.nan, np.nan, 5.0])

ser.interpolate(limit=1)
# 0    1.0
# 1    2.0
# 2    NaN
# 3    NaN
# 4    5.0

ser.interpolate(limit=1, limit_behavior="skip")
# 0    1.0
# 1    NaN
# 2    NaN
# 3    NaN
# 4    5.0
```

## Changes

* Added a new `limit_behavior` keyword (`"fill"` | `"skip"`) to:

  * `Series.interpolate`
  * `DataFrame.interpolate`
* Added validation for the new argument.
* Propagated the argument through the interpolation implementation, including the relevant ExtensionArray backends.
* Implemented `"skip"` behavior by preserving contiguous NaN runs whose length exceeds the specified `limit`.
* Updated the API documentation and docstring examples to describe the new parameter.
* Added comprehensive tests covering:

  * Series interpolation
  * DataFrame interpolation (both `axis=0` and `axis=1`)
  * ExtensionArray-backed dtypes
  * Datetime and timedelta data
  * Different `limit_direction` values
  * `limit_area`
  * Different interpolation methods (`linear`, `index`, and `time`)
  * Multiple gap configurations
  * Invalid `limit_behavior` values
  * Default behavior remaining unchanged

## Additional changes

* Suppressed `FutureWarning`s from newer versions of PyArrow in the Feather I/O tests to avoid unrelated test failures while preserving existing behavior.


---

title: BUG: `Series.to_json()` wraps `np.uint64` values ≥ `2**63` when stored in `object` dtype

labels.name: Needs Triage
labels.description: Issue that has not been reviewed by a pandas team member

body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

pd.Series([np.uint64(2**63)], dtype=object).to_json()
# '{"0":-9223372036854775808}'
```

### Issue Description

**Expected Output for Reproducible Example**

```python
'{"0":9223372036854775808}'
```

**Observed Behavior**

It appears that `np.uint64` scalars stored in `object`-dtype Series are being serialized through a signed `int64` path, causing values ≥ `2**63` to wrap to negative numbers.

```python
>>> pd.Series([np.uint64(2**63)], dtype="uint64").to_json()
'{"0":9223372036854775808}'

>>> pd.Series([np.uint64(2**63)], dtype=object).to_json()
'{"0":-9223372036854775808}'
```

**Existing tests and documentation**

- `ujson.ujson_dumps` explicitly tests Python integers up to `18446744073709551615` (`2**64 - 1`) and expects exact JSON output. [[ref]](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/f7246dccfaca04609d03820636b0caedf30672fb/pandas/tests/io/json/test_ujson.py#L540)
- `DataFrame.to_json` has a test for large uint64-looking values like `13342205958987758245`, and expects them to serialize correctly. [[ref]](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/f7246dccfaca04609d03820636b0caedf30672fb/pandas/tests/io/json/test_pandas.py#L2326)
- The docs for `to_json`/`read_json` do not appear to say "ujson only encodes up to signed int64." [[read_json ref]](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/f7246dccfaca04609d03820636b0caedf30672fb/pandas/io/json/_json.py#L535) [[to_json ref]](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/f7246dccfaca04609d03820636b0caedf30672fb/pandas/io/json/_json.py#L139)

There is one internal test comment in `pandas/tests/io/json/test_ujson.py:718`:

https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/f7246dccfaca04609d03820636b0caedf30672fb/pandas/tests/io/json/test_ujson.py#L712-L726

But that test is only avoiding `np.uint64.max` in a numpy-scalar roundtrip test. This suggests the object-scalar path may already have a known limitation around `np.uint64` values.

**Debugging Hints**

From debugging, it appears the object-scalar serialization path may be converting `np.uint64` values using the signed integer conversion (`NPY_INT64`) rather than the unsigned path (`NPY_UINT64`).

https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/f7246dccfaca04609d03820636b0caedf30672fb/pandas/_libs/src/vendored/ujson/python/objToJSON.c#L1627-L1631


If this is confirmed as a bug, I’d be happy to help work on a fix and open a pull request.

### Expected Behavior

`Series.to_json()` should preserve the value of `np.uint64` scalars regardless of whether they are stored in a `uint64` Series or an `object` Series.

### Installed Versions

<details>

pandas==3.1.0.dev0+1194.gf7246dccfa

</details>

### Feature Description

The ASan/UBsan job needs to be updated to detect memory leaks. Unfortunately, it's not as simple as setting `detect_leaks=1` because it will contain several false positives and suppressing `libpython` will ignore real memory leaks.

From my experience, it's best to build CPython from source with `--with-address-sanitizer --without-pymalloc` and the LSan becomes a lot better: fewer false positives and simpler suppression files.

AFAIK, it's not possible to use Pixi to manage Python dependencies from a custom interpreter, so probably will have to install python dependencies via `pip` or something similar.

title: BLD: honor numpy-include-dir Meson property for cross-compilation (GH#62883)
body:
closes #62883

``pandas/meson.build`` resolved the NumPy include directory by running ``numpy.get_include()`` through the build (native) Python. When cross-compiling that returns the *host* NumPy headers, where ``int64_t`` is a 64-bit ``long``; on a 32-bit target ``long`` is only 4 bytes, so pandas' compiled ``int64_t`` memoryviews disagree with the runtime NumPy's genuine 8-byte int64 arrays and import fails at the first ``int64_t[::1]`` view (``tzconversion.pyx``) with ``ValueError: Buffer dtype mismatch, expected 'const int64_t' but got 'long long'``.

Read the ``numpy-include-dir`` Meson external property first — matching what NumPy and SciPy do — and fall back to ``numpy.get_include()`` when it is unset, so cross-compilers can point pandas at the *target* NumPy headers. The reporter (Buildroot, armv7l) was already passing this property; pandas just wasn't reading it.

Also adds a configure-only CI job (``Linux-numpy-include-dir``) that sets the property to a distinct copy of the NumPy headers and asserts that path reaches the compile include flags, guarding against the property support regressing. Full cross-compilation (crossenv/qemu) is intentionally not exercised.

### Problem Description

import pandas as pd
s1=pd.Series([2,9], index=['a','b'])
s2=pd.Series([11,7], index=['b','a'])
s3=s1+s2
print(s3)

s4=s1>s2
print(s4)

When performing addition between two series object pandas searches for matching index in both and does the evaluation. If any one value is missing then it it gives nan.

But compared to arithmetic , the relational operators(>,<, <=,>=, etc) are having strict requirement that the order of the index must match. In the code above indexes a and b are both present in s1 and s2 and s1>s2 can be done as both indexes are present in both s1 and s2 but currently it is not allowed as there is a strict requirement that for relational operators the order of the indexes must also match.

It would be intutive if the requirement of index order is relaxed for relational operators and only matching index is checked.

title: PERF: prefix bloom filters for read_csv NA-value lookups
body:
With `na_filter` on (the default), every token in `read_csv`'s numeric/string converters calls `kh_get_str_starts_item` on the NA hash set. The existing filter is only a first-byte table, so default NA spellings like `"-NaN"`, `"-1.#IND"`, `"1.#QNAN"` force every `-`- or `1`-leading numeric token through a full strlen+hash lookup.

This adds two bloom layers so those tokens reject after reading 2-4 bytes:

- **starts2**: a (first byte, second byte) bitmap that rejects most tokens cheaply (`"-42"` vs `"-NaN"` differ at byte 2).
- **prefix4**: an 8192-bit bloom over the first <=4 bytes, for tokens sharing 2 bytes with an NA spelling (`"1.23"` vs `"1.#IND"` share `"1."` but differ within 4 bytes; 3 bytes is not enough: `"-1.234"` vs `"-1.#IND"` share 3).

Two refinements keep this from taxing lookups the blooms can't help:

- The bloom layers + hash lookup live in an out-of-line slow path (`kh_get_str_starts_item_slow`), so the common first-byte reject stays a tiny inline check in the per-token converter loops.
- The bool converter uses a first-byte-only variant (`kh_get_str_starts_item_expect_hit`) for its NA/true/false sets: bool tokens either reject on the first byte or are genuine hits in the true/false sets, so the deeper filters would be pure overhead there (they benchmarked as a consistent ~4-5% regression on bool columns before this split).

**Correctness**: no false negatives by construction — put and get compute identical bits for equal strings, and `kh_init_str_starts` already uses calloc so the new arrays start zeroed. `kh_str_starts` is only consumed by `pandas/_libs/parsers.pyx`; the only call-site change is the bool converter switching to the `expect_hit` variant.

## Benchmarks

2M-row single-column CSVs unless noted, default `read_csv(engine="c")`, both builds interleaved in the same run on an identical base commit, 15 paired reps x 3 reads, medians. "wins" = reps where this PR beat main.

| case | main (ms) | this PR (ms) | speedup | wins |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| floats, 90% negative | 90.9 | 82.4 | **1.103x** | 15/15 |
| wide (20 cols, int+float) | 189.4 | 175.4 | **1.080x** | 13/15 |
| ints, 50% negative | 85.7 | 81.5 | **1.052x** | 14/15 |
| floats, 50% negative | 100.6 | 95.8 | **1.051x** | 15/15 |
| ints, positive | 69.5 | 67.4 | **1.031x** | 14/15 |
| strings, N-heavy words | 143.5 | 141.0 | 1.018x | 11/15 |
| floats, scientific notation | 107.6 | 105.8 | 1.017x | 12/15 |
| floats, positive | 78.0 | 77.2 | 1.011x | 11/15 |
| floats, 10% negative | 83.0 | 82.0 | 1.011x | 12/15 |
| custom `na_values`, 50% hits | 77.0 | 75.9 | 1.015x | 7/15 |
| bools | 60.8 | 60.6 | 1.003x | 7/15 |
| NA-dense (50% literal `NaN`) | 75.4 | 75.4 | 0.999x | 7/15 |
| strings, realistic words | 123.6 | 124.9 | 0.990x | 8/15 |
| `na_filter=False` | 89.6 | 90.7 | 0.988x | 5/15 |
| adversarial strings* | 139.2 | 142.0 | 0.980x | 2/15 |

\*The constructed worst case: 100% of tokens engineered to share a full 4-byte prefix with an NA spelling (`Nonetheless`, `nulled`, `NULLIFY`, `-1.#5`), so every token passes both blooms and still misses.

Negative-leading numeric columns win most (they previously collided with the `-NaN`/`-1.#IND` first byte and now reject at byte 2). Wide real-world frames — the common case — see ~8%.

## Tradeoffs

Follow-up runs at higher sample counts (120+ samples per case) confirmed the borderline rows above are not real regressions:

- **`na_filter=False`**: 1.003x — parity. The NA set is never consulted on this path, so the blooms cost nothing; the -1.2% above was run-to-run noise.
- **Small files read in bulk**: the larger struct (+9KB: an 8KB `starts2` and 1KB `prefix4` per hash set) adds per-read init cost in theory. Measured across 200 → 20,000 rows/read it does not exceed noise — 200-row reads came out 1.02x *faster* on this PR, with no monotonic penalty as size shrinks.
- **NA-hit-dense numeric columns**: a float column that is ~50% literal `NaN` text may be ~1% slower, since each genuine NA hit now pays the two bloom layers before the hash lookup. This sits inside the noise band and needs an unusual column shape to appear.
- **Adversarial strings (~2%)**: the only measurable cost, and only for input where essentially every token collides with an NA prefix. Random bloom collisions for ordinary strings are ~0.2%.

- [x] Added an entry in the latest `doc/source/whatsnew/vX.X.X.rst` file if fixing a bug or adding a new feature.

title: PERF: reduce overhead in DataFrame reductions with axis=1 (GH#51474)
body:
Reduces overhead in `axis=1` reductions. The largest win is for single-dtype frames, which previously fell through to the expensive transpose path.

A homogeneous frame has one block, so the existing multi-block fastpath (GH-65105) required `len(blocks) > 1` and skipped it. For a 1M-row frame, `.sum(axis=1)` transposed to a 1M-column frame and spent ~35ms in a per-column dtype check before the reduction kernel even ran. Reducing the single block's values directly along axis=0 is the identical computation without that overhead.

Changes:
- Single-block frames reduce the block directly (numpy blocks via `op(..., axis=0)`, 2D EA blocks via `values._reduce`). `argmax`/`argmin` are excluded since their positional results depend on column order. Frames with few rows and many columns are left to the transpose path: their block is `(ncols, nrows)`, so reducing along axis=0 walks the long axis with a strided, barely-vectorized inner loop, and `sum`/`prod`/`mean` are faster transposed.
- The transpose path's object-dtype check is now per-block (`O(nblocks)`) instead of per-column (`O(ncols)` via `get_dtypes()`). This is what speeds up reductions that still take the transpose path, e.g. mixed-dtype `std`.
- `_maybe_null_out` short-circuits `min_count <= 0`, skipping a mask reduction that can never null anything. This is what speeds up multi-block frames already on the `_reduce_axis1` fastpath, and wide frames on the transpose path.

No new allocation is introduced on any path: peak memory is at or below the previous level for every shape measured, and materially lower for tall frames, since reducing the block directly avoids materializing the transposed frame.

Timings and peak memory (before -> after, measured against current main):

| case | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1M x 10 float64 `sum(axis=1)` | 50.6 ms / 39.1 MB | 4.2 ms / 17.2 MB |
| 1M x 10 float64 `mean(axis=1)` | 51.8 ms / 39.1 MB | 11.1 ms / 33.4 MB |
| 1M mixed-dtype `std(axis=1)` (transpose path) | 56.8 ms | 18.7 ms |
| 1M mixed-dtype `sum(axis=1)` | 18.5 ms | 9.6 ms |
| wide 4 x 2M w/ NaNs `sum(axis=1)` | 40.9 ms / 76.3 MB | 29.4 ms / 76.3 MB |
| wide 4 x 2M w/ NaNs `mean(axis=1)` | 41.2 ms / 76.3 MB | 40.7 ms / 76.3 MB |

Frames backed by extension-dtype columns (e.g. `dt64tz`) are unchanged; those already reduce via the EA fastpath after GH-56903.

Deferred: reducing a C-contiguous transpose for wide, few-row `sum`/`prod`/`mean` is measurably faster again (~2x), but allocates a full copy of the block, unbounded in the number of columns. That memory-for-speed tradeoff is left out of this PR pending discussion.

title: PERF: Series.isin for integer dtypes with small-range values

labels.name: Algos
labels.description: Non-arithmetic algos: value_counts, factorize, sorting, isin, clip, shift, diff

body:
Speeds up integer ``isin`` (:meth:\`Series.isin\`, :meth:\`Index.isin\`, :meth:\`DataFrame.isin\`) when the values being searched for span a small range, by giving the ``ismember`` hashtable kernel a dense-lookup fast path.

## What

For integer dtypes, when the searched-for values span a range no larger than ``6 * (len(arr) + len(values))`` — the same memory-constraint heuristic ``np.isin`` uses for its ``kind="table"`` strategy — ``ismember`` now scatters into a dense ``uint8`` table and answers each element with a single bounds-checked load, instead of building a khash set and probing it. A size floor (``len(arr) >= 100 or len(values) >= 100``) keeps tiny inputs on the hashtable, where the extra table allocation would not pay off. Wide-range integer inputs are unaffected and keep the existing hashtable path.

``algorithms.isin`` also gets a small carve-out: the existing ">1M comps and <=26 values" branch that dispatches to ``np.isin`` now excludes small-range integers, since the dense kernel beats ``np.isin`` there too.

## Why

The hashtable path was hash-probe bound (~13ns/probe). ``np.isin``'s sort strategy is far worse at this size ratio (~80ms vs 13ms for 1M x 10k), so the win comes from a dense table, not sorting.

## Results

1M comps x 10k values (~50% hits): **12.9ms -> 1.0ms** (``np.isin``: 3.3ms). Across comps 10-10M x values 10-10M the eligible cases improve 1.9-18x with no case regressing; results are verified byte-identical to ``np.isin`` including ``iinfo`` boundaries, full-range int64 (correctly declines the dense path), strided/read-only inputs, and empties.

title: PERF: avoid argsort of uniques in safe_sort

labels.name: Algos
labels.description: Non-arithmetic algos: value_counts, factorize, sorting, isin, clip, shift, diff

body:
Speeds up `safe_sort` (and therefore `factorize(sort=True)`, `groupby(sort=True)`, and `merge(sort=True)`) when the keys contain many unique values.

With high-cardinality keys, the sorted-groupby path spends most of its time in `safe_sort` reordering the factorized codes, and the bulk of that was two argsorts of the uniques. Three changes:

- Invert the argsort permutation with an O(n) scatter instead of a second argsort (all dtypes).
- For integer uniques whose value range is at most 4x their length, skip the argsort entirely: `np.sort` the uniques and rank them with a counting pass over the range. This also validates uniqueness for free, so the `merge` path skips its separate hashtable `unique()` check.
- Gate the counting path on ≥5000 uniques; below that the plain argsort + O(n) scatter is faster, so low-cardinality keys don't regress.

On 1M rows of int64 keys drawn from `range(2_000_000)` (~790k observed uniques), `safe_sort` drops from ~104ms to ~35ms and `df.groupby("k", sort=True)["v"].sum()` from ~145ms to ~80ms (the `sort=False` floor is ~35ms). Lower cardinalities improve proportionally with no low-cardinality regression; float/object keys get the O(n)-inverse win at scale and are neutral for small inputs.

New `SortHighCardinality` ASV benchmark added under `groupby`.

title: PERF: pool skiplist node allocations for rolling median/quantile/rank
body:
Speeds up :meth:`.Rolling.median`, :meth:`.Rolling.quantile`, and :meth:`.Rolling.rank` (and their :class:`.Expanding` counterparts) by ~1.2–1.9x, by replacing the skiplist's per-node allocation with a pooled arena.

## What changed

The skiplist backing these methods (``pandas/_libs/include/pandas/skiplist.h``) previously did 3 ``malloc``s per insert (node struct + ``next`` array + ``width`` array) and 3 ``free``s per remove, with a recursive ref-counted teardown. For a rolling reduction over N rows that's ~3N ``malloc``/``free`` pairs, and it dominated runtime — ``Series(1M).rolling(10).median()`` was ~23x slower than ``.mean()``, with a window-independent ~160ms floor pointing straight at allocation churn rather than algorithmic cost.

The skiplist size is bounded by the window, which is known at init, so nodes now come from an arena:

- **Arena node pool.** Each node and its level arrays are one allocation, bump-allocated from arena chunks (8-aligned, including on 32-bit builds), with per-level free lists so removed nodes are recycled. Steady-state rolling does zero allocator calls. Ref-counting and the recursive ``node_destroy`` are gone.
- **``skiplist_reset``.** Rewinds the arena instead of destroy+init when a window restarts (non-monotonic bounds, ``step >= window``); replaces the destroy+init pairs in all three callers in ``aggregations.pyx``. Chunks are kept in allocation order and a cursor rewinds on reset so retained chunks are refilled before any new chunk is allocated — peak memory stays at ~one window's node footprint no matter how many times the window restarts (verified: ``rolling(200_000, step=200_000)`` over 16M rows, 79 restarts, arena stays flat).
- **Per-skiplist xorshift64 level draws** instead of libc ``rand()`` + ``log2()`` — cheaper and free of shared libc state.
- **``skiplist_get_pair``** fetches two adjacent ranks in one traversal (median even-count, quantile linear/midpoint).
- **Geometric arena growth.** The first chunk is sized to the window's node budget but capped at 128KB, doubling to a 4MB cap. Windows up to ~1360 elements are a single right-sized allocation as before; larger windows reach full capacity in O(log) allocations. This bounds committed memory for windows that never fill (NaN-heavy data, since NaNs are not inserted): a ``window=40000`` at 99% NaN commits 128KB instead of 3.75MB, with resident memory and runtime unchanged.

## Benchmarks

``Series`` of 1M float64, min-of-best over an interleaved A/B (per-op speedups):

| window | median | quantile | rank |
|--------|--------|----------|------|
| 5      | 1.78x  | 1.73x    | 1.91x |
| 10     | 1.54x  | 1.60x    | 1.56x |
| 100    | 1.41x  | 1.41x    | 1.27x |
| 1000   | 1.37x  | 1.34x    | 1.22x |
| 10000  | 1.35x  | 1.32x    | 1.24x |

``expanding().median()`` 1.89x; ``step == window`` (all-reset path) 1.91x.

## Testing

``pandas/tests/window`` passes (9658 passed, slow table-method/numba cases excluded locally). ASV coverage already exists (``rolling.Methods`` / ``Quantile`` / ``Rank`` at windows 10/1000 plus expanding). Numerics at multi-chunk window sizes (250K-element windows, 10% NaN) additionally verified against ``np.nanmedian``/``np.nanquantile`` across the restart, sliding, and expanding paths.

title: PERF: reduce overhead in sorted merges and safe_sort

labels.name: Algos
labels.description: Non-arithmetic algos: value_counts, factorize, sorting, isin, clip, shift, diff

body:
Reduces the overhead of merges that sort their output. `how="outer"` always
sorts, so it was the most affected: on a 1M x 100k single-int64-key join it ran
~3.8x slower than the equivalent `how="inner"` despite near-identical output
size. Profiling showed the extra time was almost entirely avoidable work in
label sorting and indexer remapping, not inherent cost.

Changes:
- `safe_sort`: invert the sort permutation with an O(n) scatter instead of a
  second `argsort()`, and skip `argsort`+`take` when only the sorted values are
  needed. This is on the critical path of every `factorize(sort=True)`.
- `_factorize_keys`: for numeric keys, recover sorted-order codes via
  `np.sort` + a lookup in the factorizer's existing hashtable rather than
  argsorting the uniques, and pass `assume_unique`/`verify=False` through
  `_sort_labels` to skip a redundant uniqueness scan and bounds check.
- `join.pyx`: the `inner_join`/`left_outer_join`/`full_outer_join` sort paths
  now write sorter values directly during the fill loop, replacing the separate
  `_get_result_indexer` remap pass over the full-length output indexers.
- `_maybe_add_join_keys`: compute the `-1` mask once.

Verified byte-for-byte identical results and no regression across cardinality
(low/high/very-high), dtype (float, masked `Int64`, object, datetime,
`string[pyarrow]`), and join shape (dimension, many-to-many, tiny) via an A/B
build against the parent commit.

Benchmarks (min-of-n, quiesced machine):
- 1M x 100k int64 `how="outer"`: 34.7ms -> 24.5ms (-29%)
- 1M x 1M int64 `how="outer"` (~630k uniques): 192ms -> 100ms (-48%)
- inner `how="inner", sort=True`: 32ms -> 22ms (-31%)
- `factorize(sort=True)` on 1M values / 630k uniques: 89ms -> 53ms (-40%)
- `how="inner", sort=False` (control, untouched path): unchanged

title: PERF: render to_csv chunks natively, bypassing csv.writer

labels.name: Needs Discussion
labels.description: Requires discussion from core team before further action

labels.name: Mothballed
labels.description: Temporarily-closed PR the author plans to return to

body:
Renders each `to_csv` chunk into a single string in C via a new
`libwriters.write_csv_chunk`, bypassing `csv.writer` and the per-cell
Python conversions for the default dialect (`QUOTE_MINIMAL`, `doublequote`,
no `escapechar`, `errors="strict"`, single-char ASCII sep/quotechar,
≤2-char ASCII lineterminator, non-MultiIndex). Numeric, boolean, and
tz-naive datetime columns are formatted natively; floats use
`std::to_chars` (shortest round-trip) reformatted to match numpy's
value-based fixed/scientific notation. A meson try-compile probe
(`PD_HAVE_FP_TO_CHARS`) guards the float path, with a
`PyOS_double_to_string` `'r'`-mode fallback for toolchains (e.g. older
libc++ on macOS) that lack floating-point `std::to_chars`.

Columns the fast path can't render natively (`float_format`, `decimal`,
`date_format`, timedelta, period, tz-aware datetime, Interval, extension
arrays, …) are converted with the existing `get_values_for_csv` and only
assembled natively, so output stays byte-identical. Anything outside the
gate falls back to the existing `csv.writer` path. Chunks containing
strings that can't encode to UTF-8 (lone surrogates) fall back per chunk.

Speedups on 1M rows (vs the current writer): ~10x for float, int, and
bool columns, ~9x for datetimes, ~5x for strings, ~8x for a mixed 8-column
frame. The output is verified byte-for-byte identical to the `csv.writer`
path across a dtype/options matrix plus 400k random float64 / 200k random
float32 bit patterns.

Follow-up opportunities (not in this PR): reading `ArrowStringArray`
buffers directly to skip per-cell Python strings, per-chunk threading,
and a binary write path to avoid the buffer→str→re-encode round-trip.

title: PERF: typed non-boxing path for get_indexer_non_unique

labels.name: Index
labels.description: Related to the Index class or subclasses

body:
Adds a typed, non-boxing khash-based path for `Index.get_indexer_non_unique` on native numeric and datetime-like dtypes, replacing the implementation that boxed every index and target element into Python objects and matched them through a Python `set`/`dict`.

The new path maps each unique target to a dense id via the engine's typed khash table, collects matching positions in a single scan, and counting-sorts them into contiguous per-target runs. Monotonic indexes with few targets keep the vectorized `searchsorted` shortcut. `MaskedIndexEngine` takes the same path when neither side has missing values. Object dtype is unchanged; complex is excluded because khash matches complex NaNs component-wise while `is_matching_na` matches any complex NaN, and longdouble keeps the object fallback (no fused specialization).

This covers int/uint/float32/float64 directly, and datetime64/timedelta64/`Period` (via their i8 engines), `MultiIndex` (uint64 codes engine), and `Categorical` (codes engine) for free, since all route through the same integer engines.

Benchmarks (1M-row int64 index, ~100k unique, 100k targets):

- `get_indexer_non_unique`: 345ms → 14ms
- `.loc` with 100k duplicate labels: 416ms → 30ms
- float64 with NaNs: 392ms → 25ms; datetime64: 52ms → 6ms; MultiIndex: 46ms → 5ms

xref GH-15364.

title: PERF: single-pass composite-key factorization for multi-key merges
body:
Speeds up :func:`merge` when joining on multiple key columns that are all integer-like (numpy integer/unsigned/bool, datetime64, timedelta64, including tz-aware).

Previously, a multi-key merge factorized each key column separately through its own khash pass and then combined the resulting codes (`_get_join_keys` / `get_group_index`), which re-hashed the combined key — 3+ full hash passes over the data.

This adds `_fuse_int64_keys`, which fuses the integer-viewable key columns into a single int64 key per side using per-column min/max spans, so the composite key is factorized in **one** khash pass. It falls back to the existing per-column path whenever the keys are not all integer-viewable numpy arrays (object/float/masked/Arrow EAs, non-native-byteorder datetimes, uint64-mixed-with-signed pairs) or the combined key space does not fit in int64 — so behavior is unchanged. NaT almost always lands in the overflow bail (its i8 value is int64-min, making the column span ~2^63); in the one corner where it can still fuse (all dates near the datetime64[ns] lower bound), NaT participates as its i8 value, matching the fallback exactly (tested).

The fused values are order-isomorphic to lexicographic tuple order and appearance-order-isomorphic to the old combined codes, so join results are identical to the fallback for every `how`/`sort` combination (including `sort=True` ordering and NaT placement). One mechanical caveat: with `sort=False` the two encodings can disagree about whether the composite key is monotonic, flipping which branch `get_join_indexers` takes. This cannot change output — inner/left/right joins preserve the keyed side's row order in every branch, and `how="outer"` always runs with `sort=True` (`_MergeOperation` forces `self.sort` for outer).

All benchmarks below are min-of-24, with the fused path alternated against a forced-fallback baseline (interleaved to cancel drift — a single-order run turned out to inflate figures by up to ~2x from memory/thermal warmup).

## Wins

| case | fallback | fused | speedup |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1000x100 int64, N=1M, inner | 21.3 ms | 12.9 ms | 1.65x |
| narrow int8 keys, card 5x5, N=5M | 66.1 ms | 42.4 ms | 1.56x |
| 8 int16 cols, range 4, N=1M | 38.4 ms | 19.3 ms | 1.99x |
| datetime + int, low card, N=5M | 72.6 ms | 42.2 ms | 1.72x |
| high-cardinality (~N uniques), N=5M | 537 ms | 351 ms | 1.53x |

The win grows with column count (more per-column hash passes eliminated) and holds for narrow dtypes even though they incur an `astype` upcast to int64.

## Trade-off: the fallback "bail tax"

The overflow test that decides whether to fuse is based on the **value span** (`max - min + 1`) of each key column, and computing those spans requires a min/max scan over every key column. When the span product overflows int64, `_fuse_int64_keys` returns `None` and the merge runs the unchanged per-column fallback — but that min/max scan is now wasted work in front of it.

This regresses precisely when the keys are all integer-viewable **but have a wide value range with low cardinality** (e.g. sparse hashed IDs, account numbers, or scaled/epoch values). The fallback's own overflow guard (`get_group_index`) is cardinality-based rather than span-based, so it handles these inputs cheaply — the two disagree exactly in this corner, and fused adds a scan the fallback didn't need.

Measured cost, all cases where fused bails after scanning:

| case | fallback | fused | delta |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3 int64 cols, values {0, 1e9}, N=5M | 92.2 ms | 96.3 ms | +4.5% |
| 2 int64 cols, span ~1e9 (overflow at 3rd), N=5M | 114 ms | 117 ms | +2.7% |
| 2 int64 cols, span 2^62, N=5M | 116 ms | 119 ms | +1.9% |

The tax is bounded at roughly **+2–5%** and does not grow with column count (the fallback denominator grows alongside the wasted scan). Non-integer keys (object/float/masked/Arrow) bail before any scan — `_fuse_key_view` returns `None` on the first non-integer column, so the helper costs ~1 µs and those merges are unaffected. Very small frames (N < ~100) in tight loops pay a ~2% Python-overhead tax that disappears by N≈1000.

Eliminating the int64 bail tax cheaply isn't possible — knowing the span requires the scan, and dtype bounds don't help for int64 (bound is 2^64). Given the 1.5–2x wins on the common cases, the trade seems worth it, but flagging it explicitly for review.

title: PERF: faster to_datetime parsing of timezone-aware strings
body:
Parsing timezone-aware datetime strings (e.g. ``"2023-06-15 12:34:56+05:00"``) was ~20-30x slower than the equivalent tz-naive strings, because tz handling was done per element. This PR removes that per-element overhead.

For 200k unique strings:

| workload | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| ``to_datetime(strs, format="%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S%z")`` | 447 ms | 21 ms |
| ``to_datetime(strs, format="ISO8601")`` | 435 ms | 15 ms |
| ``to_datetime(strs)`` (no format) | 426 ms | 22 ms |
| ``DatetimeIndex(naive strs, tz="US/Eastern")`` | 1647 ms | 49 ms |
| ``DatetimeIndex(naive strs, tz=fixed offset)`` | 889 ms | 34 ms |
| ``DatetimeIndex(aware strs, tz="US/Eastern")`` | 1167 ms | 138 ms |

Three pieces:

- **Fixed-offset `%z` fast paths.** The `%z` sites in `array_strptime` and `convert_str_to_tsobject` built a fresh `datetime.timezone` per element and localized through `get_dst_info` (uncached for `datetime.timezone`, allocating two ndarrays per call). They now subtract the parsed offset directly. `tz_cache_key` also caches `datetime.timezone` instances (keyed on the offset alone, since the name is irrelevant to transitions) so remaining `get_dst_info` callers hit the cache.
- **Vectorized localization in `array_to_datetime_with_tz`.** Wall times are parsed tz-naive and then localized in a single vectorized `tz_localize_to_utc` call rather than one length-1 ndarray + fresh `Localizer` per element. Ints/floats (UTC epoch values), datetime/date objects (`fold`-based disambiguation), and `"now"`/`"today"` keep the per-element path to preserve behavior; wall values within a day of the int64 bounds also fall back so overflow checks still raise.
- ASV benchmarks + whatsnew.

No open issue tracks this; it addresses the long-standing gap noted in GH-9714.

## Tradeoffs / adversarial cases

I A/B'd the change against its base commit on a set of deliberately adversarial inputs. One real regression exists, plus a minor memory note.

**Near-int64-bound wall strings pay a double parse.** In `array_to_datetime_with_tz`, wall values within `2 * periods_per_day` of the int64 limits fall back to re-parsing the string *with* the tz (to keep the overflow check that would otherwise be lost in the vectorized `tz_localize_to_utc`, which wraps silently instead of raising). Those elements are therefore parsed twice:

| input (ns resolution, 20-100k elems) | base | branch | result |
|---|---|---|---|
| near-bound + slow (dateutil) parse, tz=`US/Eastern` | 26.9 µs/elem | 55.2 µs/elem | **2.05x slower** |
| near-bound + slow parse, tz=fixed offset | 26.0 µs/elem | 52.6 µs/elem | **2.02x slower** |
| near-bound + ISO parse, tz=`US/Eastern` | 9.96 µs/elem | 10.1 µs/elem | 1.4% slower |

Reachability is very low: the fallback only triggers within ~2 days of the representable limit. At ns resolution that means wall times around 2262-04-09..11 or 1677-09-21..23; at µs/ms/s resolution the bounds are year ~294247 and beyond, so it is effectively unreachable outside ns data deliberately placed at those extremes. When the parse is cheap (ISO) the doubling is ~noise; it only reaches ~2x when the expensive dateutil parser is also involved.

Options for the near-bound path:
1. **Leave as-is** (current). Simplest; ~2x only on essentially-unreachable ns-near-limit input.
2. **Localize in place instead of re-parsing** — reuse the already-parsed value and run the overflow check on it, avoiding the second string parse. Brings the near-bound case back to ~baseline at the cost of a bit more code in the hot loop. Happy to do this if reviewers prefer.

**Minor: transient memory.** The vectorized path materializes a masked copy of the wall values plus the localize result (two transient int64 arrays, ~16 B/elem) that the old in-place per-element approach didn't allocate. Negligible at normal sizes; peak memory is modestly higher for very large arrays.

For context, the same A/B showed the non-adversarial paths are neutral-to-much-faster: object arrays with no wall values (e.g. `datetime`/int) are unchanged, small-n is faster, and fixed-offset near-bound input is actually ~2.3x *faster* (the `tz_cache_key` change lets the per-element localize hit the cache).

title: BUG: select_dtypes support non-nanosecond dt64/td64 units (GH#40234)
body:
closes #40234

Stacked on GH-66120 — only the last commit is new here.

Datetime/timedelta-resolution slice of the GH-40234 fix. :meth:`DataFrame.select_dtypes` now accepts `datetime64`/`timedelta64` specs with any pandas-supported unit — `"s"`, `"ms"`, `"us"`, `"ns"` — where previously anything but `ns` raised "too specific". A unit-qualified spec, whether a string (`"datetime64[us]"`) or a numpy dtype instance (`np.dtype("datetime64[us]")`), now matches only columns with exactly that resolution; in particular `"datetime64[ns]"` now selects only `ns` columns instead of every datetime column. A unitless `"datetime64"`/`"timedelta64"` (or `np.datetime64`/`np.timedelta64`) still matches every resolution, and units pandas cannot represent (e.g. `"datetime64[D]"`) still raise.

This is the final PR in the select_dtypes stack (GH-66112 → GH-66113 → GH-66119 → GH-66118 → GH-66120 → GH-66122). Together the stack makes `select_dtypes` treat distinct dtypes as distinct across every spelling — instance, class, bare/bracketed string, and datetime unit — so merging it completes the fix for GH-40234.

title: PERF: merge_asof with by
body:
The ``by`` path in ``merge_asof`` carried a ~7x penalty relative to the no-``by`` path for what should be a cheap group partition. Root cause: the ``asof_join_*_on_X_by_Y`` kernels in ``join.pyx`` boxed each left-side by-key into a Python object and looked it up via ``__contains__`` + ``get_item`` on an ``Int64HashTable``.

Two changes:

- Rewrite the asof-by kernels to use the raw ``khash`` int64 C API (``kh_put_int64`` / ``kh_get_int64``): no per-element boxing, and a single typed lookup per left row instead of two. This is a Pareto improvement — no input makes it slower.
- In ``_AsOfMerge._get_join_indexers``, skip ``_factorize_keys`` for a single numpy by-key whose int64 representation preserves equality (int/uint/bool/datetime64/timedelta64) and pass it straight through. Matching dtypes across sides are already enforced in ``_maybe_require_matching_dtypes``. Multi-``by`` and object/string/EA by-keys keep the existing factorize path.

Benchmark (500k rows each side, sorted int ``on=`` key, 100 groups): ``by=`` goes from ~52ms (6.9x the no-``by`` path) to ~10.5ms (1.2x).

Adds an ASV case (``MergeAsof.time_by_int_many_groups``) exercising a high-cardinality by-key, which the existing cases did not cover.

## Performance: wins and the one bounded loss

I measured the factorize-skip decision in isolation (kernel on raw values = this PR, vs factorize-to-dense-codes + kernel = old behavior; everything else in ``merge_asof`` is identical between the two). 500k rows each side, ``backward``:

| by-key pattern | this PR | old (factorize) | ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| random int, 100 groups | 5.2ms | 8.6ms | **0.61x** |
| random int, ~200k groups | 15.5ms | 22.5ms | **0.69x** |
| distinct random int64 (~1M card) | 19.6ms | 56.6ms | **0.35x** |
| datetime64 day-spaced, 20k groups | 10.0ms | 15.5ms | **0.64x** |
| multiples of 2^14, 100k groups | 39.2ms | 31.3ms | **1.25x** ⚠️ |

**The loss is real but bounded.** ``kh_int64_hash_func(key) = (key>>33) ^ key ^ (key<<11)`` masked to ``n_buckets-1`` (a power of two), so the bucket index is dominated by the low bits of the key. Distinct by-values that are **exact multiples of a large power of two** collapse onto very few buckets and turn the kernel's hashtable into long probe chains. Dense factorize codes ``[0, ngroups)`` never do this, so skipping factorize exposes the kernel to those collisions. At the kernel level the penalty reaches ~2.9x (e.g. multiples of 2^20, 8192 groups: 21.9ms raw vs 7.5ms on dense codes).

Why it doesn't get worse than ~1.25x end-to-end: ``_factorize_keys`` uses the **same** khash int64 hash internally, so any value-set that collides this kernel *also* inflates the factorize cost being skipped — the two are coupled. Heavier spacings (2^20) don't regress at all because factorize itself balloons and masks the kernel loss. A sweep over spacing × cardinality caps the worst case at **1.25x** (2^14 spacing, 50k–100k groups).

Triggering the regression requires by-keys that are exact multiples of ~16384 at ~100k cardinality — pathological. Ordinary by-keys (categorical ids, small/random ints, regularly-spaced datetimes) all land in the winning column. I judged the trade worth it, but flagging it explicitly for review; happy to gate the fast path differently if a reviewer prefers.

title: BUG: select_dtypes string form of an extension dtype matches exact dtype (GH#40234, GH#59888)

labels.name: NA - MaskedArrays
labels.description: Related to pd.NA and nullable extension arrays

body:
closes #59888

Stacked on GH-66118; the diff will shrink to just the top commit once the PRs below it in the stack merge.

A string passed to :meth:`DataFrame.select_dtypes` that names a specific extension dtype now selects only columns of that exact dtype, instead of every column sharing its ``dtype.type``.

- A **bracketed** string names one parametrization and matches that instance, e.g. ``"int64[pyarrow]"`` selects only ``ArrowDtype(pa.int64())`` columns. Previously ``"int64[pyarrow]"`` matched nothing, ``"float64[pyarrow]"`` matched every numpy/masked float column, and ``"timestamp[ns][pyarrow]"`` matched a tz-aware numpy column while missing the Arrow one.
- A **bare** name matches that dtype's class (the family), e.g. ``"Int64"``/``"boolean"`` select only the nullable extension columns, no longer also matching numpy ``int64``/``bool``. Family names like ``"string"`` and ``"category"`` are unchanged.

Kind strings (``"int64"``, ``"datetime"``, ...), dtype types, dtype instances, and dtype classes are unaffected here.

With the instance (GH-66119) and class (GH-66118) slices below it in the stack, this completes the Arrow-dtype support GH-59888 asks for (the ``timestamp[ns][pyarrow]`` string now selects the Arrow column). The remaining datetime-resolution slice of GH-40234 is GH-66122.

title: BUG: select_dtypes dtype instances match exactly (GH#40234)

labels.name: ExtensionArray
labels.description: Extending pandas with custom dtypes or arrays.

body:
Stacked on GH-66113 — only the last commit is new here.

Instance-spec piece of the GH-40234 fix. A dtype *instance* (a `np.dtype` or `ExtensionDtype`, e.g. `np.dtype("int64")`, `pd.Int64Dtype()`, `pd.DatetimeTZDtype(tz="UTC")`, `pd.ArrowDtype(pa.int64())`) passed to `select_dtypes` `include`/`exclude` now matches only columns with *exactly* that dtype, instead of every column sharing `dtype.type` after unwrapping `ArrowDtype`.

Class and string specs are unchanged and still match a family of dtypes, so the loose/kind readings remain available:

- `select_dtypes(pd.Int64Dtype())` → only `Int64` columns; `select_dtypes(np.dtype("int64"))` → only numpy `int64`.
- `select_dtypes("int64")` and `select_dtypes(pd.Int64Dtype)` (string / class) still match numpy `int64`, `Int64`, and Arrow `int64` alike.

Under-specified instances stay family-matching, matching their string/class counterparts: a unitless `np.dtype("datetime64")` and a bare `pd.CategoricalDtype()` (categories `None`) select their whole family. Specific datetime-unit instances (`np.dtype("datetime64[s]")`, `pd.DatetimeTZDtype("us", tz="UTC")`) now match exactly rather than raising.

The GH-52576 branch that resolved instances via `numpy_dtype.type` is removed; the numpy-string rejection and "too specific" datetime-unit guards are preserved for the instance path.

The class-kind and string-kind pieces of GH-40234 (making `select_dtypes(pd.Int64Dtype)` / `select_dtypes("Int64")` storage-specific) are separate follow-ups, so this doesn't fully close the issue on its own.

title: BUG: select_dtypes with an ExtensionDtype subclass (GH#65366)
body:
Stacked on GH-66119; the diff will shrink to just the top commit once the PRs below it in the stack merge.

Passing an :class:`~pandas.api.extensions.ExtensionDtype` subclass (e.g. `pd.ArrowDtype`, `pd.CategoricalDtype`, `pd.DatetimeTZDtype`) to `DataFrame.select_dtypes` now selects every column whose dtype is an instance of that class, regardless of parametrization. This implements the natural "a class is a kind request" rule enabled by the preceding refactor.

Previously such classes could:
- raise `TypeError` (e.g. `pd.ArrowDtype`, `pd.DatetimeTZDtype`, `pd.PeriodDtype`),
- emit a spurious `UserWarning` about instantiating the dtype without arguments (e.g. `pd.CategoricalDtype`), or
- select the wrong columns (`pd.Int64Dtype` also matched numpy `int64`; `SparseDtype` matched all float64).

The `ExtensionDtype` base class itself matches all extension-dtype columns. Passing the `StringDtype` class in `include`/`exclude` now counts as explicitly handling `str` columns, silencing the GH-61916 object/str backward-compat warning.

title: BUG: interpolate leaving NAs unfilled for pyarrow dtypes
body:
- [x] closes #65345
- [x] Tests added and passed
- [x] All [code checks passed](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/development/contributing_codebase.html#pre-commit)
- [x] Added an entry in the latest `doc/source/whatsnew/v3.1.0.rst` file

## Problem

As diagnosed by @jorisvandenbossche in #65345, the pyarrow-native fast path added in #56347 for `method="linear"` + `limit_direction="forward"` takes over without checking whether it can actually handle the data. It computes a two-neighbor midpoint (`prev + (next - prev)/2`), so it only fills *isolated* interior NAs. Investigating the full behavior surfaced additional problems beyond the reported one:

1. **Consecutive interior NAs left unfilled** (the report): `[1, 2, 3, NA, NA, 6, 7]` → unchanged, while `Int64` gives `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]`.
2. **Trailing NAs left unfilled**: `[1, 2, NA]` with forward direction → unchanged, while `Int64` extends the last value.
3. **Integer truncation — silently wrong values**: for integer dtypes the midpoint is computed with `pc.divide_checked` on the integer type, so `[1, NA, 2]` fills with **1** instead of 1.5.
4. **Dtype inconsistency**: the fast path keeps `int64[pyarrow]`, while every other parameter combination (e.g. `limit_direction="backward"`) upcasts to `float64[pyarrow]` via the shared fallback — so the result dtype depended on which direction was requested.

## Fix

Remove the fast path so pyarrow-backed arrays always go through the shared `missing.interpolate_2d_inplace` machinery. After the change, pyarrow-backed results match the equivalent masked-dtype (`Int64`/`Float64`) results — values, NA handling, and float upcast — across all combinations of `limit_direction`, `limit`, and `limit_area` I tested (5 NA patterns × 7 parameter combinations, zero divergences).

I considered guarding the fast path instead (only isolated interior NAs + float dtype + no trailing NA), but at that point the mask analysis erases most of the benefit and it would still leave the int-truncation/upcast questions — simplest correct thing seemed to be to remove it. Happy to rework toward a guarded fast path if that's preferred.

`test_interpolate_linear` was updated for the new (masked-dtype-consistent) expectation: trailing NA now filled going forward, result upcast to `float64[pyarrow]`.

## Verification

- New regression tests: `test_interpolate_linear_consecutive_na`, `test_interpolate_linear_int_fractional` (both fail on `main`).
- `pandas/tests/extension/test_arrow.py`: 26,885 passed.
- `tests/series/methods/test_interpolate.py` + `tests/frame/methods/test_interpolate.py`: 206 passed; `tests/copy_view/test_interp_fillna.py`: 72 passed.
- `ruff check` / `ruff format` clean on changed files.

## Disclosure

This fix was developed with the assistance of an AI tool (Claude Code), with the investigation, diff and test results reviewed and owned by me — I'll respond to review feedback personally.

title: BUG: assert_categorical_equal with check_category_order=False mishandles NaN (#62008)
body:
- [x] closes #62008
- [x] Tests added and passed
- [x] All code checks passed
- [x] Added an entry in the latest ``doc/source/whatsnew/v3.1.0.rst`` file

When ``check_category_order=False``, :func:`~pandas.testing.assert_series_equal` /
``assert_categorical_equal`` compare the categoricals' *values* via
``categories.take(codes)``. Missing values have code ``-1``, and ``Index.take(-1)``
without ``allow_fill`` wraps around to the **last** category. When the two
categoricals hold their categories in a different order, the NaN position then
resolves to different labels and the comparison spuriously fails:

```python
import pandas as pd, numpy as np
left  = pd.Series(pd.Categorical(["B", np.nan, "D"], categories=["B", "D"]))
right = pd.Series(pd.Categorical(["B", np.nan, "D"], categories=["D", "B"]))
pd.testing.assert_series_equal(left, right, check_category_order=False)
# AssertionError: Series category.values are different  (before this PR)
```

This passes ``allow_fill=True, fill_value=np.nan`` to ``take`` so code ``-1`` maps
to ``NaN`` on both sides. Genuinely different values (and ``check_category_order=True``)
still raise as before.
