title: fix: Arrow interpolate fast path skips consecutive NAs (GH#65345)
body:
- [x] closes #65345
- [x] Tests added and passed
- [x] The issue describes a regression introduced by #56347

## Summary

The PyArrow-native fast path in `ArrowExtensionArray.interpolate()` uses `pairwise_diff(period=2)` which only correctly handles isolated single NAs. When consecutive NAs are present the computation silently produced wrong results instead of interpolating them.

## Root Cause

In `pandas/core/arrays/arrow/array.py`, the `interpolate()` method has a fast path for `method="linear"`, `limit_direction="forward"`, no `limit` and no `limit_area`. This fast path uses:

```python
y_diff_2 = pc.fill_null_backward(pc.pairwise_diff_checked(values, period=2))
prev_values = pa.concat_arrays([na_value, values[:-2], na_value])
interps = pc.add_checked(prev_values, pc.divide_checked(y_diff_2, 2))
return self._from_pyarrow_array(pc.coalesce(self._pa_array, interps))
```

For isolated NAs (e.g. `[a, NA, b]`), `pairwise_diff(period=2)` correctly computes `b-a` and the midpoint formula fills the gap. For consecutive NAs (e.g. `[a, NA, NA, b]`), the pairwise diff produces null values because the operation requires both positions to be non-null when the gap is larger than 2.

## Fix

Added a guard that checks for consecutive nulls using PyArrow compute (`pc.is_null` + `pc.and_kleene` on shifted slices) before taking the fast path. When consecutive NAs are detected, the method falls through to the existing generic masked-array interpolation path which handles them correctly.

## Changes

- `pandas/core/arrays/arrow/array.py`: Added consecutive-NA detection before the fast path
- `pandas/tests/extension/test_arrow.py`: Added `test_interpolate_linear_consecutive_na`

title: BUG: Series.sort_values ignore_index has no effect on already sorted Series (#65833)
body:
**Problem:** When a Series is already sorted, `sort_values()` returns early without applying `ignore_index`.

**Root cause:** The early return path (for the already-sorted case) at `pandas/core/series.py:4081` copied the Series directly without checking `ignore_index`.

**Fix:** Move the `ignore_index` index reset into the early return path for both the `inplace` and non-`inplace` branches.

Closes #65833

title: BUG: Fix nanany/nanall raising ValueError with skipna=False on nullable dtypes
body:
## Summary

Fixes #65710: `DataFrame.any(skipna=False)` and `DataFrame.all(skipna=False)` raise `ValueError: cannot convert float NaN to bool` on nullable dtypes (`boolean`, `Int*`, `Float*`), while `Series.any/all(skipna=False)` correctly returns `pd.NA`.

## Root Cause

In `nanops.nanany` and `nanops.nanall`, when `skipna=False` and NA values are present, `_get_values` preserves NaN values in the array. Then `values.astype(bool)` tries to convert NaN to bool, which raises `ValueError`.

## Fix

Check for NaN values when `skipna=False` before attempting `astype(bool)`, and return `np.nan` directly instead.

## Changes

- `pandas/core/nanops.py`: 6 lines each in `nanany` and `nanall`

Fixes #65710

  • 🌟 Adds wheel auditing with abi3audit as a default after the repair step, with new audit-requires and audit-command options (#2805)

  • 🌟 Adds pyemscripten platform tag support (PEP 783), updates Pyodide to 314.0.0a2, and adds a pyodide-eol enable flag for building end-of-life Pyodide versions (#2812, #2848)

  • 🌟 Sets up delvewheel as the default repair-wheel-command for Windows, so extension module DLLs are now bundled automatically. Skip by setting it to empty if not needed. (#2831)

  • ✨ Adds CPython 3.15 support, under the enable option cpython-prerelease. This version of cibuildwheel uses 3.15.0b2. (#2833, #2850)

    While CPython is in beta, the ABI can change, so your wheels might not be compatible with the final release. For this reason, we don't recommend distributing wheels until RC1, at which point 3.15 will be available in cibuildwheel without the flag.

  • ✨ Adds CPython 3.15 support for iOS and Android (#2857, #2858)

  • ✨ Adds Android improvements for building NumPy and related packages, including auditwheel support, pkg-config and Fortran configuration, and the xbuild-files option (#2695)

  • ✨ Adds CIBUILDWHEEL_BUILD_IDENTIFIER environment variable set to the current build identifier (e.g. cp311-manylinux_x86_64) during per-build steps (#2872)

  • ✨ Adds {project} and {package} placeholders to config-settings (#2827)

  • ⚠️ Drops support for Python 3.8 (#2686)

  • ⚠️ Removes the experimental CPython 3.13 free-threading builds and the cpython-freethreading enable option. CPython 3.14+ free-threading support remains available without the enable flag. (#2684)

  • ⚠️ Drops support for Cirrus CI, which is shutting down June 1, 2026 (#2817)

  • ⚠️ Drops GraalPy 3.11 (gp311) support, as agreed in #2741, and removes GraalPy 24-only workarounds (#2895)

  • 🔐 Adds tarfile extraction filter for safe archive extraction (#2856)

  • 🐛 Fixes UV_PYTHON not being set for before-build on Linux when using uv as the build-frontend (#2830)

  • 🐛 Fixes detection of musl libc when downloading python-build-standalone, which previously always selected the gnu asset on musl hosts like Alpine (#2889)

  • 🐛 Fixes config-settings expansion when {project} or {package} contains spaces or backslashes (#2886)

  • 🐛 Prevents deadlock when linux32 fails and forwards platform args to the sanity check (#2880, #2888)

  • 🐛 Fixes container resource leaks on start failure and during teardown (#2879, #2887)

  • 🛠 Updates Android to Python 3.13.13 and 3.14.4 (#2821)

  • 🛠 Applies Pyodide-specific patches to the Emscripten toolchain installation (#2800)

  • 🛠 Uses python -V -V for Windows build diagnostics (#2832)

  • 🛠 Simplifies pinned container image lookup (#2897)

  • 🛠 Minor fixups across error messages, OCI container, and options (#2860)

  • 💼 Adds PEP 723 metadata for bin/ scripts and drops the bin dependency group (#2819)

  • 💼 Improves Azure test reliability with retries and caching (#2890)

  • 💼 Fixes Windows GitLab CI test running (#2870)

  • 💼 Updates CI action pins and dev dependencies (#2902, #2867, #2851, #2843, #2826, #2823, #2820, #2807)

  • 💼 Adds agent and copilot setup files (#2861)

  • 💼 Uses if TYPE_CHECKING: blocks (#2866, #2864)

  • 🧪 Fixes Android tests using the uv frontend (#2809)

  • 🧪 Fixes the update-dependencies workflow to use uv to run nox (#2808)

  • 🧪 Adds unit tests for OCIContainer._get_platform_args (#2878)

  • 📚 Updates documentation for delvewheel as the default Windows repair-wheel-command, including the build diagram, schema defaults, and legal note (#2877, #2853, #2891)

  • 📚 Documents platform-specific before-build configuration (#2834)

  • 📚 Updates the "How it works" diagram with details of Android, iOS, and Pyodide builds (#2816)

  • 📚 Adds Pyodide icon and regenerates working examples data for Android, iOS, and Pyodide (#2815, #2811)

  • 📚 Adds intersphinx support for external documentation linking (#2871)

  • If multiple inputs are provided for the GitHub-internal analysis-kinds input, only code-scanning will be enabled. The analysis-kinds input is experimental, for GitHub-internal use only, and may change without notice at any time. #3892

title: [FIX: Remove trailing empty bins in pd.resample to prevent NaN padding (GH 65740)
body:
### Problem
When using `pd.resample()`, an incorrect bin boundary calculation causes an extra trailing empty bin to be generated, which pads the result with `NaN` and implicitly upcasts integer data types to `float64`.

### Solution
Adjusted the boundary/bin generation logic in `pandas/core/resample.py` to prevent appending a trailing ghost bin when the maximum timestamp aligns snugly with the interval. Reverted the incorrect assertions in `test_resample_reresample`

Closes #65740

title: CI: Fix 2.3.x CI failures from dependency and toolchain drift
body:
The `2.3.x` branch has accumulated CI failures from dependency and toolchain drift (it hasn't had a green CI run in a while), independent of any code change. This PR fixes them so `2.3.x` CI can pass again. My goal for this PR is to enable a 2.3.4 patch release that would include https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/65351.

Each fix is a focused commit (linked under each item); most mirror fixes already on `main`/`3.0.x` that were never backported.

### CI workflow
- **macOS / Windows runner images** — the `macos-13` unit-test jobs sat queued at GitHub's runner-availability limit (~24h) because `macos-13` is being deprecated and runners no longer pick up those jobs. Bump the unit-test matrix to `macos-15-intel` + `macos-15`, and the wheel builds to `macos-15-intel`, `macos-15`, and `windows-2025`, as in #62774 on `main`. A follow-up extends the same bump to the separate `python-dev` job matrix, which had also been left on `macOS-13` / `macOS-14`.
  - commit [`5a9ea0b`](https://github.com/ghackebeil/pandas/commit/5a9ea0bfb632ffe819b5ccf1395ee7abd1073c71) (main unit-test + wheels matrices)
  - commit [`71b6358`](https://github.com/ghackebeil/pandas/commit/71b6358509a6e1f0b96fa84a68b26f942df2bc10) (python-dev matrix)
- **Skip `test_gcs.py` collection on Windows + Python 3.9 (SSL trust-store bug)** — the GitHub `windows-latest` (= `windows-2025`) trust store contains a cert with malformed ASN.1 data. Python 3.9's `ssl.create_default_context()` raises `ssl.SSLError: [ASN1: NOT_ENOUGH_DATA]` while iterating the store; Python 3.10+ silently skips bad certs. The error fires during pytest **collection**: `td.skip_if_installed("gcsfs")` at module level in `test_gcs.py` triggers the chain `gcsfs` → `aiohttp` → `ssl.create_default_context()` → SSLError, so the whole file fails to collect. `main` no longer supports 3.9, so there is no upstream fix to mirror. Attempted mitigations: first commit `4cf1d35` pinned the Windows row of the unit-test matrix from `windows-latest` to `windows-2022`, on the hypothesis that an older Windows image had a different trust store — but `windows-2022` has the same offending cert, so the SSL error reproduced verbatim. The actual fix in commit `772198d` adds a module-level `pytest.skip(allow_module_level=True)` guarded by `sys.platform == "win32" and sys.version_info < (3, 10)` at the top of `test_gcs.py` (no fallback "try gcsfs" — the import itself is what fails), and reverts the `windows-2022` pin since it served no purpose. The `python-dev` (Python 3.14) matrix and the rest of the Windows row are unaffected.
  - commit [`4cf1d35`](https://github.com/ghackebeil/pandas/commit/4cf1d3559b5234205113e9cee76dd2d955eae352) (initial `windows-2022` pin attempt — did not fix the bug)
  - commit [`772198d`](https://github.com/ghackebeil/pandas/commit/772198d265ff1781a9e80099042221a0be819708) (module-level skip in `test_gcs.py` + revert the pin)
- **Cap `pytest` to `<9.1` across CI / dev environments** — pytest 9.1 (released 2026-06-13) made duplicate parametrization of an already-parametrized fixture an error rather than a warning, breaking collection of 4 tests (`test_new_axis`, `test_intersection`, `test_replace_series_datetime_tz`, `test_to_html`). This first hit the pip-based `Linux-32-bit` job; once conda-forge also promoted 9.1, the conda-based jobs (e.g. `Copy-on-Write 3.10`) broke too. Cap to `<9.1` in the pip install lines in `unit-tests.yml` (mirroring #65883 on `main`) and additionally in the conda env yamls (`ci/deps/actions-*.yaml` except the min-versions file), `environment.yml`, and `requirements-dev.txt`. The min-versions yaml and `pyproject.toml` are left at `pytest>=7.3.2` because the `validate-min-versions-in-sync` hook strictly compares the pytest spec across them and `_optional.py` (it scans for the literal `- pytest>=` substring and does a `split(">=")` on the toml spec).
  - commit [`cd3f93b`](https://github.com/ghackebeil/pandas/commit/cd3f93bb730f25ae33f94716bd2866dfbdfa453b) (pip-based jobs in `unit-tests.yml`)
  - commit [`fd10117`](https://github.com/ghackebeil/pandas/commit/fd10117a7d612e956316525f43a6cb6df8ad02e8) (conda env yamls + `environment.yml` + `requirements-dev.txt`)
- **Cap `matplotlib` to `<3.11` in CI / dev environments** — matplotlib 3.11.0 (released a few days ago) deprecated the `locs` attribute and changed color-comparison semantics, causing ~200 plotting tests to fail across the unit-test matrix (`test_time_formatter` in `test_converter.py`, `test_default_colors_named_undefined_prop_cycle` in `test_style.py`, `test_df_legend_labels_time_series` in `test_frame_legend.py`, and others). Upstream #65742 covers part of this on `main`, but only touches `test_style.py` / `test_series.py` / `test_boxplot_method.py` and doesn't fix `test_converter.py` or `test_frame_legend.py`. pandas 2.3.x does not target matplotlib 3.11; cap `<3.11` in the conda env yamls (`ci/deps/actions-*.yaml`), `environment.yml`, and `requirements-dev.txt`. The pip install extras in `pyproject.toml` are left as-is because the `validate-min-versions-in-sync` hook only tolerates a bare `>=` there.
  - commit [`0be3de2`](https://github.com/ghackebeil/pandas/commit/0be3de25c18bca235f0a4f9527ccb4f270d04f9a)

### Unit-test matrix
- **`test_list_getitem_slice_invalid`** — pyarrow >= 22 changed the `ArrowInvalid` message for a zero slice step. Assert only the exception type via `tm.external_error_raised(pa.ArrowInvalid)`, as in #64057 on `main`. The `pa_version_under11p0` branch is kept (unlike #64057) since `2.3.x` still supports `pyarrow>=10.0.1`.
  - commit [`82ec040`](https://github.com/ghackebeil/pandas/commit/82ec040ed381d8066a4a0869b5c9b94865736982)
- **`test_dataframe_to_sql_empty[postgresql_adbc_conn]`** — the unconditional xfail `XPASS(strict)`s now that the ADBC postgres driver is `>= 1.2`. Guard the xfail by driver version (`< 1.11`); matches the `3.0.x` fix #65261 (the same guard is on `main`, landed via #65196).
  - commit [`9d590f0`](https://github.com/ghackebeil/pandas/commit/9d590f03b90a2d961275bffd6b4a0e05615e7c22)
- **`test_np_fix`** — under Copy-on-Write this test is numpy-dependent: it raises `ValueError: putmask: output array is read-only` on some numpy versions and passes on others, so a strict CoW xfail either fails or `XPASS(strict)`es depending on the job. Make the CoW xfail **non-strict** so it's green either way. (On `main` the test/decorator was dropped once CoW became the default in 3.0; `2.3.x` keeps the test because CoW is opt-in here.)
  - commit [`e097b40`](https://github.com/ghackebeil/pandas/commit/e097b40736f28b79fedc2bf8378419bd13bc7242)
- **Windows timestamp-with-tz pyarrow tests** (`test_from_sequence_of_strings_pa_array[…tz…]`, `test_arrow_timestamp_resample`, `test_interchange_from_non_pandas_tz_aware`) — these xfail on Windows expecting a "tzdata not found" `pa.ArrowInvalid`, but pyarrow `>= 22` bundles tzdata, so they `XPASS(strict)`. Guard each with `pa_version_under22p0`, as in #63905 on `main`; this adds `pa_version_under22p0` to `pandas.compat`.
  - commit [`e980e8b`](https://github.com/ghackebeil/pandas/commit/e980e8bff0bbced33cf9b8bf266b3e22142bbfe6)
- **`test_no_track_times`** — `AssertionError`: with HDF5 `>= 2`, `track_times=False` produces non-deterministic files, so the two checksums differ. Add the version-guarded `xfail(Version(tables.hdf5_version) >= Version("2"))`, as in #64829 on `main`.
  - commit [`bc162a5`](https://github.com/ghackebeil/pandas/commit/bc162a5c2e0f1f21a3713ce64327d0fae5acd125)

### pre-commit.ci
- **pyupgrade** crashed under pre-commit.ci's Python 3.14 (`tokenize.cookie_re` became a bytes pattern). Pin the hook's `language_version` to `python3.13`. Bumping pyupgrade (as `main` did) isn't viable here: newer versions rewrite annotations to single-arg `Generator[...]`, which the pinned `mypy 1.8.0` can't parse.
  - commit [`cb6348f`](https://github.com/ghackebeil/pandas/commit/cb6348fb962a5259f896c1fa1a57386c80bf0d0f)
- **validate-min-versions-in-sync** — realign `ci/deps/actions-311-downstream_compat.yaml` `s3fs`/`scipy` floors to the minimums declared in `pandas/compat/_optional.py` (the script's source of truth).
  - commit [`26ab7e5`](https://github.com/ghackebeil/pandas/commit/26ab7e59ac0c399acbca46428703fc7e2d58e760)

### Code Checks
- **`docstrings` (EX03)** — fix `E121` (3→4-space continuation indent) in the `DatetimeArray` example.
  - commit [`baafa72`](https://github.com/ghackebeil/pandas/commit/baafa7274bbc05b625f93ce0535b5e496f55c9b9)
- **`mypy` / `mypy (stubtest)` / `pyright reportGeneralTypeIssues`** — pyarrow 24 ships `py.typed` but its dynamically generated `pyarrow.compute` functions aren't statically declared, breaking the pinned `mypy 1.8.0` / `pyright 1.1.339`. Treat `pyarrow.*` as untyped for mypy (`follow_imports = "skip"`); add `_arrow_string_mixins.py`, `arrow/accessors.py`, and `io/parquet.py` to the pyright `reportGeneralTypeIssues` exclude; and `# type: ignore[assignment]` the `pa = None` fallback in `test_get_dummies.py`. (Upstream instead bumped mypy/pyright, which isn't viable on `2.3.x`'s pinned toolchain.)
  - commit [`a940a35`](https://github.com/ghackebeil/pandas/commit/a940a3596133ede38e6f5b66ce9a892d27f884ba)

### Doc Build
- **`io.rst`** — an executed `read_xml` example fetched `s3://pmc-oa-opendata/.../PMC1236943.xml`, now removed, raising `FileNotFoundError` (surfaced only as the opaque "Unexpected exception in io.rst" in the parallel build). Make it a static `code-block`, as in #56762 on `main`.
  - commit [`31d250f`](https://github.com/ghackebeil/pandas/commit/31d250feb46a5f9f5affb04e866174d928bfc566)

No whatsnew entry (CI/test-only changes).

**This pull request was generated with AI assistance (in case that was not obvious).**

title: BUG: Clarify Series ndarray subclass assertion message
body:
closes #65770

Clarifies the `assert_series_equal` failure message for Series backed by different `ndarray` subclasses. The assertion still raises for value-array class mismatches, but now labels that mismatch as `Series values` instead of implying the Series class itself differs.

- [x] closes #65770 (Replace xxxx with the GitHub issue number)

title: BUG: escape SQL identifiers in ADBCDatabase to prevent injection (GH#65065)
body:
Closes #65065

## Problem
`ADBCDatabase` interpolated table and schema names directly into SQL 
f-strings in three methods without quoting, causing failures for any 
identifier containing spaces, reserved words, or special characters:

- `read_table`: `SELECT * FROM {table_name}`
- `to_sql`: `DROP TABLE {table_name}` (if_exists='replace' path)  
- `delete_rows`: `DELETE FROM {table_name}`

## Fix
Add `_get_valid_adbc_name()` module-level helper function that applies 
ANSI SQL double-quote escaping, mirroring the existing 
`_get_valid_sqlite_name()` pattern. Apply it to all three vulnerable 
call sites.

The `adbc_ingest()` call in `to_sql` is unaffected — it accepts name 
and schema as separate parameters handled internally by the ADBC driver.

## Tests
Added `test_adbc_identifier_quoting` covering all three code paths 
using a table name with a space (`"my table"`).

Note: similar fix attempted in #65066 which has gone stale.

title: DOC: Fix malformed type for read_csv/read_table quoting parameter
body:
- [x] closes #65813
- [x] All code checks passed (`ruff check`, line length within 88).

## Problem

In the `read_csv` and `read_table` docstrings, the `quoting` parameter's type spec was wrapped across two physical lines:

```
quoting : {0 or csv.QUOTE_MINIMAL, 1 or csv.QUOTE_ALL,
    2 or csv.QUOTE_NONNUMERIC, 3 or csv.QUOTE_NONE}, default csv.QUOTE_MINIMAL
    Control field quoting behavior per ``csv.QUOTE_*`` constants. ...
```

numpydoc only treats the **first** line after `name :` as the type, so the overflow (`2 or csv.QUOTE_NONNUMERIC, ...`) was parsed as the start of the *description*. The type therefore bled into the description in the rendered docs (see the issue for the rendered output).

## Fix

The full enumeration cannot fit on a single line within the 88-char limit, so the type is written in a compact `{0, 1, 2, 3} or csv.QUOTE_* constant` form and the explicit value/constant mapping is moved into the description, where it renders correctly:

```
quoting : {0, 1, 2, 3} or csv.QUOTE_* constant, default csv.QUOTE_MINIMAL
    Control field quoting behavior per ``csv.QUOTE_*`` constants:
    ``0`` or ``csv.QUOTE_MINIMAL``, ``1`` or ``csv.QUOTE_ALL``,
    ``2`` or ``csv.QUOTE_NONNUMERIC``, ``3`` or ``csv.QUOTE_NONE``.
    Default is ``csv.QUOTE_MINIMAL`` (i.e., 0), which implies that only
    fields containing special characters are quoted (e.g., characters
    defined in ``quotechar``, ``delimiter``, or ``lineterminator``).
```

The same fix is applied to both `read_csv` and `read_table` (which share this parameter documentation). I also balanced the trailing parenthesis in the description, which was previously left unclosed.

I verified with numpydoc's `NumpyDocString` parser that the type and description now parse into separate fields (no bleed), and that all changed lines are ≤ 88 characters. No whatsnew note is added, per the contributing guide's guidance for documentation-only changes.

title: DataFrame.to_string gained an `ending_header` keyword argument (GH#32296)
body:
Closes #32296

### Description
This PR adds a new keyword argument `ending_header` to `DataFrame.to_string()`. When set to `True`, the column headers (the same header shown at the top) are repeated as a footer after the last row of data.

This is particularly useful for wide or tall DataFrames where the original header has scrolled off the screen – users can see the column names again at the bottom without having to scroll back up.

### Changes
- Added `ending_header: bool = False` to `DataFrame.to_string()` signature, overloads, and docstring.
- Propagated the flag through `DataFrameRenderer.to_string()` and `StringFormatter`.
- Implemented logic in `StringFormatter` to append the header row(s) at the end when `ending_header=True` and the DataFrame is non‑empty and header is enabled.
- The footer uses the same column widths and formatting as the top header, including MultiIndex columns and index name rows.
- Updated documentation (whatsnew v3.1.0).
- Added comprehensive tests for various scenarios (basic, MultiIndex, empty DataFrame, truncated output, `header=False`, `show_dimensions`, custom header aliases, single row/column, etc.).

### Usage Example
```python
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame(np.random.random((4,3)), columns=['a','b','c'])
print(df.to_string(ending_header=True))
```
Output:
```
          a         b         c
0  0.151196  0.933293  0.319235
1  0.501800  0.745816  0.734992
2  0.935173  0.140886  0.654070
3  0.803266  0.944231  0.379065
          a         b         c
```

title: BUG: to_parquet (pyarrow) opens local path twice
body:

For a local filesystem path, the pyarrow engine resolved the path through `get_handle` in `_get_path_or_handle` and then handed the string to pyarrow, which opened the same path a second time through its own C++ I/O. The redundant open wasted a syscall on POSIX and, on filesystems that finalize a file's contents on close, let the empty pandas-side descriptor close last and truncate pyarrow's output to 0 bytes (silent data loss).

This skips `get_handle` for local paths and passes the string straight to pyarrow, reproducing the `~` expansion and parent-directory check that `get_handle` previously performed. Non-fsspec URLs (e.g. http/https) still route through `get_handle`, since pyarrow cannot fetch those.

title: BUG: to_parquet (pyarrow engine) opens the local file path twice

labels.name: Needs Triage
labels.description: Issue that has not been reviewed by a pandas team member

body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import builtins
import os

import pandas as pd

# Spy on Python-level opens of the destination path.
target = "test.parquet"
opens = []
real_open = builtins.open

def spy_open(file, *args, **kwargs):
    if os.path.abspath(os.fspath(file)) == os.path.abspath(target):
        opens.append(args)
    return real_open(file, *args, **kwargs)

builtins.open = spy_open
try:
    pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3]}).to_parquet(target, engine="pyarrow")
finally:
    builtins.open = real_open

print(f"pandas opened the destination {len(opens)} time(s) at the Python level")

# Observed: 1  -> pandas opens the file itself via get_handle...
# ...but pyarrow ALSO opens the same path through its C++ layer and does the
# actual writing, so the path is opened twice per to_parquet call.

# On Linux this is also visible at the syscall level:
# strace -f -e trace=openat python -c \
#  "import pandas as pd; pd.DataFrame({'a':[1]}).to_parquet('x.parquet')" 2>&1 \
#  | grep -c 'x.parquet'
# two openat() calls for the same path
```

### Issue Description

For a local filesystem path, `to_parquet` with the pyarrow engine resolves the path through `pandas.io.common.get_handle` inside `_get_path_or_handle`, then unwraps the handle's .name back to a string and hands that string to pyarrow. pyarrow then opens  the same path a second time through its own (memory-mapped, multithreaded) C++ I/O layer, which is where the read/write actually happens. So every local-path call opens the destination/source twice.

Consequences:
- On POSIX: a wasted `open()`/`close()` syscall pair on every call (minor, but pointless).
- On filesystems that finalize a file's contents when the descriptor is closed (e.g. certain write-once / object-store backed filesystems): the empty pandas-side descriptor is closed after pyarrow has written and closed its own, so the empty one wins and the file is silently truncated to 0 bytes - data loss with no error raised.

### Expected Behavior

A local path should be opened exactly once. pandas should hand the string path directly to pyarrow (which opens it itself), without first opening it via `get_handle`. The repro above should print 0 Python-level opens of the destination, and strace should show a single `openat()` for the path.

(Non-fsspec URLs such as http(s):// still need `get_handle`, since pyarrow can't fetch those - only genuine local paths should skip it.)

body:

- [x] I have reviewed and followed all the contribution guidelines
- [x] If I used AI to develop this pull request, I prompted it to follow `AGENTS.md`.

## Description

This PR enhances [`DataFrame.set_axis`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.set_axis.html) and [`Series.set_axis`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.Series.set_axis.html) in two ways,
and fixes a docstring placement issue.

### 1. Callable support for `labels`

`labels` can now be a callable. As discussed in #61493, this was a missing feature in this method and other related methods. The callable receives the **full current axis
`Index`** (not individual labels) and must return the new labels. This is the
key distinction from `.rename`, which calls a function element-wise and
therefore cannot be used to cases that the entire `index`/`column` is needed, such as flatten a `MultiIndex` in a chain:

```python
# Flatten MultiIndex columns
(
    pd.DataFrame({("A", 1): range(3), ("B", 2): range(10, 13)})
    .set_axis(lambda cols: ["_".join(map(str, t)) for t in cols], axis=1)
)
```

### 2. `index=` and `columns=` keyword arguments

`index=` and `columns=` are now accepted as alternatives to `(labels, axis=)`,
consistent with `DataFrame.rename`'s calling convention:

```python
df.set_axis(columns=["X", "Y"])                        # equivalent to axis=1
df.set_axis(columns=lambda cols: cols.str.lower())     # callable + keyword
df.set_axis(index=lambda idx: idx + 1)                 # callable on row index
```

Both additions can be combined. Mutually exclusive combinations raise
`TypeError` with a clear message.

### 3. Docstring fix in `Series.set_axis`

The `.. deprecated:: 3.0.0` notice for the `copy` keyword was incorrectly
placed at the top of the docstring body (before the `Parameters` section)
rather than nested under the `copy` parameter description. This is corrected
to match the convention used in all other pandas methods.

## Motivation

Chained pandas processing where the axis labels are dynamic or unknown
upfront requires a verbose `.pipe(lambda df: df.set_axis(..., axis=1))`
workaround today. This change eliminates that workaround while keeping
the API consistent with existing methods (`rename`, `rename_axis`).

body:
### Pandas version checks

### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

names = ['alice', 'bob', 'charle']

bananas = pd.Series([10, 3, 9], index=names, dtype="UInt8")
oranges = pd.Series([3, 11, 6], index=names, dtype="UInt8")
fruits_jan = pd.DataFrame({'bananas': bananas, 'orange': oranges})

bananas = pd.Series([6, 1], index=names[:-1], dtype="UInt8")
apples  = pd.Series([8, 5], index=names[1:],  dtype="UInt8")
fruits_feb = pd.DataFrame({'bananas': bananas, 'apples': apples})

df = fruits_jan.add(fruits_feb, fill_value=0)
print(df.dtypes)


  Actual output:
  apples     Float64
  bananas      UInt8
  orange     Float64
  dtype: object

  Expected output:
  apples     UInt8
  bananas    UInt8
  orange     UInt8
  dtype: object
```

### Issue Description

  Issue Description

  When two DataFrames with nullable integer dtypes and non-overlapping columns are combined using `DataFrame.add` with a `fill_value`, columns that are absent from one of the DataFrames are silently
  promoted from their original nullable integer dtype (e.g. `UInt8`) to `Float64` in the result. Only columns present in
  both DataFrames retain their dtype.

  This is inconsistent with the equivalent Series operation, which correctly preserves the nullable integer dtype:
```
  s1 = pd.Series([10, 20, 30], index=list("abc"), dtype="UInt16")
  s2 = pd.Series([12, 22, 32], index=list("acd"), dtype="UInt16")
  print((s1 + s2).dtype)  # UInt16 — dtype preserved
```


### Expected Behavior

The original extended dtype is preserved

When converting a NumPy masked array, masked elements should be preserved as pandas missing values (`<NA>`), and conversion behavior should remain consistent.

title: BUG: apply into to nested mappings in to_dict(orient=index)
body:
Fixes GH#65778

## Summary

`DataFrame.to_dict(orient='index', into=...)` did not apply the
`into` parameter to the nested per-row mappings. The outer result
correctly used the requested mapping type, but each inner per-row dict
was a plain `dict`, ignoring `into` entirely.

This was inconsistent with `orient='records'`, which already applies
`into` to each per-row mapping.

## Reproducer

```python
import pandas as pd

class MyDict(dict):
    pass

df = pd.DataFrame({'A': [1, 2], 'B': ['x', 'y']})
out = df.to_dict(orient='index', into=MyDict)

type(out)        # MyDict  (correct)
type(out[0])     # dict    # BUG: should be MyDict
```

## Expected

The inner per-row mapping should also respect `into`, e.g.
`type(out[0]) is MyDict`.

## Fix

Wrap the inner mapping construction in `into_c(...)` in all three
sub-branches of the `orient == 'index'` branch in
`pandas/core/methods/to_dict.py`:

- all-object columns
- mixed / extension columns
- all-non-object columns

This mirrors the existing `orient == 'records'` pattern.

## Tests

`pandas/tests/frame/methods/test_to_dict.py` should be extended with
new regression cases for GH#65778. Suggested additions are documented
alongside the patch in the verification harness (see
`to_dict_test/test_to_dict_patch_addition.py` for the exact
parameterised test cases).

A self-contained 30-test verification harness is provided in
`to_dict_test/` that exercises the patched `to_dict.py` in
isolation (without requiring the full pandas build). The harness was
also run against the original unpatched code, where 14 of the 30 tests
fail — precisely the `orient='index'`-related ones — confirming the
tests correctly capture the bug.

Fixes #65778

When using DataFrame.to_dict(orient="index", into=...), the into parameter was only applied to the outer mapping. Inner row mappings were always plain dict.

This fix replaces all three dict() calls in the orient=="index" branch with into_c(), ensuring both outer and nested mappings use the specified mapping constructor.

title: BUG: fixed-format HDFStore storer shape reports phantom row for empty objects
body:
closes #37235

`HDFStore.get_storer(...).shape` returned `(1, N)` for a fixed-format `Series` or `DataFrame` stored with zero rows, instead of `(0, N)`.

Empty arrays are written *un-transposed* as a `(1,)*ndim` sentinel placeholder (see `write_array_empty`), with the true shape stashed in the `_v_attrs.shape` attribute — while non-empty arrays are stored transposed with their real shape on disk. `SeriesFixed.shape` and `BlockManagerFixed.shape` read the on-disk sentinel and never consulted `_v_attrs.shape`, so they reported the phantom length-1 axis.

Both properties now detect the empty sentinel (the same `_v_attrs.shape` marker `read_array`/`read_index_node` already rely on) and use the true stored shape, reversing it in the block-manager case to match the transposed layout used for non-empty blocks.

title: BUG: HDFStore.select where query on categorical column matched NaN rows (GH-22977)
body:
closes #22977

A `where` query on a categorical data column for a value that is **not one of the categories** was translated to the code `-1` — which is also the sentinel code pandas uses for missing (`NaN`) values. As a result the query incorrectly matched `NaN` rows the user never requested (and, symmetrically, dropped them from `!=` queries).

```python
df = pd.DataFrame({"col": pd.Categorical(["a", "b", np.nan, "a"])})
df.to_hdf(path, key="df", format="table", data_columns=["col"])

pd.read_hdf(path, "df", where='col == "z"')   # "z" not a category
# before: returns the NaN row
# after:  empty, matching `df[df["col"] == "z"]`
```

The exact example in the issue was already addressed by GH-57608 / GH-39420; this fixes the remaining manifestation when the categorical column contains missing values. A non-category value is now mapped to a sentinel distinct from `-1`, so such a query matches no rows for `==`/`in` and all rows for `!=`, matching in-memory `Categorical` comparison semantics (`ops.invalid_comparison`).

title: BUG: to_hdf PerformanceWarning names columns that are not mixed (GH-28460)

labels.name: Warnings
labels.description: Warnings that appear or should be added to pandas

body:
closes #28460

When `DataFrame.to_hdf` writes the fixed format, same-dtype columns are consolidated into a single block. For object blocks the `PerformanceWarning` inferred the dtype of the *whole* block, so if any column was non-string the block inferred as `mixed` and **every** column in the block was listed in the message — including pure-string columns that, written on their own, take the `inferred_type == "string"` branch and emit no warning.

This infers per column on the warning path and lists only the columns that are not plain strings (using `lib.is_string_array` rather than `lib.infer_dtype`).

Note the pandas-3.0 string dtype default already mitigates the issue's canonical example — a plain string column now gets its own `str`-dtype block and the dedicated VLArray write path, so it is never falsely flagged. The bug remains reachable whenever multiple genuine object columns share a block (forced `astype(object)`, or `future.infer_string=False`), and becomes obsolete once object string columns are gone (GH-8640).

title: BUG: clearer error for over-complex HDFStore.select where (GH-39752)

A `where` expression with more than 31 OR-ed conditions over indexed columns overflows numexpr's input limit inside PyTables' indexed-query path (`_table__where_indexed` combines one boolean array per OR-ed term in a single `numexpr.evaluate` call). title: BUG: clear error for arithmetic HDFStore.select where-clauses
body:
closes #41100

Arithmetic expressions in an `HDFStore.select` `where` clause (e.g. `"(A % 3) == 0"`) previously raised an opaque PyTables `TypeError`. During query pruning the comparison was silently dropped, leaving a non-boolean `(A % 3)` that PyTables then rejected with `condition `(A % 3)` does not have a boolean type`.

PyTables support is in maintenance mode, so rather than grow the query grammar to evaluate arithmetic, this raises an informative `NotImplementedError` pointing to a working alternative:

```python
NotImplementedError: arithmetic operations are not supported inside an HDFStore
'where' filter; instead store a precomputed column as a data_column and query
that, or read the data and apply the filter in pandas (e.g. df[df['A'] % 3 == 0]).
```

### Notes
- The guard sits at the top of `BinOp.prune` and keys off `ARITH_OPS_SYMS`. This is precise: comparison/boolean operators become `Condition`/`Filter`/`Joint` ops, so arithmetic is the only operator class reaching that point. It catches both nested (`(A % 3) == 0`) and bare (`A + 1`) forms.
- On `main` no arithmetic `where` clause works today — every form already errors opaquely — so this strictly improves the failure mode without changing anything that currently functions.

title: WARN: read_hdf nested OR query may hit PyTables index bug (GH#50598)

labels.name: Warnings
labels.description: Warnings that appear or should be added to pandas

body:
closes #50598

## Problem

Reading an HDF5 table with a nested `where` of the form `"(A & B) | (C & D)"` over indexed columns can silently return **incorrect** results (dropping matching rows), and the result depends on the physical row order (GH-50598).

I root-caused this to PyTables, not pandas:
- pandas generates a correct condition string and just passes it to `table.read_where()` (the post-read filter is `None`).
- Calling `read_where()` directly with that condition (no pandas in the loop) reproduces the wrong row count; brute-force row iteration over the same condition gives the correct count.
- Removing the column indexes makes `read_where()` correct again.

The bug fires only when **all** of these hold:
1. the `(A & B) | (C & D)` shape — an `OR` whose operands are themselves multi-column `AND`s;
2. the queried columns are indexed (pandas indexes `data_columns` by default);
3. the table spans more than one chunk (`chunkshape[0] < nrows`) — single-chunk tables are always correct.

This is also why the reporter couldn't build a synthetic repro: they were missing condition 3.

## This PR

The fix belongs upstream, so this just detects that exact query shape at read time and emits a `UserWarning` pointing at the workarounds (write with `index=False`, or run the `OR` branches as separate queries and `concat`). The predicate is intentionally precise, so it stays silent on safe queries: single `AND`, single-column `OR`, `OR` of two single-column conditions, single-chunk tables, and `index=False`.

It is a warning, not a hard raise: the structural pattern is necessary but not sufficient (whether results are actually wrong is data-dependent), so raising would break correct queries.

title: BUG: clearer error for HDFStore data column named 'index' (GH-41437)
body:

Writing a `DataFrame` with `format='table'` and a column named `'index'` as a `data_columns` entry (including `data_columns=True`) raised an opaque `IndexError: tuple index out of range` from deep inside `write_data`.

The implicit row index is stored under the reserved cname `'index'`, so a data column of the same name collides with it in the table description dict. The duplicate key silently dropped a column, leaving `self.dtype.names` one entry short and overrunning during the reshape.

This is the single-index analogue of GH-6208 (a `MultiIndex` level named `'index'`), which already raises a clear error. This PR raises a parallel `ValueError` instead:

```
cannot use a column named 'index' as a data_column; 'index' is reserved for the implicit row index
```

A plain (non-data) column named `'index'` is unaffected and still round-trips.

title: BUG: read_hdf fails on old files with freq=None on non-datetimelike indexes (GH-33186)
body:
closes #33186

Old pandas (``<=0.15.x``) wrote a ``freq=None`` attr on *every* index node of a fixed-format frame, including non-datetimelike ones (integer/string indexes). On read, ``GenericFixed._get_index_factory`` treated the mere presence of the ``freq`` attr as a signal to route a plain ``Index`` through the ``TimedeltaIndex`` factory, which fails — historically with ``TypeError: Unexpected keyword arguments {'freq'}`` and currently with ``ValueError: Could not convert 'x' to NumPy timedelta``.

The fix only treats a **non-None** ``freq`` as meaningful, so a genuine ``TimedeltaIndex`` (which stores a real ``freq``) still round-trips while these legacy indexes read back as their original integer/string ``Index``.

Verified against the actual ``beads1.h5`` attached to GH-33186 (a real pandas 0.15.2 file): it now reads back to the expected ``(66, 8)`` frame.

`GenericFixed.write_array` (the `format="fixed"` writer) stores `object`-dtype columns — the common case for string data — in a PyTables `VLArray`. That `create_vlarray` call was the only array-creation path in the method that did not pass `filters=self._filters`. Because the HDF5 file is opened without file-level filters, a `VLArray` created with no `filters` argument inherits `complevel=0`, so **string columns were never compressed in fixed format**, regardless of the `complib`/`complevel` passed to `to_hdf`. This is what produced the dramatic file-size blow-up in GH-45286 (reporter saw ~65x on string-heavy data).

The fix passes the store's filters through, matching the sibling `BaseStringArray` and numeric `carray` paths just above/below it.

On a synthetic frame shaped like the reporter's data (object-dtype string columns), saving per-key dropped the file from **114 MB → 10.5 MB**.

The existing `test_complibs` only exercised numeric data (`np.ones`), so the `VLArray` path was never covered — hence the gap. The new `test_complib_object_dtype_compressed` writes an `object`-dtype column and asserts the resulting `VLArray` node carries the requested filter; it fails on `main` and passes with this change.

Note: with pandas 3.0's default `str` dtype, `read_csv`-loaded strings now take the already-filtered `BaseStringArray` path, so today this only affects genuine `object`-dtype columns. The new test forces `object` dtype to lock in the fix.

title: BUG: HDFStore.select raises clear error for columns-in-where with iterator/chunksize (GH-12953)
body:
closes #12953

Previously ``store.select(key, where="columns=['A']", chunksize=...)`` (or ``iterator=True``) raised a cryptic ``KeyError: 'column [columns] not found in the table'``.

A column selection embedded in the ``where`` expression is a column *projection*, not a row filter, so it cannot be applied via the row coordinates used for chunked/iterated reads — only via the ``columns`` argument (which already works with iteration). The full, non-iterator read of ``where="columns=[...]"`` is unaffected.

`HDFStore.select` now raises an informative ``NotImplementedError`` for this combination, pointing users to the equivalent ``columns`` argument:

```
selecting columns through the 'where' expression (e.g. "columns=['A']") is not
supported with 'iterator' or 'chunksize'; use the 'columns' argument instead
```

The check fires eagerly when ``select(...)`` is called (not mid-iteration) and covers pure column selections, negation (``columns!=[...]``), and combined ``row-condition & columns=[...]`` expressions — each of which previously surfaced the same ``KeyError``.

title: BUG: read_hdf of categorical column with a category equal to nan_rep

labels.name: Missing-data
labels.description: np.nan, pd.NaT, pd.NA, dropna, isnull, interpolate

body:
closes #21741

When a `format="table"` HDF5 file is read back, a categorical column's categories are decoded using `nan_rep` (default `"nan"`). If `"nan"` was a genuine category string, it becomes an actual `NaN` category that must be stripped. The stripping code subtracted a per-*category* cumsum from the per-*row* `codes` array:

```python
codes[codes != -1] -= mask.astype(int).cumsum()._values
```

These two arrays only line up by accident, so reading raised `ValueError: operands could not be broadcast together` whenever `#rows != #categories`, and silently mis-mapped codes when they happened to match. It also never mapped codes pointing at the dropped `NaN` category to `-1`.

Replaced with an explicit old→new code remap: surviving categories are renumbered to their compacted positions, and codes that pointed at the dropped `NaN` category map to `-1` (missing).

Note the `'nan'`-string → `NaN` conversion itself is the long-standing `nan_rep` collision (writing with a different `nan_rep` avoids it, see GH-9604); this PR only makes the read non-crashing and correct rather than changing that lossy write behavior.

title: BUG: HDFStore.remove with large "in" where clause deleted all rows (GH-17567)
body:
closes #17567

- [x] closes #17567
- [x] Tests added and passed
- [x] All code checks passed
- [x] Added an entry in the latest `doc/source/whatsnew/v3.1.0.rst` file

A `where` clause that selects on more than 31 values (e.g. `"index in [...]"`) is too large for numexpr, so it is realized as a **post-read filter** rather than a numexpr condition. `Selection.select_coords` ignored that filter and returned every row coordinate via `np.arange(start, stop)`. `HDFStore.select` masked this because `read_coordinates` re-applied the filter afterward, but `HDFStore.remove` (via `AppendableTable.delete`) used the raw coordinates — so it **deleted the entire table** instead of only the matching rows.

This moves the filter application into `select_coords` itself, so both `read_coordinates` and `delete` get the correct coordinates from a single code path.

There were previously no `remove`-with-`where` tests in the suite (every `.remove(...)` call removed a whole node), which is why this went unnoticed since GH-17567 was filed. Added a regression test parametrized over a small selector (≤ 31, numexpr-condition path) and a large one (> 31, filter path); it fails on the large case without the fix.

title: BUG: to_hdf to a key deletes nested keys stored beneath it (GH-17267)
body:
closes #17267

Writing a pandas object to an HDF5 key with `DataFrame.to_hdf` / `HDFStore.put` silently deleted any keys nested beneath that key:

```python
pd.Series(np.zeros(20)).to_hdf("t.h5", key="All/atest")   # -> ['/All/atest']
pd.Series(np.zeros(10)).to_hdf("t.h5", key="All")         # -> ['/All']   <- /All/atest gone
```

`HDFStore._identify_group` overwrote an existing key by calling `remove_node(group, recursive=True)`, which nukes the entire subtree — including child keys, which are separate pandas objects. This is distinct from the documented recursive behavior of `HDFStore.remove` / `del store[key]` (those still work as documented); a plain `put` clobbering a sibling key is an unintended data-loss path.

Since storers only ever write leaf nodes under their group (never child groups), any child *group* under a key is necessarily another key. The fix removes only the data nodes (and resets stale attributes) of the object stored at the target key when nested keys are present, leaving those keys intact. When there are no nested keys, the existing recursive-remove path is unchanged, so no orphan nodes are left behind on a normal overwrite.

Tested across fixed/table formats, repeated overwrites, and format/dtype changes of the parent key.

title: BUG: HDFStore.select bus error on strict-alignment platforms (GH-54396)
body:
closes #54396

PyTables stores HDF5 compound types **packed** (no inter-field padding). When a frame's index serializes to an odd-width leading field (e.g. a string `Index` → `S3`), the `float64` `values_block_*` field lands at an unaligned byte offset:

```
[('index', 'S3'), ('values_block_0', '<f8', (100,))]   # values_block_0 at byte offset 3
```

`DataCol.convert` extracted that field as a numpy **view** (no copy), so the unaligned buffer (`ALIGNED=False`, `ptr % 8 == 3`) propagated all the way into the result `DataFrame`'s block. A subsequent boolean `.loc` filter calls the Cython `take_2d` kernel, which does raw 8-byte `float64` loads via pointer arithmetic. On x86 those unaligned loads just work; on strict-alignment **32-bit ARM** (AArch32 `LDRD`/`VLDR.64`) they alignment-fault → **SIGBUS**, matching the odd addresses in the reporter's UBSAN trace. The sibling `IndexCol.convert` already copies, which is why only the data block crashed.

The fix realigns the extracted field with a copy, but only when it is actually unaligned. Int/Datetime-index tables put the float block at offset 8 (already aligned), so the common path is unchanged — the copy only fires for the rarer unaligned layouts.

The new regression test is platform-independent: it asserts the read-back block is aligned, which fails on `main` and passes here, so no ARM hardware is needed to guard against this.

title: BUG: to_dict(orient='index') ignores into for nested mappings
body:
Fixes #65778

`DataFrame.to_dict(orient="index", into=...)` applied the `into` mapping type to the outer mapping but built the nested per-row mappings with a plain `dict`. The `dict` and `records` orients already wrap their nested mappings with the standardized `into` type, so `orient="index"` was inconsistent and contradicted the `into` docstring, which says it applies to all Mappings in the return value.

This wraps the three nested-mapping constructions in the `orient="index"` branch with `into_c`, mirroring the `records` orient. The `tight` and `split` orients are unaffected since their nested structures are lists, not mappings.

Added a regression test parametrized over OrderedDict and defaultdict across the three dtype paths, plus a whatsnew entry.

title: BUG: `DataFrame.to_dict(orient="index", into=...)` does not apply `into` to nested mappings

labels.name: IO Data
labels.description: IO issues that don't fit into a more specific label

body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd


class MyDict(dict):
    pass


df = pd.DataFrame(
    {"A": [1, 2], 
    "B": ["x", "y"]}
)

out = df.to_dict("index", into=MyDict)

print(out)
print(type(out))
print(type(out[0]))

assert isinstance(out, MyDict)
assert isinstance(out[0], MyDict)  # fails
```

### Issue Description

Running the code above raises an `AssertionError` like below.

```python
{0: {'A': 1, 'B': 'x'}, 1: {'A': 2, 'B': 'y'}}
<class '__main__.MyDict'>
<class 'dict'>
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
AssertionError                            Traceback (most recent call last)
Cell In[19], line 22
     18 print(type(out))
     19 print(type(out[0]))
     20 
     21 assert isinstance(out, MyDict)
---> 22 assert isinstance(out[0], MyDict)  # fails

AssertionError:
```

This suggests `DataFrame.to_dict(..., into=...)` applying `into` only to the outer mapping when `orient="index"`.

In the example above, the outer returned object is `MyDict`, but each nested row mapping is a plain `dict`.

I checked whether this behavior is intended, but the docstrings of both functions
```python
pandas.core.frame.DataFrame.to_dict()
pandas.core.methods.to_dict.to_dict()
```

describe the result as `dict-like`, but do not clarify whether nested mappings should also respect `into`:
```
    Parameters
    ----------
    orient : str {'dict', 'list', 'series', 'split', 'tight', 'records', 'index'}
        Determines the type of the values of the dictionary.
    ...
    - 'index' : dict like {index -> {column -> value}}
```

I also inspected the `to_dict` implementation in `pandas.core.methods.to_dict`.
I believe this behavior comes from the following three return paths in the `elif orient == "index"` branch:
- plain dict is used directly:
```python
            return into_c(
                (t[0], dict(zip(df.columns, map(maybe_box_native, t[1:]), strict=True)))
                for t in df.itertuples(name=None)
            )
```
```python
            return into_c(
                (t[0], dict(zip(columns, t[1:], strict=True)))
                for t in df.itertuples(name=None)
            )
```
- a dict comprehension is used directly, bypassing `into_c` for the nested mapping:
```python
            return into_c(
                (
                    t[0],
                    {
                        column: maybe_box_native(v)
                        if i in object_dtype_indices_as_set
                        else v
                        for i, (column, v) in enumerate(
                            zip(columns, t[1:], strict=True)
                        )
                    },
                )
                for t in df.itertuples(name=None)
            )
```

This could be fixed by using the standardized mapping constructor `into_c` for the nested row mappings as well. For example, the dict-comprehension branch could be changed to:
```python
            return into_c(
                (
                    t[0],
                    into_c(
                        (
                            column,
                            maybe_box_native(v)
                            if i in object_dtype_indices_as_set
                            else v,
                        )
                        for i, (column, v) in enumerate(
                            zip(columns, t[1:], strict=True)
                        )
                    ),
                )
                for t in df.itertuples(name=None)
            )
```


With this change, the following code passes:
```python

class MyDict(dict):
    pass


df = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "A": [1, 2],
        "B": ["x", "y"],
    }
)


out = to_dict(df, "index", into=MyDict)


print(out)
print(type(out))
print(type(out[0]))

assert isinstance(out, MyDict)
assert isinstance(out[0], MyDict)  # success
```

```
{0: {'A': 1, 'B': 'x'}, 1: {'A': 2, 'B': 'y'}}
<class '__main__.MyDict'>
<class '__main__.MyDict'>
```

I would be happy to open a pull request for this.

### Expected Behavior

Expected behavior:
```python
result = df.to_dict(orient="index", into=MyDict)

type(result)
# <class '__main__.MyDict'>

type(result[0])
# <class '__main__.MyDict'>
```

In other words, the result should be equivalent to:
```
MyDict(
    {
        0: MyDict({"A": 1, "B": "x"}),
        1: MyDict({"A": 2, "B": "y"}),
    }
)
```

title: BUG: assert_series_equal ignores check_series_type=False for ndarray subclass-backed Series on exact comparison path  #65770

labels.name: AI Slop
labels.description: Suspected of being AI-generated, which is not welcome.

body:
Here you go:

---

Title

BUG: assert_series_equal fails with ndarray subclass when check_series_type=False

---

Description

Closes #65770

Problem

pd.testing.assert_series_equal raised an AssertionError when comparing two Series that had the same values, dtype, and index but one was backed by a plain np.ndarray and the other by an np.ndarray subclass, even when check_series_type=False was passed.

This happened because inside assert_numpy_array_equal, the function assert_class_equal was called unconditionally with no way for check_series_type=False to flow down and skip it.

The error message was also misleading. It said "Series classes are different" but was actually showing the backing array classes like ndarray vs OtherArray, not the Series classes.

```
Reproduction

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

class OtherArray(np.ndarray):
    pass

arr = np.array([1])
left = pd.Series(arr)
right = pd.Series(arr.view(OtherArray))

assert left.equals(right)
pd.testing.assert_series_equal(left, right, check_series_type=False)
```

What I Did To Fix It

1. Added a check_class parameter to assert_numpy_array_equal with default True for backward compatibility

2. Made assert_class_equal conditional on check_class inside assert_numpy_array_equal

3. Passed check_class=check_series_type when calling assert_numpy_array_equal inside assert_series_equal so the flag properly propagates down

4. Added check_series_type parameter to assert_frame_equal and passed it down to assert_series_equal so DataFrame column comparisons are also fixed

### Issue Description

`pd.testing.assert_series_equal` fails when comparing two equal `Series` objects if one is backed by a plain `np.ndarray` and the other is backed by an `np.ndarray` subclass, even when `check_series_type=False` is passed.

In the reproduction, you can observe that the two Series have the same dtype, values, index, and compare equal via `Series.equals`, but `assert_series_equal` still fails because it checks the concrete class of the internal backing arrays.

The error message is also misleading: it reports “Series classes are different”, but the classes shown are the backing array classes (`ndarray` vs `OtherArray`), not the `Series` classes.

title: BUG: Fix pivot_table margins dropping valid rows when aggfunc is a dict
body:
- [x] closes #65765
- [x] Tests added and passed
- [x] All code checks passed

**What happened:**
When `pivot_table` is called with `margins=True`, `dropna=True`, and a dictionary passed to `aggfunc` (e.g., `{'Salary': 'sum', 'Age': 'mean'}`), the internal `_add_margins` function was applying a blanket `data.dropna()` across all rows before calculating the margins. This caused valid data in one column to be dropped if a `NaN` existed in a completely different column for that row.

**The fix:**
I updated `_add_margins` in `pivot.py` to only apply the blanket `dropna` if `aggfunc` is *not* a dictionary (preserving the required behavior for `crosstab`). When `aggfunc` is a dictionary, it now passes the full DataFrame through, allowing the `.agg()` function to handle `NaN` values gracefully on a per-column basis.

title: PERF: read_csv faster for float columns
body:
**Stacked on GH-65350** (`perf-read_csv-end-offsets`), rebased onto its current tip — which now also threads the token length into *integer* parsing. Two commits ride on top of GH-65350 here: *"PERF: read_csv faster for float columns"* and a small *"CLN: review cleanups for read_csv token-length changes"*. This PR targets `main`, so the diff still shows GH-65350's content too; it collapses to just these two commits once GH-65350 merges. For review, read the float commit in isolation.

Threads the C tokenizer's known token length into the float converter so `precise_xstrtod` skips its per-field end-of-token scan on the `fast_float` fast path. The length comes from the `_token_len` helper GH-65350 adds (derived from adjacent `word_starts` entries), so there's no new data structure. The public `pd_parser` capsule `precise_xstrtod` keeps its signature — a thin wrapper forwards to a new `precise_xstrtod_with_end`.

## Bench

1M × 8 float columns, warm cache, best-of-15. A/B on the current branch tip: the baseline is the same build with the float threading reverted (the converter scans for each token's end, as before this PR), so the two differ only by this optimization. Best / median over 3 interleaved build-and-measure rounds:

| build | best | median |
|---|---:|---:|
| base (threading reverted) | 472.9 ms | 487.3 ms |
| this PR | 421.2 ms | 433.4 ms |

~11% faster (best and median). Int/string/mixed columns are unaffected (those paths are untouched).

title: DOC: fix misleading deprecated DataFrameXchg type in from_dataframe docstring (#63111)
body:
- [x] closes #63111
- [ ] [Tests added and passed](https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/dev/development/contributing_codebase.html#writing-tests) if fixing a bug or adding a new feature
- [ ] All [code checks passed](https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/dev/development/contributing_codebase.html#pre-commit).
- [ ] Added [type annotations](https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/dev/development/contributing_codebase.html#type-hints) to new arguments/methods/functions.
- [ ] Added an entry in the latest `doc/whatsnew/vX.X.X.rst` file if fixing a bug or adding a new feature.

## Summary

Documentation-only change.

The `df` parameter of `from_dataframe` (`pandas/core/interchange/from_dataframe.py`) was documented solely as type `DataFrameXchg`, which refers to the now-deprecated dataframe interchange protocol. However, `from_dataframe` itself is not deprecated: it first checks for an `__arrow_c_stream__` method (routing through pyarrow) and only then falls back to `__dataframe__`. The documented type was therefore misleading, as reported in #63111.

This updates the `df` parameter's documented type so it reflects both accepted inputs:
- `ArrowStreamExportable` — objects supporting the Arrow PyCapsule Interface (an `__arrow_c_stream__` method)
- `DataFrameXchg` — objects supporting the legacy dataframe interchange protocol (a `__dataframe__` method)

This follows @MarcoGorelli's suggestion in the issue thread to update the type to use the `ArrowStreamExportable` hint from the [Arrow PyCapsule Interface typehints](https://arrow.apache.org/docs/format/CDataInterface/PyCapsuleInterface.html#protocol-typehints).

No code behavior changes, so no new tests or `whatsnew` entry are required.

title: DOC: Fix text visibility in dark mode for getting started data cards

labels.name: AI Slop
labels.description: Suspected of being AI-generated, which is not welcome.

body:
Addresses #65062.

The `.gs-data-title` and `.gs-data-list` elements in the getting started tutorials did not have an explicit text color set. In dark mode, the inherited text color from Bootstrap's card components remains dark, making the "Data used for this tutorial" text invisible against dark backgrounds.

This PR adds `color: var(--pst-color-text-base)` to both selectors, which follows the pydata-sphinx-theme convention and ensures text remains visible in both light and dark modes.

title: BUG: Fix core dump in fillna on ArrowDtype(pa.null())
body:
closes #65483

Fixes a core dump when calling `fillna` on `ArrowDtype(pa.null())` columns.

`fillna` ends up calling PyArrow's `fill_null` or `replace_with_mask` kernels, but both of those crash with a C++ assertion failure when given a `null` type array.

Since a null array can only ever contain nulls, replacing nulls with nulls just gives back the exact same array. I just added a quick early return in `_safe_fill_null` and `_replace_with_mask` to bypass the PyArrow bug entirely and avoid the crash.

title: STYLE: enforce "|".join([...]) for message-regex alternations in tests
body:
Human here: I think we should move from the old `msg = foo|bar` to the new `msg = "|".join(["foo", "bar"])`.  I've seen the old pattern can hide things like a trailing extra `|` which makes the regex useless.  The new one is also more conducive to adding comments about what cases need each pattern and trimming down cases to move toward more consistent messages.

-----

Adds a pre-commit check that flags a bare top-level `|` in `msg`/`match=` regexes in the test suite, nudging toward the more readable

```python
msg = "|".join(["first message", "second message"])
```

instead of `msg = "first message|second message"`. An alternation that is genuinely part of one message (e.g. `cannot (add|subtract)`) should be grouped rather than joined.

### The check
- `bare_pipe_alternation_in_message` in `scripts/validate_unwanted_patterns.py`, wired into `.pre-commit-config.yaml` (scoped to `pandas/tests/`).
- AST-based: only flags a **top-level, unescaped** `|`, so it ignores `(a|b)` groups, `[a|b]` character classes, and `\|`. f-strings are handled; `"|".join([...])` and `match=<name>` are not flagged.
- Covered by unit tests in `scripts/tests/test_validate_unwanted_patterns.py`.

### Cleanup
Converts the existing offenders so the suite passes under the new rule: genuine multi-message alternations to `"|".join([...])`, and inline alternations to grouped `(a|b)`.

title: PERF: restore to_datetime caching for duplicated input with an explicit format
body:
GH-65409 added an O(1) early-bail to `should_cache` that disabled caching whenever an explicit `format` was passed, on the premise that `array_strptime` is always fast enough that caching can't help.

That premise only holds for ISO-style formats. For slower strptime formats (e.g. `%d%b%y`, `%z` offsets, `%d-%m-%Y`) on highly-duplicated input, caching parses only the *unique* values and is a large win. Disabling it caused 5-15x slowdowns, surfaced by the asv perf tracker in [pandas-dev/asv-runner#137](https://github.com/pandas-dev/asv-runner/issues/137#issuecomment-4435676943):

| Benchmark | regressed | restored |
|---|---|---|
| `ToDatetimeFormat.time_exact` | 121 ms | 12 ms |
| `ToDatetimeFormat.time_no_exact` | 118 ms | 13 ms |
| `ToDatetimeFormat.time_same_offset` | 366 ms | 43 ms |
| `ToDatetimeFormat.time_different_offset_to_utc` | 353 ms | 25 ms |
| `ParseDateComparison.time_to_datetime_format_DD_MM_YYYY` | 6.1 ms | 1.1 ms |

This drops the `format` bail (and the now-unused `format` parameter on `should_cache`); format inputs again go through the normal duplication-based cache decision. The genuinely-safe O(1) bails from GH-65409 — numeric `unit` and already-datetime dtypes — are kept, since those are vectorized conversions where deduplicating can never help.

The one input the `format` bail helped (ISO + low cardinality) reverts to its small pre-existing overhead on a sub-2ms, non-tracked path; distinguishing fast-parse ISO from slow-parse formats was flagged as out of scope in GH-65380 and isn't worth re-introducing a 5-15x regression to chase.

Also moves the GH-65409 whatsnew note out of the frozen `v3.0.0` file (that PR is not in any released 3.0.x) and into `v3.1.0`, scoped to the cases that actually improve.

title: DEPR: deprecate DataFrame construction from ragged list of sequences
body:
Constructing a `DataFrame` from a list of sequences whose lengths don't match silently pads the shorter rows out to the longest with `NaN`:

```python
>>> pd.DataFrame([[1, 2], [3, 4, 5]])

0  1  2  NaN
1  3  4  5.0
```

This is surprising and rarely intentional. This PR deprecates it (emitting a `Pandas4Warning`) so that it can raise in a future version. The detection lives in `_list_to_arrays`, so it covers list-of-lists, list-of-tuples, and the generic-sequence fallback path. Equal-length input, list-of-`Series`, and list-of-`dict` construction are unaffected.

title: BUG: inplace where/mask corrupting multi-column 2D datetimelike blocks

labels.name: Indexing
labels.description: Related to indexing on series/frames, not to indexes themselves

labels.name: Regression
labels.description: Functionality that used to work in a prior pandas version

labels.name: Internals
labels.description: Related to non-user accessible pandas implementation

body:
Regression from GH-64620 (unreleased), so no whatsnew entry.

`EABackedBlock.putmask` reorients `mask` to the block's storage layout (`mask = mask.T`) but never did the same for `new`. On a multi-column 2D extension block (datetime64 / timedelta64 / datetime64tz / period), an inplace `where`/`mask` therefore filled masked cells from the wrong column:

```python
df = pd.DataFrame({"a": pd.date_range("2000-01-01", periods=3),
                   "b": pd.date_range("2010-01-01", periods=3)})
other = pd.DataFrame({"a": pd.date_range("2020-01-01", periods=3),
                      "b": pd.date_range("2030-01-01", periods=3)})
cond = pd.DataFrame({"a": [True, False, True], "b": [False, True, False]})

ref = df.where(cond, other)                          # correct (non-inplace)
d2 = df.copy(); d2.where(cond, other, inplace=True)
ref.equals(d2)        # False before this PR, True after
```

The fix transposes `new` alongside `mask`, mirroring the `value = value.T` that `EABackedBlock.setitem` already applies. `new` is a read-only input, so transposing it is correct regardless of whether `.T` is zero-copy (`dtype._can_fast_transpose`) — transposing the destination `values` is what GH-64620 deliberately avoided, and this PR still doesn't.

The non-inplace `where`/`mask` path goes through `EABackedBlock.where` (which transposes `values` into a fresh block) and was never affected.

title: BUG: DataFrame(list_of_arrays) with ragged same-dtype rows

labels.name: Regression
labels.description: Functionality that used to work in a prior pandas version

body:
The uniform-dtype fast path added in GH-64958 assumed every row had the
same length: it took the column count from the first row only
(`ncols = len(data[0])`) and indexed every row by that width.

For ragged rows of a single dtype this misbehaved in two ways:

```python
pd.DataFrame([np.array([1, 2]), np.array([3, 4, 5])]).to_numpy().tolist()
# -> [[1, 2], [3, 4]]   # the 5 was silently dropped

pd.DataFrame([np.array([1, 2, 3]), np.array([4, 5])])
# -> IndexError: index 2 is out of bounds for axis 0 with size 2
```

The entry condition (`treat_as_nested`) only inspects `data[0]`, so
same-dtype arrays of differing lengths still reach this path.

This gates the fast path on uniform row lengths; ragged rows now fall
through to the existing object/pad path and are padded to the longest
row with `NaN`, matching list-of-lists behavior (and the existing
`test_construct_from_listlikes_mismatched_lengths`).

No whatsnew: GH-64958 is unreleased, so this regression never shipped.

title: BUG: unstack corrupting source DataFrame via Copy-on-Write aliasing

labels.name: Regression
labels.description: Functionality that used to work in a prior pandas version

body:
Fixes a Copy-on-Write aliasing regression introduced by GH-65107.

GH-65107 added a zero-copy fast path: when the `MultiIndex` is already sorted and the unstacked level is the last level, `_Unstacker.get_new_values` returns a *view* of the block values rather than a `take_nd` copy. For single-block frames and `Series`, the view is tracked via `_Unstacker.get_result`'s `add_references` logic. But for multi-block (non-consolidated) frames, unstack goes through `BlockManager.unstack` → `Block._unstack`, which built the result block with `refs=None`. CoW therefore never tracked the sharing, and mutating the unstack result wrote through to the source `DataFrame`:

```python
idx = pd.MultiIndex.from_product([["a", "b"], [1, 2]])
df = pd.DataFrame({"x": [1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0], "y": ["p", "q", "r", "s"]}, index=idx)
res = df.unstack()
res.iloc[0, 0] = 999.0
df["x"].tolist()  # [999.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0] -- source corrupted
```

This fixes `Block._unstack` to track the reference when the unstacked values alias `self.values`, mirroring the `add_references` logic in `get_result`. The zero-copy view from GH-65107 is preserved; CoW now triggers a copy before either object is mutated.

No whatsnew entry: GH-65107 landed in the unreleased 3.1.0 dev cycle, so this regression was never in a released pandas.

title: BUG: get_indexer_non_unique raising ZeroDivisionError on empty index

labels.name: Indexing
labels.description: Related to indexing on series/frames, not to indexes themselves

body:
Fixes a `ZeroDivisionError` in :meth:`Index.get_indexer_non_unique` when called on an empty index against a non-empty target.

The binary-search heuristic guard evaluates `len(stargets) < (n / (2 * n.bit_length()))`, which divides by zero when the index is empty (`n == 0`, `(0).bit_length() == 0`). The `stargets and ...` short-circuit only guards an empty *target*, not an empty *index*. An empty index matches nothing, so this now returns an all-missing result early — which also sidesteps a degenerate resize loop in the fallback path.

- The non-masked `IndexEngine.get_indexer_non_unique` has had this since GH-54746 (shipped in v2.2.0 through v3.0.2).
- The masked `MaskedIndexEngine.get_indexer_non_unique` regressed in GH-64674 (3.1-dev only, unreleased).

```python
>>> import pandas as pd
>>> pd.Index([], dtype="Int64").get_indexer_non_unique(pd.Index([1, 2], dtype="Int64"))
ZeroDivisionError: division by zero   # before
(array([-1, -1]), array([0, 1]))      # after
```

A regression test covers both the masked (`Int64`/`Float64`/`boolean`) and non-masked (`int64`/`float64`/`object`) engines.

title: BUG: strftime %Y not zero-padded for years before 1000

labels.name: Regression
labels.description: Functionality that used to work in a prior pandas version

body:
Restores 4-digit-minimum zero-padding for the `%Y` directive in the array `strftime` fast path.

The directive-map optimization added in GH-64609 mapped `%Y` to `{0}` (no padding), so `Series.dt.strftime` / `DatetimeIndex.strftime` rendered years before 1000 without zero-padding:

```python
>>> ser = pd.Series(np.array(["0005-06-15", "0999-01-01"], dtype="M8[s]"))
>>> ser.dt.strftime("%Y").tolist()
['5', '999']        # main; this PR -> ['0005', '0999']
>>> ser.dt.strftime("%Y/%m/%d").tolist()
['5/06/15', '999/01/01']   # main; this PR -> ['0005/06/15', '0999/01/01']
```

`%Y` now maps to `{0:04d}`, matching `datetime.strftime` / `Timestamp.strftime` and `str(Timestamp(...))`, which already zero-pad the year to 4 digits. Other directives (`%m %d %H %M %S %f`) were already padded and are unchanged; 4-digit years are unaffected.

### Scope

This fixes the directive-map (custom-format) path — the regression introduced by GH-64609. The broader cross-platform consistency tracked in GH-58179 is **not** fully resolved here: the default repr and the `%Y-%m-%d` / `%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S` `basic_format` paths still render years before 1000 unpadded, and the scalar `Timestamp.strftime` slow path remains OS-dependent for `%Y`. Those are left for a follow-up.

No whatsnew entry: GH-64609 has not shipped in a release (it is only in `3.1.0.dev0`; latest release is `v3.0.2`), so this regression was introduced and fixed within the same unreleased cycle.

title: BUG: Incoherent dynamic dtype changes in `.map()`

labels.name: Needs Discussion
labels.description: Requires discussion from core team before further action

body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.

### Issue Description

In `a.map(b)`, when both a and b are Series and b's dtype is non-nullable, Pandas dynamically changes the output dtype if it can't match all the keys.

This behaviour changed in the nightlies vs. 3.0; however I am seeing inconsistencies which make little sense to me.

### Use case 1: Not all elements of `a.values` are in `b.index`
```python
a = pd.Series([1, 2])
b = pd.Series([10, 20], index=[2, 3])
```
output (pandas 3.0): np.float64
output (pandas 3.1 nightly): np.float64

### Use case 2: Some values of `a` are NULL
```python
a = pd.Series([1, None], dtype="Int16")
b = pd.Series([10, 20], index=[2, 1])
```
output (pandas 3.0): np.float64
output (pandas 3.1 nightly): Float64

```python
a = pd.Series([1, None], dtype="int16[pyarrow]")
b = pd.Series([10, 20], index=[2, 1])
```
output (pandas 3.0): np.float64
output (pandas 3.1 nightly): double[pyarrow]

### Use case 3: All values of `a` are NULL
```python
a = pd.Series([None, None], dtype="Int16")
b = pd.Series([10, 20], index=[2, 1])
```
output (pandas 3.0): np.float64
output (pandas 3.1 nightly): Int16

```python
a = pd.Series([None, None], dtype="int16[pyarrow]")
b = pd.Series([10, 20], index=[2, 1])
```
output (pandas 3.0): np.float64
output (pandas 3.1 nightly): double[pyarrow]


### Expected Behavior

IMHO there should be no difference in output in the three use cases.
Any of these output dtypes make sense to me:  

- `np.float64` (pandas 3.0 behaviour); on the principle that if `b.dtype` was a numpy dtype it should remain one even at the cost of loss of accuracy
- ` Int64`, or in other words the Pandas nullable equivalent of `b.dtype` (so Int8 if `b.dtype` is `np.int8`, etc.)
- `int64[pyarrow]`, or in other words the PyArrow nullable equivalent of `b.dtype`


### Installed Versions

pandas                            3.0.3
pyarrow                           24.0.0 

vs.

pandas                3.1.0.dev0+968.g384dfb2679
pyarrow               25.0.0.dev70

title: ENH: fallback to zoneinfo Python API (for correct tz localization) for distant dates
body:
Attempt for the third option mentioned in https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/65712: Use our fast-path for a "normal" range (eg up to 2100) to cover most use cases, and then for dates after that, use the zoneinfo python API directly as a slower fallback.

This is adding back a modified version of https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/65481, but then inside the general for-loop to fallback per value, instead of always for zoneinfo tz objects.

I tried parametrizing some of of the `tz_localize` tests for a current year and a distant year, to have some coverage for this fallback.

If we would go with this PR, then https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/65705 (expanding the cached transition data's range to 2262 instead of 2100) might not be needed
