title: BUG:  `groupby` cumprod/cummin/cummax returns `Float64` for nullable integers when group key contains `NA`

labels.name: NA - MaskedArrays
labels.description: Related to pd.NA and nullable extension arrays

body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
      "key": ["a", None, "a"],
      "val": pd.array([2, 3, 4], dtype="Int64"),
})

g = df.groupby("key")

print(g["val"].cumsum().dtype)   # Int64   (correct)
print(g["val"].cumprod().dtype)  # Float64 (expected Int64)
print(g["val"].cummin().dtype)   # Float64 (expected Int64)
print(g["val"].cummax().dtype)   # Float64 (expected Int64)
```

### Issue Description

`groupby().cumprod()`, `groupby().cummin()`, and `groupby().cummax()` return `Float64` instead of preserving the nullable integer dtype, e.g. `Int64`, when the group key contains NA values and `dropna=True`. 

`groupby().cumsum()` is not affected ( it already handles this case correctly following #58811 ) . The same handling is missing from group_cumprod and group_cummin_max.

### Expected Behavior

The dtype of the output should match the input nullable integer dtype.

title: BUG: to_datetime origin path silently ignored errors='coerce' (GH-63419)
body:
## Summary

Follow-up to GH-63915. The coerce handling here amends that unreleased fix, so there is no whatsnew entry.

- ``_adjust_to_origin`` now forwards ``errors`` to ``to_timedelta`` so out-of-bounds offsets become ``NaT`` under ``errors="coerce"`` instead of raising.
- Forwarding alone only coerced values that overflow ``to_timedelta`` itself (beyond ~1.07e14 days with ``unit="D"``); values that fit a timedelta but where ``origin + value`` overflows the result resolution still raised, making coercion magnitude-dependent. The addition is now wrapped:
  - under ``errors="coerce"``, entries whose sum cannot be represented in the addition's resolution become ``NaT`` (all-``NaT`` when the origin itself is not representable in the result resolution, e.g. ``origin=datetime(1, 1, 1)`` with ``unit="ns"``);
  - under ``errors="raise"``, the bare ``OverflowError``/``OutOfBoundsTimedelta`` escaping the addition is translated to ``OutOfBoundsDatetime``.
- Tidied the wrapper at the ``to_datetime`` call site:
  - dropped the dead ``ABCSeries`` branch in the ``utc`` block — after ``_adjust_to_origin``, ``arg`` is always a ``DatetimeArray`` or scalar ``Timestamp``, never a ``Series``;
  - dropped the redundant ``Timestamp`` ``isinstance`` check, since ``Timestamp.tz_localize`` covers it;
  - moved the lazy ``from pandas import Series`` import inside the ``is_series`` branch where it is actually needed.

## Test plan

- [x] ``test_origin_errors_coerce_overflow`` covers ``errors="coerce"`` across magnitude bands (in-bounds, addition overflow, ``to_timedelta`` overflow) for list/Series/scalar inputs, and ``errors="raise"`` exception types.
- [x] ``test_origin_errors_coerce_overflow_boundary`` asserts the exact cutoff value: last representable day succeeds, the next becomes ``NaT`` (coerce) or raises ``OutOfBoundsDatetime`` (raise).
- [x] ``test_origin_oob_for_unit_coerce`` covers the unrepresentable-origin all-``NaT`` case.

title: BUG: DataFrame.min/max axis=1 on dt64tz frames with NaT returning NaT or raising TypeError (GH-65500)

labels.name: Multi-Block
labels.description: Issues caused by the presence of multiple Blocks

body:
closes #65500

## Summary

Two fixes for `DataFrame.min`/`max(axis=1)` on tz-aware frames with `NaT`, reported in GH-65500:

1. **Regression** (unreleased, introduced by GH-65105): multi-block same-tz dt64tz frames returned `NaT` rows under the default `skipna=True`; mixed-tz frames got a silently wrong single-tz result.
2. **Long-standing bug**: the issue's headline repro — different timezones plus `NaT` — raised `TypeError: '>=' not supported between instances of 'Timestamp' and 'float'`, on released pandas as well. The same defect broke any object-dtype `min`/`max` with NAs alongside values not comparable with `float`, e.g. `Series(["a", "b", np.nan]).max()`.

## Root cause and fix

**1. Fast-path regression.** GH-65105 admitted 2D `ExtensionArray` blocks into the `axis=1` fast path (`_reduce_axis1`), which reduces with `np.fmin`/`np.fmax`. Those coerce a 2D EA to object dtype and do not skip `NaT`. Per review feedback the fast path is now restricted to numpy-backed non-object blocks, and EA frames fall back to the pre-GH-65105 routing: same-dtype EA frames take the GH-54341 flatten/groupby fast path (NA-correct, dtype-preserving); mixed-dtype frames fall through to the transpose path and coerce to `object`. This is also a perf win, not a trade-off: `np.fmax.reduce` on a 2D `DatetimeArray` degrades to elementwise object-speed dispatch, ~55-80x slower than the groupby path that replaces it (100k×10 multi-block dt64tz `max(axis=1)`: 814ms → 10ms). Numpy-backed frames keep the GH-65105 fast path unchanged.

**2. Object-dtype NA fill.** `nanops._nanminmax` filled NA positions with float `±inf` before reducing, so the reduction compared `Timestamp >= -inf` and raised. NA entries are now filled with a valid value from the same reduction slice — duplicating an existing value can never change a min/max, and always compares cleanly. All-NA slices still return NA, and genuinely incomparable data (e.g. `["a", 1, nan]`) still raises.

Out of scope: `idxmin`/`idxmax` (`nanargmin`/`nanargmax`) retain the `±inf` fill and still raise on object data with NAs — a value fill could relocate the arg result, so that fix needs index-mapping on the valid subset. Object-dtype `skipna=False` NA-propagation quirks are likewise pre-existing and untouched.

## Notes

- Whatsnew entry under 3.1.0 Numeric for the object-dtype fix (affects released versions). The GH-65105 regression itself never shipped, so it gets no separate note.

## Test plan

- [x] New tests: object-dtype min/max with NAs (strings, tuples, mixed-tz Timestamps, all-NA), frame `axis=1` mixed-tz with `NaT` under both `skipna` modes, and mixed-tz fall-through asserting values and `object` dtype.
- [x] Exhaustive `axis=1`-vs-transpose parametrization aligned so the dt64tz×dt64tz pairing exercises a same-dtype multi-block + `NaT` scenario across all reduction methods.
- [x] Suites green: frame/series/reductions/nanops/groupby/resample/indexes/arrays/extension/dtypes/apply/reshape/computation (~150k tests).
- [x] `pre-commit` and `pyright` clean.

title: BUG: read_excel with index_col and parse_dates=True fails to create a DatetimeIndex when used with the pyarrow backend
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

# Create example dataframe and write to excel
df = pd.DataFrame({"A": [1, 2, 3]}, index=pd.date_range("2026", periods=3, freq="MS"))
df.to_excel("test.xlsx")

# Read the excel file using the default numpy_nullable backend
excel_df = pd.read_excel("test.xlsx", index_col=0, parse_dates=True, dtype_backend="numpy_nullable")
print("Is DatetimeIndex:", isinstance(excel_df.index, pd.DatetimeIndex))
print(excel_df.index)
# Can be converted to a PeriodIndex
excel_df.index.to_period("M")

# Read the excel file using the pyarrow backend
excel_df = pd.read_excel("test.xlsx", index_col=0, parse_dates=True, dtype_backend="pyarrow")
print("Is DatetimeIndex:", isinstance(excel_df.index, pd.DatetimeIndex))
print(excel_df.index)
# Can't be converted to a PeriodIndex
excel_df.index.to_period("M")
```

### Issue Description

When calling ``pd.read_excel`` with ``index_col`` and ``parse_dates=True`` the DataFrame has a DatetimeIndex when used with the default numpy_nullable backend but not when called with the pyarrow backend. This leads to unexpected follow up errors, trying to call for example ``df.index.to_period`` on the result.

I would expect the dtype_backend to have no influence on the IndexType of the returned DataFrame, i.e. the index type of read_excel with ``index_col``, ``parse_dates=True`` and ``dtype_backend="pyarrow"`` should also be a DatetimeIndex.

title: PERF: skip redundant `take()` copies in `_Unstacker.sorted_labels` when indexer is identity
body:
## Problem Description

When `_indexer_is_identity` is `True` (the MultiIndex codes are already in the required order -- the common case for `from_product` / monotonic `from_arrays` data unstacking the last level), `sorted_labels` still ran `[line.take(indexer) for line in to_sort]`, allocating one O(N) copy per label dimension. `_indexer_is_identity` is already a `cache_readonly` (it gates `_make_sorted_values`), so the new guard is free.

The bottleneck was identified when profiling `xarray` operations.

## Output of ``pd.show_versions()``

N/A (performance-only change, no API change).

## Benchmark

`Series.unstack("x0")` on a fully-sorted Cartesian-product MultiIndex:

| input | before (ms) | after (ms) | speedup |
|---|---|---|---|
| 5x4 (2-level)      | 0.200 | 0.203 | ~1.0x (below noise) |
| 10x10x10 (3-level) | 0.300 | 0.290 | ~1.0x (below noise) |
| 100x90             | 0.441 | 0.391 | 1.13x |
| 200x92             | 0.672 | 0.557 | 1.21x |
| 10x10000           | 4.161 | 3.448 | 1.21x |

Profiling confirms 3 `ndarray.take` calls per `unstack` in the baseline drop to
0 in the patched version (for the identity case).

ASV benchmarks added in `asv_bench/benchmarks/unstack_cartesian.py`.

title: BUG: Conversion from np.ma.masked_array to pd.array does not preserve missing values
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

a = np.ma.array([1, 2, 3, 4], mask=[False, True, False, True])

# BUG: mask is ignored completely
pd.array(a)
# Output:
# <IntegerArray>
# [1, 2, 3, 4]
# Length: 4, dtype: Int64

# For comparison, pd.Series handles the mask but changes dtype to float
pd.Series(a)
# Output:
# 0 1.0
# 1 NaN
# 2 3.0
# 3 NaN
# dtype: float64
```

### Issue Description

NumPy [masked arrays](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/maskedarray.generic.html#what-is-a-masked-array) are used to define arrays with missing values, similar to pandas extension arrays. However, converting to `pd.array` currently ignores the mask completely and masked values appear as regular values.

Converting to `pd.Series` does respect the missing values, but the dtype is converted to `float` and the original dtype is not preserved in all cases.

This behavior is inconsistent with user expectations and with how `pd.Series` handles masked arrays.

The same issue occurs with string masked arrays where the mask is also ignored by `pd.array`.

### Expected Behavior

Masked values should be converted to pd.NA and the appropriate nullable dtype should be preserved, such as Int64 or string, instead of ignoring the mask or coercing to float.

>>> pd.array(a)
<IntegerArray>
[1, <NA>, 3, <NA>]
Length: 4, dtype: Int64

### Installed Versions

pandas: 3.0.0
numpy: 2.3.5
python: 3.12.9

title: BUG: raise on timedelta64 multiplication / division / sum overflow (GH-43178)
body:
- closes #43178

## Summary

Make ``timedelta64`` overflow handling consistent and overflow-safe across multiplication, division, and `sum`:

- ``TimedeltaArray.__mul__`` with an integer scalar/array silently wrapped on int64 overflow. It now routes through a new Cython ``mul_overflowsafe`` helper (analogous to ``add_overflowsafe``) that raises ``OverflowError`` instead.
- ``TimedeltaArray.__mul__`` with a float scalar/array silently saturated to ``int64.max`` on overflow. It now goes through a ``_mul_float_overflowsafe`` path that bounds-checks the float result and raises ``OverflowError``, while preserving ``NaT`` and propagating ``NaN`` multipliers as ``NaT``. The check compares against ``2**63`` rather than ``int64.max``: ``int64.max`` (``2**63 - 1``) is not exactly representable in float64 and rounds up to ``2**63``, so a product landing exactly on ``2**63`` (e.g. ``Timedelta(2**62, "ns") * 2.0``) would otherwise slip past the check and silently saturate on the cast.
- ``__truediv__``/``__floordiv__`` with a float scalar/array silently saturated the same way (``tdi / 0.4`` is the same operation as ``tdi * 2.5``); scalar ``Timedelta`` already raised. They now raise ``OverflowError``. The check is detection-only — numpy still computes the result values — so quotient semantics are unchanged and zero/``NaN`` divisors keep returning ``NaT``. (Integer divisors cannot overflow and are untouched.)
- An **unsigned** multiplier above ``int64.max`` previously wrapped to a negative ``int64`` in the ``astype("i8")`` cast *before* the overflow check ran, silently multiplying by the wrong value. It now raises ``OverflowError`` in both the scalar and array branches. Python int multipliers below ``int64.min`` likewise raise with the same message.
- An integer product landing exactly on ``int64.min`` is representable in int64 but is the ``iNaT`` sentinel, so it previously came back as a silent ``NaT``. ``mul_overflowsafe`` now raises ``OverflowError`` for it. (The float path already raised, since its bounds check is symmetric at ``2**63``.)
- Multiplying by ``inf`` now raises ``OverflowError``, matching scalar ``Timedelta * inf`` behavior; numpy returns ``NaT`` here. A ``nan`` multiplier still returns ``NaT``.
- ``Series.sum`` on an overflowing ``timedelta64`` reduction raised a plain ``ValueError``. It now raises ``OutOfBoundsTimedelta`` (a ``ValueError`` subclass).

Perf: the scalar-integer multiply and scalar-float divide checks first bounds-check the products/quotients of the ``i8`` extremes, so the common no-overflow case keeps a vectorized numpy op (~1.1x raw numpy at 1M elements, vs ~6.6x through the per-element Cython loop). ``NaT``-containing arrays fall back to the NaT-aware slow paths.

Before, on ``timedelta64[ns]``:

```
>>> td = pd.Timedelta(100000, "D").as_unit("ns")
>>> x = pd.Series([td, td])
>>> x * 2          # silent overflow → -13504 days +00:25:26.290448384
>>> x / 0.4        # silent saturation → 106751 days 23:47:16.854775807
>>> x.sum()        # ValueError
```

After:

```
>>> x * 2          # OverflowError: Overflow in int64 multiplication
>>> x * 2.5        # OverflowError: Overflow in timedelta multiplication
>>> x * np.inf     # OverflowError: Overflow in timedelta multiplication
>>> x / 0.4        # OverflowError: Overflow in timedelta division
>>> x.sum()        # OutOfBoundsTimedelta: overflow in timedelta operation
```

Known remaining gap: an object-dtype multiplier array (``tdi * np.array([2, 2], dtype=object)``) still wraps silently, because that path multiplies raw ``np.timedelta64`` scalars elementwise; this is fixed upstream in numpy.

## Test plan

- [x] New `test_td64arr_mul_int_overflow` and `test_td64arr_mul_float_overflow` over Series/Index/DataFrame/array boxes
- [x] New `test_td64arr_mul_uint_overflow` (unsigned multiplier above ``int64.max``, Python int below ``int64.min``) and `test_td64arr_mul_float_overflow_boundary` (product landing exactly on ``2**63``)
- [x] New `test_td64arr_mul_int_min_boundary` — integer product landing exactly on ``int64.min`` raises instead of silently returning ``NaT``
- [x] New `test_td64arr_mul_inf_raises` and `test_td64arr_mul_nan_returns_nat`
- [x] New `test_td64arr_mul_preserves_nat` — ``NaT`` survives the overflow-safe int and float paths (the ``iNaT`` sentinel is ``-2**63``, so it would otherwise trip the new overflow checks)
- [x] New `test_td64arr_div_float_overflow` (truediv/floordiv, scalar and array divisors) and `test_td64arr_div_float_zero_nan_still_nat` — zero/``NaN`` divisors keep returning ``NaT``
- [x] New `test_td64arr_mul_div_overflow_non_nano` — overflow bounds are per-unit int64 (``m8[s]``), not nanosecond-specific
- [x] Updated `test_td64_summation_overflow` to expect `OutOfBoundsTimedelta`
- [x] Updated `tslibs.test_api` namespace test for the new `mul_overflowsafe` export
- [x] `pandas/tests/arithmetic/`, `pandas/tests/reductions/`, `pandas/tests/extension/`, `pandas/tests/series/test_reductions.py`, `pandas/tests/test_nanops.py`, `pandas/tests/tslibs/`, `pandas/tests/scalar/timedelta/`, `pandas/tests/indexes/timedeltas/`, `pandas/tests/arrays/timedeltas/` all pass locally

title: BUG: to_julian_date ignored timezone (GH-54763)
body:
- closes #54763

## Summary

`Timestamp.to_julian_date` and `DatetimeIndex.to_julian_date` were computing the Julian date from the **local wall-clock** representation, so two timestamps referring to the same UTC instant in different timezones returned different values:

```python
>>> pd.Timestamp("1858-11-17", tz="UTC").to_julian_date()
2400000.5
>>> pd.Timestamp("1858-11-17", tz="US/Mountain").to_julian_date()
2400000.5  # wrong; should be ~2400000.79 (00:00 Mountain == 07:00 UTC)
```

JD is an absolute-time concept (cf. `Timestamp.timestamp` / POSIX seconds, which already returns the UTC instant), so the fix routes tz-aware inputs through the naive UTC instant before computing. Behavior for tz-naive inputs is unchanged.

The implementation is a single early-return in each method — naturally vectorized for the array path via `tz_convert("UTC").tz_localize(None)`, no per-element Python loop. Supersedes the stale GH-60280.

title: DOC: explain why and/or/not cannot be used with pd.NA
body:
- closes #49828

## Summary

GH-49828 reports that `pd.NA and X`, `pd.NA or X`, and `not pd.NA` all raise `TypeError: boolean value of NA is ambiguous`, while the mirrored forms (`True and pd.NA`, `False or pd.NA`, etc.) sometimes succeed. This is not a bug — it's the unavoidable interaction of two design points:

1. `bool(pd.NA)` raises by design (GH-38224) — pandas refuses to guess truthiness of an unknown.
2. Python's `and`/`or`/`not` keywords always call `bool()` on their operand and cannot be overridden via dunders.

The asymmetry users see is just Python short-circuiting: `and`/`or` only call `bool()` on the **left** operand, so when `pd.NA` happens to be on the right, `bool()` is never invoked.

`&`/`|`/`~` work correctly via `__and__`/`__or__`/`__invert__` and already implement Kleene logic.

This PR adds a paragraph to the `NA in a boolean context` section of the user guide spelling out exactly this: why the keywords can't work, why the position-dependent behavior happens, and that `&`/`|`/`~` are the supported alternatives.

I considered also expanding the `TypeError` message itself with the `&`/`|`/`~` hint, but `bool(pd.NA)` is hit from many contexts (`if pd.NA:`, `assert pd.NA`, library code doing `if x == y:`, etc.) where that hint would be misleading. The docs are the right venue for the explanation.

## Test plan

- [x] No code/runtime change, so existing tests still pass
- [x] `pre-commit` passes (sphinx-lint, rst lint, etc.)

title: BUG: pandas.DataFrame.max fails on datetime64[ns, ...] columns with different time zones and NaT in the data

labels.name: Missing-data
labels.description: np.nan, pd.NaT, pd.NA, dropna, isnull, interpolate

body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [ ] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

ONE_TZ = pd.Timestamp("2026-01-01 15:13:44.01234567", tz="Europe/Budapest")
OTHER_TZ = pd.Timestamp("2026-01-01 15:13:44.01234567", tz="Europe/Moscow")

# Example (works): different timezones, no NaT
df1 = pd.DataFrame({"time1":[ONE_TZ, ONE_TZ], "time2":[OTHER_TZ, OTHER_TZ]})
df1.max(axis=1) # Works

# Example (works): same timezone, with NaT
df2 = pd.DataFrame({"time1":[ONE_TZ, ONE_TZ], "time2":[ONE_TZ, pd.Timestamp("")]})
df2.max(axis=1) # Works

# Example (fails): different timezone, with NaT
df3 = pd.DataFrame({"time1":[ONE_TZ, ONE_TZ], "time2":[OTHER_TZ, pd.Timestamp("")]})
df3.max(axis=1) # Fails, as soon as we have a NaT
```

### Issue Description

In dataframes with datetime64 columns, max() fails with a `TypeError: '>=' not supported between instances of 'Timestamp' and 'float'` when 2 different timezones and NaT values are both present. As long as we have 1 timezone or no NaTs, everything works as expected. The default behavior of max() is skipping nans, and NaT is interpreted as such correctly with the same timezone. Once the timezone is different, it is treated as a float and the comparison fails.

It seems like during the max() operation, since timezones differ, rows are coerced into an `object` dtype. The NaT is leaking into the underlying numpy amax as a float instead of being safely skipped or masked out before the comparison occurs.

### Expected Behavior

Truly skipping NaTs as a default in max() before attempting the comparison of the remaining datetime64 values.

title: BUG: fix check if pyarrow is installed in cython lib - use existing constant
body:
In https://github.com/apache/arrow/pull/49912 it was noticed that the trick of `sys.modules["pyarrow"] = None` to let python think that pyarrow is not installed, does not work for imports in cython (while in case of a python `import pyarrow`, that gives a ModuleNotFoundError, which is an ImportError sublcass).

Now, this is not really a bug in pandas, but since we already have tried to import pyarrow in the `pandas.compat` module before we get to import `pandas._libs.lib`, we can also just reuse the knowledge of pyarrow being available or not, instead of doing a new try/except.  
And that then also makes the `sys.modules` hack work again.

title: PERF: remove special casing for zoneinfo in tz_localize_to_utc
body:
https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/64379 already fixed the zoneinfo performance issues in the UTC -> wall time code path (i.e. what you need when accessing parts of the time like the hour), but the wall time -> UTC code path was also still having its custom (slow) zoneinfo handling. This PR removes that, to reuse the transitions/deltas from https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/64379

>>> dti = pd.date_range("2020-01-01", periods=1_000_000, freq="1min", tz="Europe/Brussels").tz_localize(None)
>>> %timeit dti.tz_localize("Europe/Brussels", ambiguous="infer")

title: Cache BlockManager.get_dtypes result for repeated calls
body: BaseBlockManager.get_dtypes was rebuilding an O(nblocks) object array on every call from hot paths like df.dtypes, fillna, select_dtypes, and iloc setitem. This change caches the per-column dtypes array on the manager and invalidates it alongside the existing _interleaved_dtype hook at every block-mutation site. get_dtypes returns a copy of the cache so df.dtypes (which wraps the array in a Series with copy=False) does not share storage across calls. On a 1000-column, 335-block frame the warm-cache path drops from about 47 us to 2.7 us. Fixes #65382.

title: BUG: fix Index.get_indexer pd.NA vs NaN inconsistency (GH#65419)
body:
## Summary
When calling `get_indexer` with an ndarray containing `pd.NA` on an index containing `np.nan`, the results were inconsistent with the list input.

## Root Cause
In `_maybe_cast_listlike_indexer`, when the target is a list, `ensure_index` normalizes `pd.NA` to `np.nan` via `Index.__new__` -> `sanitize_array`. However, when the target is already an ndarray (has `.dtype` attribute), this normalization was skipped.

## Fix
Added handling in `_maybe_cast_listlike_indexer` to fillna `pd.NA` to `np.nan` when both self and target have object dtype, ensuring consistent matching behavior.

## Example
```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

idx = pd.Index([np.nan, 'b'])

# Before fix: ndarray path returned -1, list path returned 0
idx.get_indexer([pd.NA])  # array([0]) - correct
idx.get_indexer(np.array([pd.NA], dtype=object))  # array([-1]) - WRONG

# After fix: all return array([0])
idx.get_indexer(np.array([pd.NA], dtype=object))  # array([0])
```

Fixes #65419

body:
## Summary

- Replaces the long-commented-out `test_string_column_above_2GB` (originally needing >5GB RAM) with a buffer-aliased version that exercises the same int32-offset boundary using ~150MB.
- Constructs a logically >2GB `pa.string()` ChunkedArray from a single 150MB data buffer referenced by 20 single-string chunks. `pyarrow.ChunkedArray.combine_chunks()` on this input raises with the exact `offset overflow while concatenating arrays` error from GH-55606, confirming the test exercises the real failure mode rather than a proxy.
- Drives `pd.StringDtype(storage="pyarrow").__from_arrow__(...)` end-to-end. Since `pc.cast` to `large_string` preserves chunked structure (and pyarrow shares the underlying data buffers across the cast), physical RSS stays bounded.

This only covers the pyarrow-storage branch of `__from_arrow__`. The python-storage branch goes through `arr.to_numpy(zero_copy_only=False)` which materializes Python `str` objects, so buffer aliasing doesn't help there — that branch isn't reasonably testable at >2GB and isn't covered here.

## Test plan

- [ ] `pytest pandas/tests/io/test_parquet.py::TestParquetPyArrow::test_string_column_above_2GB -v`
- [ ] Confirm it runs in <5s and stays well under 1GB RSS

title: BUG: DateOffset arithmetic not supported for date32[pyarrow] (GH#57168)
body:
Closes #57168

## Problem
`pd.Series(..., dtype="date32[pyarrow]") + pd.offsets.MonthEnd()` raised
`ArrowTypeError: No temporal attributes found on object` because
`_arith_method` tried to box the `DateOffset` as a `date32` scalar.

## Fix
Added a branch in `ArrowExtensionArray._arith_method` to detect
`pd.DateOffset` operands on date-typed arrays and apply the offset
element-wise via `to_pylist()`, then reconstruct the Arrow array.

## Tests
- Added parametrized tests for `MonthEnd`, `MonthBegin`, `Day`, `DateOffset`
- Added null-handling test

title: BUG: keep fsspec OpenFile alive for chained URL reads

labels.name: IO Data
labels.description: IO issues that don't fit into a more specific label

body:
Closes #65462

Should be tested by our existing tests by removing the fsspec upper pin and updating the lock file

In the end this is actually an issue on our side and not a regression in fsspec:

`pandas.io.common._get_filepath_or_buffer` opened fsspec URLs with `fsspec.open(...).open()`, which thus immediately discards the intermediate `OpenFile` object (the result of the first `open()` call). 
And fsspec documents that the `OpenFile` must stay alive while the returned file handle is in use. And because of an upstream fix, dropping it early now causes reads to fail with `ValueError: seek of closed file` with a Tar filesystem.

So the change here keeps that object alive, and returns it in the `IOArgs`, and then ensures we explicitly call `close()` on that object as well.

title: BUG: `Series.values` returns inconsistent type (`ndarray` vs `MaskedArray`) depending on whether DataFrame rows are pre-sorted by groupby key

labels.name: Algos
labels.description: Non-arithmetic algos: value_counts, factorize, sorting, isin, clip, shift, diff

body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

print(pd.__version__)

bins = np.linspace(0., 100., 101)
xc   = 0.5 * (bins[1:] + bins[:-1])

for label, x, y in [
    ("non-empty, y sorted by bin",   np.ma.array([0.1, 0.2, 0.3]), np.array([25., 50., 75.])),
    ("non-empty, y unsorted by bin", np.ma.array([0.1, 0.2, 0.3]), np.array([50., 75., 25.])),
    ("empty",                        np.ma.array([], dtype=float),  np.array([])),
]:
    df = pd.DataFrame()
    df["x"] = x
    df["y"] = y
    df = df.loc[:, ["x", "y"]]
    df.reset_index(inplace=True)
    df["bin"] = pd.cut(df["y"].values, bins=bins, labels=[str(c) for c in xc])
    for name, grp in df.groupby("bin", observed=False):
        print(f"{label}: {type(grp['x'].values).__name__}")
        break
```
prints
```
3.1.0.dev0+824.gb00d4f6710
non-empty, y sorted by bin: MaskedArray
non-empty, y unsorted by bin: ndarray
empty: MaskedArray
```

### Issue Description

When a `numpy.ma.MaskedArray` column is stored in a DataFrame and groups are iterated via `groupby(..., observed=False)`, the type returned by `Series.values` depends on whether the rows happen to be pre-sorted by the groupby key and on whether the DataFrame is empty. The same column, same dtype, same group, just different row ordering or DataFrame size, produces either `ndarray` or `MaskedArray`.

### Expected Behavior

`Series.values` should return a consistent type regardless of whether the underlying DataFrame rows are sorted, unsorted, or empty. Given the column dtype is numeric (e.g. `float64`), `ndarray` is the expected return type in all three cases.

title: BUG: Ensure consistent index naming when merging with empty DataFrames
body:
This PR fixes an inconsistency reported in #22921 where merging an empty DataFrame with a non-empty DataFrame via `left_on`/`right_index` (or `left_index`/`right_on`) inadvertently preserved the named index from the non-empty DataFrame. 

Previously, when one side was empty, `_get_join_info` bypassed standard join index creation and fell back to `copy()`/`take()` on the populated axis, dragging along its index metadata. This updates the logic to construct a fresh `default_index(n)` when one side is empty. The length `n` is correctly calculated based on the `how` parameter (e.g., `n = len(right)` for an outer join with an empty left DataFrame).

Parametrized tests have been added to ensure consistency across all join types (`inner`, `left`, `right`, `outer`).

title: API: tracker for single-element listlike RHS inconsistency in setitem

labels.name: Indexing
labels.description: Related to indexing on series/frames, not to indexes themselves

labels.name: Master Tracker
labels.description: High level tracker for similar issues

labels.name: Needs Discussion
labels.description: Requires discussion from core team before further action

body:
`obj[key] = [42]` (or `np.array([42])`) does different things depending on the accessor, the key shape, the dtype, and the block structure of unrelated columns:

```python
df = pd.DataFrame({"x": [10, 20, 30], "y": [40, 50, 60]},
                  index=["a", "b", "c"]).astype(object)

# list RHS
df.loc["a", "x"]      = [42]            # cell stores [42]
df.loc["a", ["x"]]    = [42]            # cell stores 42
df.loc[["a"], ["x"]]  = [42]            # cell stores 42
df.iloc[0, 0]         = [42]            # cell stores [42]
df.iloc[0, [0]]       = [42]            # cell stores 42
df.at["a", "x"]       = [42]            # cell stores [42]

# np.array RHS — yet another set of outcomes
df.loc["a", "x"]      = np.array([42])  # cell stores array(42)   (0-D!)
df.loc["a", ["x"]]    = np.array([42])  # cell stores np.int64(42)
df.loc[["a"], ["x"]]  = np.array([42])  # cell stores 42
df.iloc[0, 0]         = np.array([42])  # cell stores array(42)
df.iloc[0, [0]]       = np.array([42])  # cell stores np.int64(42)
df.at["a", "x"]       = np.array([42])  # cell stores array(42)
```

Six open issues describe pieces of this directly. Filing as a single umbrella so they can be considered together.

## Bull's-eye open issues

**#16864 (2017) — One item lists are assigned into dataframes as single items.** `df.loc[[0,1], 'new_col'] = [['one_item'], ['one_item']]` stores `'one_item'` (the inner string) in each row instead of `['one_item']` (the list). The reporter wanted to populate a list-valued column row-by-row and was surprised that single-element nested lists got unwrapped while multi-element ones didn't.

**#25806 (2019) — Effect of assigning list to DataFrame cell depends on unrelated column's type.** `df.loc['a', 'foo'] = ['123']` stores `['123']` on a fresh DataFrame, but the *same* assignment on the same DataFrame stores `'123'` once an unrelated column has been cast to float. Behavior depends on the block layout, not on user intent. Same example shows `.at` and `.loc` diverging on the same input.

**#30649 (2019) — `df.at[...] = ['some list']` doesn't set object dtype on column creation.** Setting a list via `.at` to a non-existent column creates the column with the wrong dtype; the first row stores the unwrapped scalar `'a'` while subsequent rows (after the column exists) correctly store `['a']`. Same accessor, same RHS, two different outcomes depending on whether the column already exists.

**#35006 (2020) — Different behavior when setting a list(scalar) to entire column vs filtered rows.** `df["new"] = list_of_arrays` produces one outcome; `df.loc[mask, "new"] = list_of_arrays` produces another, even when the mask matches every row. Multi-step repro showing four "expected" cases and two "unexpected" ones with the same RHS construction.

**#53565 (2023, regression from 2.0) — Reassigning a Series index with a 1-D length-1 ndarray loses dimension.** First `s['whatever'] = np.array([1])` stores shape `(1,)` as expected. *Second* assignment of the same value collapses to shape `()`. Reproducible 1.5 → 2.0 regression, no movement since.

**#57923 (2024) — Inconsistent implicit conversion of 1-arrays inside DataFrames.** `df.at[0, 0] = np.arange(2)` stores `array([0, 1])`; `df.at[1, 0] = np.arange(1)` stores `np.int64(0)`. Length-1 ndarrays get silently unwrapped to scalars where length-2+ ndarrays don't, on the same accessor with the same dtype. Reporter notes pandas can be tricked into holding 1-arrays via `applymap`, demonstrating the unwrap is at the setitem boundary and not a storage limitation.

## Closely related — broader setitem consistency

- **#26333 (2019)** — REGR: assigning a tuple/scalar-with-length to an object-dtype cell stopped working in 0.23, "Must have equal len keys and value when setting with an iterable".
- **#46544 (2022)** — `DataFrame.loc` and `DataFrame.__setitem__` give different results for the same 2-D ndarray RHS.
- **#57962 (2024)** — `df.loc[1, 2] = np.zeros(3)` into an object-dtype cell raises despite the dtype permitting it (1.4 → 2.x regression).
- **#61223 (2025)** — `.at` setting an iterable fails when the column doesn't yet exist, succeeds afterwards.
- **#15490 (2017)** — `.at` / `.loc` modifies the DataFrame even when the assignment raises.
- **#45769 (2022)** — MultiIndex `loc` with an n×2 list assignment fails despite shape match.
- **#62369 (2025)** — API question on what dtype setitem-with-expansion should infer.

## Umbrella / meta

- **#55935 (2023)** — PDEP-6: setitem casting (the standing umbrella for setitem semantic decisions).
- **#27911 (2019)** — API: when to cast list-like to ndarray, check len match (the arithmetic-side analog of this question).
- **#60218 (2024)** — ERR: consistent error messages for unsupported setitem values.

## Adjacent — same family, peripheral

- **#42549 (2021)** — list-like objects broadcast to each row (1.3 regression caused by `is_list_like` not detecting some sequences).
- **#46974 (2022)** — DataFrame setitem with DataFrame RHS doesn't align column names.
- **#51386 (2023)** — `Series.__setitem__` with Series value: alignment vs replacement question.
- **#53996 (2023)** — DOC: is the behavior of setitem with repeated keys defined?
- **#57765 (2024)** — Setting a 2-D numpy array as a column uses only the first column.
- **#61026 (2025)** — Setting column with 2-D object-dtype array raises.

Original-intent context for the carve-outs that any fix would need to revisit: **#19474** (the explicit unwrap-on-listlike-LHS), **#37629** (nested-container preservation), **#44103** (force-split-path for scalar-row + listlike-col).

## Why one tracker

These six bull's-eye issues are not separate bugs in separate corners — they're the same inconsistency surfacing at six different accessor / dtype / shape / expansion-vs-existing combinations, on a code path that has accumulated independent decision points at multiple layers. Discussing them in one place makes the matrix visible and lets any fix (or deprecation) be evaluated against all six at once rather than one at a time.

title: PERF: speed up read_sas for compressed SAS7BDAT files

labels.name: Mothballed
labels.description: Temporarily-closed PR the author plans to return to

body:
## Summary

Two changes targeting the compressed-file hot path in ``read_sas``:

1. **RLE/RDC decompression**: replace per-byte loops in ``rle_decompress`` and ``rdc_decompress`` with ``memcpy``/``memset`` for byte runs. Bounds are asserted once per opcode block instead of per byte. The RDC long-pattern path keeps the byte-by-byte loop for the overlap case (``ofs < cnt``) where intentional pattern repetition requires byte-by-byte semantics; the non-overlap case is ``memcpy``. ``process_byte_array_with_data`` drops the per-byte ``buf_get`` and uses ``memcpy`` for the column copy — this generalizes the ``lngt == 8`` fast path from #65363 with no extra branch.

2. **Per-page subheader pointers**: replace the Python list-of-tuples ``_current_page_data_subheader_pointers`` with two preallocated int64 arrays. Move the per-page subheader-walk loop out of Python's ``_process_page_metadata`` into a new module-level Cython ``collect_page_subheaders`` that reads pointer fields directly from the cached page (with inline byteswap), looks up the signature index via the existing 32/64-bit lookup tables, writes data subheaders into the int64 arrays, and only bounces non-data subheaders back to the Python processors. ``readline()`` then indexes the arrays directly with no GIL acquire and no tuple unpack. This is the win on compressed files where every page is a meta page and every row goes through a tuple lookup.

## Benchmarks

Inner-loop ``Parser.read`` time/row (baseline = ``main``):

| file (compression, rows/page) | before | after | speedup |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| test_meta2_page (RDC, 1000) | 1.20 µs | 0.34 µs | **3.6×** |
| test3  (RDC, 10) | 2.24 µs | 1.61 µs | 1.4× |
| test11 (RDC, 10) | 2.22 µs | 1.60 µs | 1.4× |
| test2  (RLE, 10) | 1.74 µs | 1.38 µs | 1.3× |
| test12 (RLE, 10) | 1.64 µs | 1.31 µs | 1.3× |

End-to-end vs. pyreadstat: ``test_meta2_page`` (the realistic many-rows-per-meta-page shape for compressed files) goes from 1.46× slower than readstat to **0.72×** (28% faster). The 10-row test files remain dominated by metadata parsing + DataFrame construction, which is the target of #65364.

xref #47339

title: BUG: Index.str.split/rsplit/findall return ndarray on object path
body:
- xref GH-64798, GH-20285

After GH-64798, `Index.str.split`, `Index.str.rsplit`, and `Index.str.findall` with `expand=False` raise `TypeError` on object/string-dtype Indexes, because the per-row Python lists are unhashable and can no longer be wrapped in an `Index`.

This restores functionality by returning an `ndarray[object]` of lists instead of attempting to construct an Index. Per Joris's suggestion in GH-64798 (returning an array, mirroring the historical precedent for some Index methods).

| `object`, `string[python]`, `string[pyarrow]`, `"str"`, default | returns `ndarray[object]` |

## Summary

- Adds a regression test for GH-56996 covering `to_timedelta(np.int32(0), unit="D")` and similar sub-int64 NumPy integer scalars.
- The original `OutOfBoundsTimedelta` was incidentally fixed by GH-63302 (`Timedelta.__new__` integer branch now short-circuits through `np.timedelta64(value, unit)` for non-`ns` units, avoiding the NEP 50 path in `cast_from_unit`).

The integer fast-path added in GH-63302 means that path is no longer reachable from `to_timedelta`/`Timedelta` for integer scalars with a non-`ns` unit, but a regression test ensures it stays that way.

title: BUG: Period.strftime crashes on Windows for invalid format strings
body:
## Summary

title: BUG: Timestamp with 1-3 digit BC year silently drops leading '-' (GH-55954)
body:
## Summary
- The iso8601 fast path required exactly 4 digits for the year, so strings like `"-111-01-01"` fell through to `dateutil`, which silently strips the leading `"-"` and parses as a positive year (so `Timestamp("-111-01-01") == Timestamp("111-01-01")` was `True`).
- Extend the iso8601 parser to accept 1-4 digit BC years, matching `numpy.datetime64` behavior.
- Raise `DateParseError` for non-iso strings starting with `"-"` (e.g. `"-12:30"`, `"--12-01-01"`) rather than letting `dateutil` silently mishandle them.

## Behavior change

| Input | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| `Timestamp("-111-01-01")` | year 111 (silently wrong) | year **-111** ✓ |
| `Timestamp("-12-01-01")` | year 2001-12-01 | year **-12** ✓ |
| `Timestamp("-9-1-1")` | 2001-09-01 | year **-9** ✓ |
| `Timestamp("-0111-01-01")` | year -111 | year -111 (unchanged) |
| `Timestamp("-2000-01-01")` | year -2000 | year -2000 (unchanged) |
| `Timestamp("-12:30")` | 0001-01-01 12:30 (silently wrong) | `DateParseError` |

`pd.Timestamp("-111-01-01") == pd.Timestamp("111-01-01")` is now `False`, matching `np.datetime64`.

## Out of scope
`to_datetime("-0111-01-01")` still mishandles the negative sign because it goes through `_guess_datetime_format` + `array_strptime`, a different code path. That's a separate pre-existing bug.

closes #55954

title: BUG: restore array-level state and avoid object roundtrip in DataFrame._append_internal
body:
## Summary

Follow-up to GH-65094, addressing the [next-to-last review comment](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/65094#issuecomment-3502023527) from @jorisvandenbossche.

GH-65094 removed the per-column casting loop in `_append_internal` under the assumption that `_post_expansion_casting` in `_LocationIndexer.__setitem__` made it redundant. That's not equivalent for two reasons:

1. **Correctness**: `_post_expansion_casting` rebuilds via `pd_array([], dtype=...)`, so EAs whose state lives on the *array* (e.g. geopandas CRS) lose that state.
2. **Performance**: when `find_common_type` falls back to `object` (e.g. `ArrowDtype(pa.struct(...))` + `object` row), concat materializes the whole column to object and post-cast rebuilds — Joris's 1M-row example regresses ~170× on this hardware.

This PR reintroduces the pre-cast loop, but conditionally:
- skip columns where the row's inferred dtype already matches the original (avoids the unconditional `_cast_pointwise_result` overhead the original loop paid)
- skip plain-object original columns (post-cast is a no-op anyway)

For columns we do pre-cast, the original `ExtensionArray`'s *instance* `_cast_pointwise_result` runs — which is what carries array-level state (CRS, etc.) into the row's value. Concat then takes the same-dtype fastpath and `_post_expansion_casting` is a no-op.

## Benchmarks (best-of-N, same hardware)

Joris's `ArrowDtype(pa.struct(...))` 1M-row example:

| state | time |
|---|---|
| pre-GH-65094 (loop unconditionally restored) | 1.53 ms |
| current `main` (GH-65094 merged) | 262.5 ms |
| this PR | 1.41 ms |

GH-65094's own 500-iter microbenchmark, on this machine:

| dtype | current `main` | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| `int64` | 0.127 s | 0.123 s |
| `Int64` | 0.142 s | 0.154 s |
| `int64[pyarrow]` | 0.190 s | 0.195 s |
| `string[pyarrow]` | 0.138 s | 0.141 s |
| `object` | 0.125 s | 0.124 s |

The `int64`/`object` benchmarks keep GH-65094's gains because their dtype-equality / object-orig short-circuits fire first. The EA microbenchmarks regress 2–8% on the small-N hot path — the cost of restoring per-row pre-casting for the EA cases. I'd argue that's worth it to avoid the catastrophic regression on the large-N case GH-65094 was supposed to be improving in the first place.

## Test plan

- [x] `pandas/tests/extension/` + `pandas/tests/indexing/` — 46608 passed, 0 failures
- [x] `pyright pandas/core/frame.py` — clean
- [x] `pre-commit run --files pandas/core/frame.py` — clean
- [x] Manually verified array-level state preservation with a synthetic geopandas-style EA (state on `array.tag`, analogous to CRS): `tag="EPSG:4326"` survives the append on this PR, becomes `None` on current `main`.

I have not added a regression test in the repo — the geopandas case can't be tested directly without a new test dependency, and the closest synthetic reproduction needs a ~70-line custom `ExtensionArray`. Happy to add one if reviewers want — let me know which form you'd prefer.

title: CI: lowercase types-pymysql/types-pyyaml to fix mamba 2.6.0 shard lookup
body:
## Summary

- Lowercase ``types-PyMySQL`` → ``types-pymysql`` and ``types-PyYAML`` → ``types-pyyaml`` in ``environment.yml`` and ``requirements-dev.txt``.
- Fixes the Code Checks job that has been failing on every PR since 2026-04-29 ~21:00 UTC with:

  ```
  error    libmamba Could not solve for environment specs
      The following package could not be installed
      └─ types-pymysql =* * does not exist (perhaps a typo or a missing channel).
  ```

## Root cause

[mamba 2.6.0](https://github.com/mamba-org/mamba/releases/tag/2.6.0) was released on 2026-04-29 14:04 UTC and made **sharded repodata the default**. Shard keys on conda-forge are normalized to lowercase (the feedstock recipe sets ``package.name: {{ name|lower }}``), and the new shard lookup is case-sensitive. Mixed-case entries in ``environment.yml`` therefore stop resolving — even though the packages still exist on the channel.

The Unit Tests workflow is unaffected because it switched to pixi; only Code Checks (and the doc build) still go through ``setup-micromamba`` + ``environment.yml``.

The mamba-org/setup-micromamba action is already pinned by SHA in our workflow, but it downloads the latest micromamba binary on each run, which is why a pure upstream change broke us without any workflow edit.

## Test plan

## Summary

- Fixes a label-equality check in `_get_merge_keys` that compared `lk == rk` directly. NaN compares unequal to itself, so `merge(left_on=np.nan, right_on=np.nan)` failed to drop the right-side duplicate column. `pd.NA` on either side raised `TypeError: boolean value of NA is ambiguous`.

title: BUG: Index.get_indexer matches pd.NA against NaN for list input but not ndarray input

labels.name: Indexing
labels.description: Related to indexing on series/frames, not to indexes themselves

body:
`Index.get_indexer` gives different answers for `[pd.NA]` (list) vs `np.array([pd.NA], dtype=object)` on a NaN-containing index. The list path normalizes `pd.NA` to NaN; the ndarray path doesn't. `Index.get_loc` (scalar lookup) also matches. This propagates into `Index.drop`, which routes through `com.index_labels_to_array` (producing an ndarray) and so cannot drop a NaN-labeled entry given `pd.NA`.

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

idx = pd.Index([np.nan, "b"])

idx.get_loc(np.nan)                              # 0
idx.get_loc(pd.NA)                               # 0  <- matches

idx.get_indexer([pd.NA])                         # array([0])   <- matches
idx.get_indexer(np.array([pd.NA], dtype=object)) # array([-1])  <- doesn't
idx.get_indexer(pd.Index([pd.NA]))               # array([-1])  <- doesn't

idx.drop([pd.NA])   # KeyError: '[<NA>] not found in axis'
idx.drop([np.nan])  # works
```

Surfaces from `merge`: a DataFrame built with `{pd.NA: ...}` has columns coerced to a NaN label, so `merge(left_on=pd.NA, right_on=pd.NA)` resolves keys correctly via `_get_label_or_level_values` (which uses `get_loc`) but fails on the `right_drop` path via `_drop_labels_or_levels` -> `Index.drop`.

The scalar-lookup paths (`get_loc`, list `get_indexer`) treat `pd.NA` as matching NaN; the array-lookup paths (ndarray/Index `get_indexer`, `Index.drop`) don't. Either both should match, or neither should.

title: BUG: DataFrame.loc setitem-with-expansion preserves dtype for list-like values (GH-42099)
body:
## Summary

Fixes two FIXMEs in `pandas/core/indexing.py`:

- **Stale FIXME (line 1040)** — `_expand_ellipsis` already raises `IndexingError` if more than one Ellipsis is present (a few lines above), so the comment was no longer accurate. Removed.
- **Real bug (line 2471, GH-42099)** — `_setitem_new_column` seeded a brand-new column from a list-like value via `infer_fill_value(value)`, which produced wrong fill values for several common cases:
  - `df.loc[[0, 1, 2], "data"] = ["a", "b", "c"]` filled unselected rows with the literal string `"n"`. Chain: `np.asarray([\"a\",\"b\",\"c\"])` infers dtype `<U1`, then `np.array(np.nan, dtype=\"<U1\")` casts `nan` to `\"nan\"` and truncates to width 1 → `\"n\"`. Wider strings would have produced `\"na\"`, `\"nan\"`, etc. — same root cause, less obviously wrong.
  - `df.loc[[0, 1, 2], "data"] = [True, False, True]` raised `TypeError` because the column was first initialized as float64, and writing booleans into it triggered `LossySetitemError`.

The fix mirrors the existing `is_array_like(value)` branch: convert the list to an array via `sanitize_array`, build an NA-filled column with `take_nd`, then write the values directly. The follow-up `_setitem_with_indexer` call is no longer needed for this branch since values are already written.

title: BUG: Categorical.map with defaultdict replaces NA with NaN

labels.name: Missing-data
labels.description: np.nan, pd.NaT, pd.NA, dropna, isnull, interpolate

body: closes #62710 ## Problem `Series.map()` on a categorical column with a `defaultdict` and `na_action=None` incorrectly replaces `NA` values with `float("NaN")` instead of mapping them through the defaultdict's default factory. **Reproducer (before fix):** The non-categorical column `a` correctly returns `True`, but the categorical column `b` returns `NaN` at row 2 instead of `True`. ## Root Cause In `Categorical.map` (`categorical.py`), the NA value was computed using `mapper.get(np.nan, np.nan)` for dict-like mappers. For a `defaultdict`, `.get()` bypasses `__missing__` and returns `None` instead of invoking the default factory — that `None` then gets cast to `float("NaN")` during Series construction. ## Fix Use `mapper[np.nan]` (which honors `__missing__`) with a `KeyError` fallback for dict-like mappers, matching the behavior already used for callable mappers. **After fix:** ## Tests Added two regression tests in `pandas/tests/arrays/categorical/test_map.py`: - `test_map_defaultdict_na_action_none` — verifies NA is passed through the default factory - `test_map_defaultdict_na_action_ignore` — verifies NA is preserved when `na_action="ignore"`

title: CI: pin pyodide-build to fix venv pip wrapper crash
body:
## Summary

The `Pyodide build` CI job has been failing on `main` since pip 26.1 was released. `pyodide venv` generates a pip wrapper that runs on the host CPython but patches `sys.platform` to `"emscripten"` before invoking pip. pip 26.1 bumped its vendored urllib3 to a version whose `urllib3.contrib.emscripten` package imports `js` eagerly, so every pip invocation in the venv crashes with:

```
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'js'
  at .venv-pyodide/.../pip/_vendor/urllib3/contrib/emscripten/fetch.py:45
```

This is upstream issue [pyodide/pyodide-build#339](https://github.com/pyodide/pyodide-build/issues/339), fixed in [pyodide/pyodide-build#341](https://github.com/pyodide/pyodide-build/pull/341) by importing `pip._vendor.urllib3` before patching `sys.platform`. The fix is merged on `main` but not yet released.

Pin `pyodide-build` to the merge commit (`471889b`) until a release containing the fix ships.

body:

- [ ] Added an entry in the latest `doc/source/whatsnew/vX.X.X.rst` file if fixing a bug or adding a new feature.

## Summary

Speeds up `pandas.tseries.frequencies.to_offset` string parsing. Stacked on top of GH-65390 (remove `_offset_map` cache); review/merge that first.

The big win is on tick-resolution offsets ("h", "min", "s", "ms", "us", "ns", "D"). The previous implementation built a `Timedelta(1, unit=name)`, called `delta_to_tick` to wrap it as a Tick, then multiplied by `float(stride)` — which calls `Tick.__mul__(float)`, which calls `np.isclose` on every invocation. That last step alone dominated profiles. Now we look the prefix up in a small `{name: (TickKlass, factor)}` dict and construct the Tick subclass directly for integer strides; fractional strides like "2.5min" still fall through to the old path so unit-promotion semantics are preserved.

A few smaller wins on the non-tick path:
- Drop `int(np.fabs(stride) * stride_sign)` (numpy scalar dance) in favor of explicit sign-aware Python int multiplication, mirroring the tick path.
- Convert `_warn_about_deprecated_aliases` and `_validate_to_offset_alias` to `cdef`. Both are only called from `to_offset`, so no public-API impact.
- Cache `alias.upper()` in `_validate_to_offset_alias` (was being called up to 3 times).
- Precompute `c_PERIOD_AND_OFFSET_DEPR_FREQSTR.values()` as a frozenset (was an O(n) values-view lookup per call).
- Walk the regex split by index rather than `zip(split[0::4], split[1::4], split[2::4])` — drops three list-slice copies and the zip object on every call.

## Perf

Microbench, per-call timings (Python 3.13, M-series mac):

| freq | before | after | speedup |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `"h"` | 10.6 µs | 0.84 µs | **12.6x** |
| `"5min"` | 10.6 µs | 0.93 µs | **11.4x** |
| `"D"` | 10.8 µs | 0.91 µs | **11.9x** |
| `"3s"` | 10.5 µs | 0.77 µs | **13.7x** |
| `"3D"` | 10.8 µs | 0.90 µs | **12.0x** |
| `"-3D"` | 10.7 µs | 1.02 µs | **10.5x** |
| `"1D1h"` | 21.5 µs | 1.59 µs | **13.5x** |
| `"5h30min"` | 25.0 µs | 4.55 µs | **5.5x** |
| `"ME"` | 2.04 µs | 1.08 µs | **1.9x** |
| `"BMS"` | 2.30 µs | 1.02 µs | **2.3x** |
| `"YS-MAR"` | 2.50 µs | 1.50 µs | **1.7x** |
| `"B"` | 2.20 µs | 1.23 µs | **1.8x** |
| `"2.5min"` | 17.5 µs | 16.9 µs | 1.0x (intentionally unchanged) |

`BaseOffset` passthrough, `None`, and `timedelta` paths are unchanged.

Also adds asv benchmarks (`ToOffset`, `ToOffsetPassthrough`) since none existed for `to_offset`.

title: PERF: skip redundant Index.equals calls in pd.concat
body:
### Problem

`pd.concat` compares the same logical pair of indexes twice:

1. `union_indexes` → `all_indexes_same` (`indexes/api.py:337`) walks the inputs pairwise (`first.equals(idx)` for each other), and returns `indexes[0]` when they all match.
2. Then `_get_result` (`reshape/concat.py:652`) re-runs `new_labels.equals(obj_labels)` per obj to decide whether reindexing is needed — re-asking the same question.

In the common case where input frames are separately-constructed with content-equal-but-identity-distinct column indexes, ~50% of all `Index.equals` calls under `pd.concat` are this duplicate.

### Numbers (per call, inputs pre-built outside the timer)

| workload | before | after | speedup |
|---|---|---|---|
| 100 frames, 50 cols, single-block float | 0.62 ms | 0.50 ms | **1.25x** |
| 1000 frames, 50 cols, single-block float | 6.76 ms | 5.70 ms | 1.19x |
| 100 frames, 20 cols, multi-block (dict-built) | 0.64 ms | 0.49 ms | **1.31x** |
| 20 sibling-tables, axis=1, 1000 rows | 0.19 ms | 0.15 ms | 1.25x |
| 200 frames built fresh + concat (read-many-files) | 7.96 ms | 7.58 ms | 1.05x |

"After" estimated by short-circuiting duplicate `(id(self), id(other))` pairs with a per-concat memoization cache.

### Beneficiary

Patterns that build frames separately then concat them: `pd.concat([pd.read_csv(f) for f in files])` and equivalents.

`groupby.apply` and `pd.concat([df.iloc[a:b] for ...])` see **zero** `Index.equals` calls (slices share the parent's Index identity, `_get_distinct_objs` collapses them) — this change is a no-op for those.

### Proposed change

Return an `all_equal` flag from `union_indexes` when it takes the `all_indexes_same`-True branch, and thread it through `_get_combined_index` → `new_axes` → `_get_result`. When True, `_get_result` skips the per-obj `equals` and uses empty indexers.

Happy to put up a PR.

title: CLN: remove _offset_map cache in offsets.pyx
body:
## Summary

Removes the `_offset_map` dict cache inside `_get_offset` (offsets.pyx). It was added in 2012 (commit `0cc1a3d`) when offset construction was slow enough that caching alias→offset lookups was worth it.

Today the cache buys very little:
- Construction itself is ~0.3 µs; the cache saves ~0.3 µs at the bare-`_get_offset` level and ~0.5 µs at the realistic `to_offset(non-tick)` level (~5–25%).
- Tick aliases (`D`, `h`, `min`, `s`, `ms`, `us`, `ns`) bypass `_get_offset` entirely, so the cache never serves them.
- `to_offset` itself never returned cached identity even with the cache, because the trailing `offset * int(np.fabs(stride) * stride_sign)` step always produces a fresh instance. So `to_offset(name) is to_offset(name)` was already `False` for every name, and equality is preserved.

After the change, `_get_offset` is just `prefix_mapping[split[0]]._from_name(*split[1:])` with the existing error wrapping.

title: BUG: Timedelta.total_seconds drops sub-microsecond nanosecond component
body:
- closes #46819

## Summary

`Timedelta.total_seconds()` combines days, seconds, and microseconds but silently drops the sub-microsecond nanosecond component. For example, ``Timedelta(nanoseconds=999).total_seconds()`` returned ``0.0`` instead of ``9.99e-7``, and ``Timedelta("1us 500ns").total_seconds()`` returned ``1e-6`` instead of ``1.5e-6``. The fix adds the missing ``self._ns / 1_000_000_000`` term.

A pre-existing ``# TODO: add nanos/1e9?`` comment had flagged this. The existing ``test_total_seconds_scalar`` regression test silently passed because ``assert_almost_equal`` defaults to 5-decimal tolerance, hiding the up-to-456 ns error.

title: PERF: Speed up Timedelta.total_seconds
body:
## Summary

- `_Timedelta.total_seconds()` reads `_d/_h/_m/_s/_ms/_us` directly instead of going through the `days`, `seconds`, and `microseconds` `@property` descriptors. ~3.3x faster on a microbenchmark (~118 ns → ~36 ns/call).

title: TYP: tighten Timestamp/Timedelta round/floor/ceil return types
body:
## Summary

- `Timestamp.round/floor/ceil` end with `result.tz_localize(self.tz, ambiguous=ambiguous, nonexistent=nonexistent)` when tz-aware, so they really can return `NaT` when `ambiguous='NaT'` or `nonexistent='NaT'`. - `Timedelta.round/floor/ceil` carried the same TODO, but the implementation has no tz path: `_round` only ever returns `self`, returns `Timedelta._from_value_and_reso(...)`, or raises `OutOfBoundsTimedelta`/`ValueError`. The TODO was stale and is removed without a signature change.

>>> dti = pd.DatetimeIndex(['2023-11-05 01:30:00']).tz_localize('US/Eastern', ambiguous=[True])
>>> dti[0].floor('h', ambiguous='NaT')

title: PERF: cache BlockManager.get_dtypes() result

labels.name: Internals
labels.description: Related to non-user accessible pandas implementation

body:
### Problem

`BaseBlockManager.get_dtypes()` (`pandas/core/internals/managers.py:339`) rebuilds an object array on every call:

```python
def get_dtypes(self) -> npt.NDArray[np.object_]:
    dtypes = np.array([blk.dtype for blk in self.blocks], dtype=object)
    return dtypes.take(self.blknos)
```

It's called from a number of hot paths — `df.dtypes`, `DataFrame.fillna` (`generic.py:6391`), `select_dtypes`/`_get_numeric_data`, `DataFrame.apply` (`frame.py:15751`), `unique_dtypes` in repr/info (`generic.py:7136`), and twice per `iloc` setitem (`indexing.py:944, 975`). For wide, fragmented managers each call is O(nblocks) Python iteration plus an object-array allocation.

### Numbers (1000-col DataFrame, 335 blocks, mixed f8/i8/object)

| call | current | with cache | speedup |
|---|---|---|---|
| `mgr.get_dtypes()` | 47 us | 0.08 us | **608x** |
| `df.dtypes` | 58 us | 8.7 us | **6.7x** |

Caching saves the full cost on cache hits; `df.dtypes` retains ~8 us of unavoidable Series-construction overhead.

### Proposed change

Add a `_dtypes_cache` attribute on the manager, populated lazily in `get_dtypes()` and invalidated alongside the existing `_blknos` / `_interleaved_dtype` cache hooks (`managers.py:1411, 1497` and other block-mutation sites). The same invalidation pattern is already in place — adding one more entry is mechanical.

### Caveats

- The cached array must not be mutated in place by callers. A quick audit of callers shows they only read it (equality checks, `.take`, iteration) — no in-place writes — but worth confirming during review.
- `SingleBlockManager` already has only one block; the cache is still cheap and consistent.

Happy to put up a PR.

In non-ISO8601 cases we use dateutil's parser, but this is 1) not-optimized pure-python and 2) parses some strings that we probably should raise on, e.g.:

"Jan"
"10am"
"5th"
"1234"

The hard part here is deciding exactly what cases we want to allow and a deprecation cycle for cases that we disallow.

Using a regex with a fixed set of formats would be significantly faster (preliminary benchmarks are 5-15x on cases with month name sand 100x on cases with "AM" or "PM").

Running list of issues that this might address: #17265

title: PERF: skip to_datetime cache=True overhead for input shapes where it cannot help
body:
#### Summary

`to_datetime(..., cache=True)` (the default) unconditionally runs the
`_maybe_cache` machinery — `Series(dtype=object)` construction +
`should_cache` which iterates up to 500 elements of the input — even on
inputs where `_convert_listlike_datetimes` is going to dispatch to a
non-parsing path or a path where caching has been measured to never help.
On these inputs `cache=True` is strictly slower than `cache=False`, by
margins ranging from a few percent to **~520×** at the worst.

All five "no-help" conditions are identifiable in O(1) time, before any
sampling, just by looking at `arg.dtype`, the `unit` kwarg, and the
`format` kwarg.

#### Affected input shapes (all O(1) to detect)

1. `unit is not None` — input is dispatched to `_to_datetime_with_unit`,
   which is a vectorized cast; caching cannot help.
2. `arg.dtype` is `np.dtype("M8[*]")` — already datetime64; `_convert_listlike_datetimes` short-circuits.
3. `arg.dtype` is `DatetimeTZDtype` — already tz-aware; short-circuits.
4. `arg.dtype` is `ArrowDtype` with `type is Timestamp` — short-circuits.
5. `format is not None and format != "mixed"` — `array_strptime` is fast
   enough that `pd.unique()` + `Series.map()` costs as much as just
   re-parsing; `cache=True` is never a measurable win on this path.

#### Reproducer

```python
import time
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd


def best(fn, k=5):
    fn()  # warmup
    times = []
    for _ in range(k):
        t0 = time.perf_counter()
        fn()
        times.append(time.perf_counter() - t0)
    return min(times)


def bench(label, arg, **kwargs):
    t_off = best(lambda: pd.to_datetime(arg, cache=False, **kwargs))
    t_on = best(lambda: pd.to_datetime(arg, cache=True, **kwargs))
    print(f"{label:<35s}  off={t_off*1000:7.2f}ms  on={t_on*1000:7.2f}ms  on/off={t_on/t_off:.2f}x")


n = 100_000
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

arr_unit = np.arange(n, dtype="int64")
arr_dt64 = pd.date_range("2020-01-01", periods=n, freq="s").to_numpy()
idx_tz = pd.date_range("2020-01-01", periods=n, freq="s", tz="US/Eastern")
base_iso = pd.date_range("2020-01-01", periods=100, freq="s").strftime("%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S").to_numpy()
arr_iso = base_iso[rng.integers(0, 100, n)]

bench("unit='s' int", arr_unit, unit="s")
bench("datetime64 ndarray", arr_dt64)
bench("DatetimeIndex tz=US/Eastern", idx_tz)
bench("ISO strings, format=...", arr_iso, format="%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S")
```

#### Measurements

On `main` (today, n=100k unless noted):

| Input | `cache=False` | `cache=True` | Ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| `unit='s'` int (10% unique) | 0.07 ms | 0.78 ms | **11.0×** slower |
| `unit='s'` int (n=100k all-unique) | 0.07 ms | 0.92 ms | **13.4×** slower |
| `datetime64[ns]` ndarray | 0.03 ms | 0.07 ms | 2.6× slower |
| `DatetimeIndex` w/ tz (any n) | 0.01 ms | 6.15 ms | **~520×** slower |
| `ArrowDtype` timestamp (any n) | 0.01 ms | 0.64 ms | ~50× slower |
| ISO + explicit format (n=10k, 100 unique) | 0.82 ms | 1.19 ms | 1.45× slower |
| ISO + explicit format (n=10k, 10 unique) | 0.80 ms | 1.26 ms | 1.57× slower |

The DatetimeTZ case is the worst: `should_cache` does
`set(islice(arg, 500))`, which on a tz-aware DatetimeIndex materializes
500 `Timestamp` Python objects (~6 ms), and that cost is paid regardless
of `n`. A `to_datetime` round-trip on an already-converted `DatetimeIndex`
of any size is dominated entirely by this useless sampling step.

#### Where the caching gate lives

`pandas/core/tools/datetimes.py`:

- `_maybe_cache` is called from the dispatch in `to_datetime` (lines ~1081, 1090, 1104) **before** `_convert_listlike_datetimes` runs its dtype short-circuits (lines ~367–412).
- `should_cache` (lines 156–213) does the iteration that costs ~6 ms on tz-aware DTIs.

#### Proposed fix

Add an O(1) early-bail at the top of `_maybe_cache`:

```python
if cache:
    if unit is not None:
        return cache_array
    arg_dtype = getattr(arg, "dtype", None)
    if (
        lib.is_np_dtype(arg_dtype, "M")
        or isinstance(arg_dtype, DatetimeTZDtype)
        or (isinstance(arg_dtype, ArrowDtype) and arg_dtype.type is Timestamp)
    ):
        return cache_array
    if format is not None and format != "mixed":
        return cache_array
    ...
```

`unit` would need to be threaded from the dispatch sites (currently bound
in the partial only). No behavior change — every one of these inputs hits
a short-circuit / non-parsing path in the next call.

#### Out of scope (separate follow-ups)

- `format=None` on ISO strings where format inference succeeds → strptime path. Same loss profile as the explicit-format case, but only detectable by deferring the cache decision past format inference.
- `should_cache`'s `unique_share=0.7` threshold is calibrated for the slow
  dateutil path and is too generous for fast-parse inputs that get past
  the O(1) gate.

#### Pandas version
pandas `main` @ `501e319b0b`.

title: BUG: nansem with mask + skipna=False + axis returns scalar nan instead of array
body:
closes #65373

Problem: nansem with mask + skipna=False + axis={0,1} returned a scalar
np.nan instead of an array due to an early return that ignored the axis
argument entirely.

Fix: Narrowed the early return guard to axis=None only. For axis=0/1,
nanvar already propagates nan correctly per-slice, so the early return
was unnecessary and wrong.

title: BUG: nansem with mask + skipna + axis={0,1} returns scalar np.nan instead of array of np.nan
body:
### Pandas version checks

### Reproducible Example

```python
import numpy as np
from pandas.core.nanops import nansem

values = np.array(
    [
        [np.nan, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0],
        [0.0, np.nan, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0],
        [0.0, 1.0, np.nan, 3.0, 4.0],
        [0.0, 1.0, 2.0, np.nan, 4.0],

        [False, False, True, False, False],
        [False, False, False, True, False],
        [False, False, False, False, True],
        [True, False, False, False, False],

# expected: np.array([np.nan, np.nan, np.nan, np.nan, np.nan])
```

`nansem`, contrary to other reductions in nanops, returns a scalar `np.nan` instead of an array of `np.nan` in the example above.

title: BUG: str.replace hangs indefinitely on empty pattern with PyArrow backend
body:
- [x] closes #64941
- [x] Tests added and passed if fixing a bug or adding a new feature
- [ ] All code checks passed.
- [ ] Added type annotations to new arguments/methods/functions.
- [x] Added an entry in the latest `doc/source/whatsnew/v3.1.0.rst` file if fixing a bug or adding a new feature.
- [x] I have reviewed and followed all the contribution guidelines
- [x] If I used AI to develop this pull request, I prompted it to follow `AGENTS.md`.

## Problem

`Series.str.replace("", ...)` with a PyArrow-backed Series hangs indefinitely, catching kill signals, making the process unresponsive. The hang also reproduces in CI (e.g. skrub-data/skrub#1772).

Root cause: PyArrow's `replace_substring` / `replace_substring_regex` enters an infinite loop when given an empty pattern (apache/arrow#39149). After substituting at position 0, the loop advances by `len("") = 0` and never moves forward.

A previous fix (GH#56404, GH#56406) guarded against negative `max_replacements`, but empty patterns were not addressed.

## Fix

In `_arrow_string_mixins._str_replace`, detect `pat == ""` before calling into PyArrow and fall back to element-wise Python processing, which replicates Python's own semantics:

```python
"abcd".replace("", "")   # -> "abcd"        (no-op)
"abcd".replace("", "X")  # -> "XaXbXcXdX"  (insert at every position)
```

Both `regex=True` (via `re.sub`) and `regex=False` (via `str.replace`) paths are handled. `None` / `NA` values are preserved.

## AI disclosure

I used Claude Code (claude-sonnet-4-6) to locate the hang site and draft the fix. I reviewed the logic — checking that `re.sub("", ...)` and `str.replace("", ...)` produce identical output for the empty-pattern case, and that the `n` / `count` semantics map correctly — before committing.

title: DOC: `to_numeric` "Returns" is missing Index and scalars, may have other problems
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that the issue still exists on the latest versions of the docs on `main` [here](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/)


### Location of the documentation

https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/reference/api/pandas.to_numeric.html

> **Returns:**
> **ret**
> Numeric if parsing succeeded. Return type depends on input. Series if Series, otherwise ndarray.

### Documentation problem

The documentation is missing these return types:

### Index

1-d specifically

Example:
```py
>>> pd.to_numeric(pd.Index(['0']))
Index([0], dtype='int64')
```

Source:
https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/be0642f7cb8900282a43b53cd50cf00a05161ed6/pandas/core/tools/numeric.py#L318-L323

### Scalars

Example:
```py
>>> pd.to_numeric('0')
np.int64(0)
```

Source:
https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/be0642f7cb8900282a43b53cd50cf00a05161ed6/pandas/core/tools/numeric.py#L202-L210

https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/be0642f7cb8900282a43b53cd50cf00a05161ed6/pandas/core/tools/numeric.py#L324-L325

### Additionally

"Numeric if parsing succeeded" implies there's a different return type if parsing failed, but the function would actually **raise** in that case (instead of returning), if I understand correctly. Or it would return NaN, but that's still a numeric type, even though it's called "not a number".

Also, the `dtype_backend` parameter says: "Back-end data type applied to the resultant **DataFrame**", but `to_numeric` can't return a DataFrame as far as I know. I tried it just to confirm:
```py
>>> pd.to_numeric(pd.DataFrame([0]))
TypeError: arg must be a list, tuple, 1-d array, or Series

>>> pd.to_numeric(pd.DataFrame([0]), dtype_backend='pyarrow')
TypeError: arg must be a list, tuple, 1-d array, or Series

>>> pd.to_numeric(pd.DataFrame([0]), dtype_backend='numpy_nullable')
TypeError: arg must be a list, tuple, 1-d array, or Series
```

### Suggested fix for documentation

I don't understand all the ins and outs of the function, but I'll try my best:

Change "Returns" to:
> **Returns:**
> **numeric**
> Return type depends on input. For numeric inputs, the type is preserved. For scalars: `int` if possible, otherwise `float`. For 1-d: Series if Series, Index if Index, otherwise ndarray.

Change `dtype_backend` paramter to: "Back-end data type applied to the resultant Series or Index"

title: Test: Add regression test for DataFrame.sum() with negative values and NaN
body:
## What does this test?
Adds a regression test to ensure `DataFrame.sum()` correctly handles:
- Negative numbers
- NaN values (ignored by default)  
- Mixed positive/negative columns

## Why is this needed?
Currently there is no explicit test for the combination of:
1. Negative values
2. NaN values in the same DataFrame
3. Multiple columns with different signs

This is common when working with:
- Financial data (profits/losses)
- Temperature changes
- Performance metrics (gains/losses)

## Test Verification
The test verifies that:
- NaN values are ignored (not included in sum)
- Negative values are summed correctly
- Works with multiple columns having different signs

Example:
```python
df = DataFrame({
    "losses": [-100, np.nan, -50, -25],  # Sum: -175
    "gains": [50, 100, np.nan, 75]       # Sum: 225
})
df.sum()  # Returns {"losses": -175.0, "gains": 225.0}

title: BUG: select_dtypes ExtensionDtype handling (GH#40234, GH#59888)

labels.name: ExtensionArray
labels.description: Extending pandas with custom dtypes or arrays.

body:
- closes #40234
- closes #59888

## Summary

`select_dtypes` routed every spec through `infer_dtype_from_object`, collapsing EA and numpy dtypes into a shared `dtype.type` / `issubclass` matching space. This caused several unrelated issues:

- `select_dtypes("Int64")` and `select_dtypes(pd.Int64Dtype)` silently matched numpy `int64` columns as well as the Int64 EA (GH-40234).
- `select_dtypes(include=["datetime64[ns]"])` silently matched Arrow `timestamp[ns][pyarrow]` columns, and `include=["timestamp[ns][pyarrow]"]` returned empty (GH-59888).
- Passing a parameterized EA class like `pd.ArrowDtype` or `pd.DatetimeTZDtype` as a spec emitted a spurious `UserWarning: Instantiating X without any arguments`.

Resolves the conflation by routing user-facing dtype specs into three distinct buckets:

- **Numpy scalar types** (`np.int64`, `np.dtype("int64")`) — match by `issubclass` on `dtype.type`. Storage-specific.
- **`ExtensionDtype` requests** — class → match any instance of that class (kind), instance → exact `==` (identity).
- **Kind-name strings** (`"int64"`, `"float64"`, `"datetime"`, `"bool"`, ...) — match by `(dtype.kind, dtype.itemsize)` across numpy, masked, and Arrow backends.

The third bucket gives us the kind reading reviewers asked for: `select_dtypes("int64")` selects every int64 column regardless of storage (numpy, Int64Dtype, ArrowDtype), `select_dtypes("datetime")` selects naive numpy, tz-aware DatetimeTZDtype, and Arrow timestamp columns alike. Type-based specs (`np.int64`, `pd.Int64Dtype()`) remain storage-/identity-specific.

EA-parseable strings unify under one rule: bracket-free strings (`"category"`, `"string"`, `"Int64"`) are class (kind) requests, bracketed strings (`"datetime64[ns, UTC]"`, `"timestamp[ns][pyarrow]"`) are instance (identity) requests. The hand-maintained legacy alias map shrinks to just `"datetimetz"`/`"datetime64tz"` (the strings that don't parse via `pandas_dtype`).

As a natural consequence, passing an EA class (e.g. `pd.ArrowDtype`, `pd.DatetimeTZDtype`) now works as a "kind" request matching any instance of that class, with no warning. For `StringDtype` and `CategoricalDtype` the kind reading spans backends: `"string"`/`"str"`/`str` also match Arrow `string`/`large_string`/`string_view` columns (as on main, where the `numpy_dtype` unwrap provided this), and `"category"` also matches Arrow `dictionary` columns. This keeps `DataFrame.plot.scatter(..., c=...)` working with Arrow-backed string columns (the scatter include list relies on `"string"`/`"category"`).

`get_dummies` previously relied on the `ArrowDtype` → `numpy_dtype` unwrap to include Arrow string columns via `include=["object"]`. Its two `select_dtypes` calls are replaced by a local `_is_encodable` predicate fed to `BlockManager._get_data_subset`, preserving existing behavior (GH-56273) without reintroducing the cross-class match. The predicate checks `is_object_dtype` last, since it raises for Arrow `string_view` columns (`ArrowDtype.type` is not implemented for them — a pre-existing gap that also makes the eventual encode raise, on main and here alike).

### Behavior changes

- EA instance specs (e.g. `DatetimeTZDtype("UTC")`, `ArrowDtype(pa.int64())`) now match by exact dtype equality. To match "any tz" / "any Arrow int", pass the class instead.
- `select_dtypes(np.int64)` (the numpy *type*) no longer matches `Int64` EA columns — but `select_dtypes("int64")` (the string *kind*) selects both, plus Arrow int64.
- `select_dtypes("datetime")` / `"datetime64"` now match `DatetimeTZDtype` and Arrow timestamp columns in addition to numpy `datetime64`. Previously matched numpy only.
- As fallout of the previous point, `DataFrame.describe()` with the default `include=None` now includes tz-aware datetime columns, consistent with tz-naive ones (which it has included since 2.0). Whatsnew note added under Timezones.

## Test plan

- [x] New tests for GH-40234, GH-59888 (both halves + symmetric Arrow-int case), parameterized-class warning elimination, class-as-kind semantics for `ArrowDtype` / `DatetimeTZDtype` / `CategoricalDtype`, kind-string matching across backends for int64/float64/datetime, and the Python-`str` route under `future.infer_string`
- [x] New tests: `"string"`/`StringDtype` and `"category"`/`CategoricalDtype` matching Arrow-backed columns (include and exclude), scatter `c=` with an Arrow string column, `describe()` default including tz-aware columns
- [x] Existing `test_select_dtypes.py` suite passes (53 pass, 4 existing skips)
- [x] Broader pass across `frame/`, `dtypes/`, `extension/`, `arrays/`, `reshape/`, `plotting/`, `window/`, `io/json/` (85,341 pass, no regressions)
- [x] `pre-commit`, `mypy`, `pyright` clean
