title: PERF: speed up read_sas string columns

labels.name: Strings
labels.description: String extension data type and string data

labels.name: Mothballed
labels.description: Temporarily-closed PR the author plans to return to

body:
## Summary

For `read_sas` on SAS7BDAT files with string columns, the Cython parser
previously produced one Python `bytes` object per cell, then the Python
side called `Series.str.decode` followed by `.astype("str")`. This PR
adds two fast paths that skip most of that work plus a related
`DataFrame` construction speedup. xref GH-47339.

- **pyarrow large_string fast path** (default when `using_string_dtype()`
  is on and the resolved `StringDtype` storage is pyarrow): the Cython
  loop writes utf-8 bytes + int64 offsets + per-cell validity directly
  into per-column buffers, which are wrapped via `pa.Array.from_buffers`
  in `_chunk_to_dataframe`. utf-8 source bytes are memcpy'd verbatim and
  validated after assembly; latin-1 expands to utf-8 inline; other
  single-byte encodings (ascii, cp1252) translate through a cached
  256-entry utf-8 lookup table.

- **direct-str fallback**: when the pyarrow path doesn't apply but the
  encoding is utf-8/latin-1/ascii, the Cython loop writes Python `str`
  directly via `PyUnicode_FromStringAndSize` / `PyUnicode_DecodeLatin1` /
  `PyUnicode_DecodeASCII`, so the per-cell `Series.str.decode` pass is
  skipped.

- `_chunk_to_dataframe` now builds a list of arrays and uses
  `DataFrame._from_arrays(verify_integrity=False)` instead of a dict ->
  `DataFrame` round-trip, which removes per-column `Series` wrapping
  and `_homogenize`/reindex.

## Behavior fixes

- Files with duplicate column names: each column now keeps its own data;
  the old dict-based construction silently filled every duplicate with
  the last column's data (whatsnew bug-fix entry included).
- Truncated files (data pages end before the header's `row_count`) raise
  a clear `ValueError` instead of an incidental Series length-mismatch
  error — or, for all-string files on the new path, silently returning
  partial data.
- Bytes invalid for the declared encoding raise `UnicodeDecodeError` on
  every path, matching the previous strict per-cell decode — including
  utf-8 sequences split across cell boundaries, where pyarrow's
  validation error type would otherwise leak.
- `mode.string_storage="python"` keeps returning python-backed
  `StringArray` columns (the fast path only engages for pyarrow storage).
- Compressed files whose worst-case string buffer (declared width x
  nrows x expansion) exceeds 1 GiB fall back to the object path, since
  declared widths can far overstate the actual data; `chunksize=` reads
  stay under the cap.

## Benchmarks

End-to-end on the test fixtures (`encoding="latin-1"`, default
`infer_string=True`), measured on the initial commit:

| file | before | after | speedup |
| --- | --: | --: | --: |
| productsales.sas7bdat (1440 × 10, 5 str) | 2.05 ms | 0.42 ms | 5.12x |
| load_log.sas7bdat (2097 × 8, 7 str) | 3.34 ms | 0.66 ms | 5.19x |
| many_columns.sas7bdat (3 × 392, 6 str) | 9.24 ms | 2.55 ms | 3.62x |
| test5.sas7bdat (10 × 100, 25 str) | 4.83 ms | 0.96 ms | 5.04x |
| test1.sas7bdat (10 × 100, 25 str) | 4.88 ms | 0.94 ms | 5.18x |

For users without pyarrow or with the legacy object dtype, the same
files get ~2.3-3.3x from the direct-str fallback + `_from_arrays`
changes alone.

## Test plan

- [x] `pytest pandas/tests/io/sas/` (127/127 pass; 10 new tests covering
  strict decode errors, invalid utf-8 incl. cell-boundary splits,
  `string_storage="python"`, duplicate column names, truncated files,
  and the compressed buffer cap)
- [x] mypy / pyright clean
- [x] pre-commit clean
- [ ] CI

title: PERF: speed up read_sas for full-precision numeric columns
body:
## Summary

The SAS7BDAT cython parser's inner loop copies bytes from the page buffer into ``byte_chunk`` one byte at a time via ``buf_get`` (a memoryview-indexed read with an assert). The vast majority of SAS numeric columns are stored as full-precision 8-byte doubles, where this loop can be replaced by a single 8-byte load/store. Shorter widths (3–7 bytes) keep the existing per-byte path.

xref #47339

## Benchmarks

156 real-world SAS7BDAT files, best of 5–25 iterations per file, on macOS / Apple Silicon:

| Bucket               | n   | min   | median | max   |
|----------------------|----:|------:|-------:|------:|
| Large (>1 MB)        |   7 | 1.01× | 1.62×  | 1.82× |
| Medium (100KB–1MB)   |  12 | 0.93× | 0.99×  | 1.72× |
| Small (<100KB)       | 137 | 0.82× | 0.98×  | 1.07× |

Top files by absolute time:

```
file                          size_kb     rows  cols  str   before    after  speedup
dr1iff_c.sas7bdat               87457   131164    82    0   70.6ms   39.6ms   1.78x
drxiff_b.sas7bdat               84769   143004    74    0   68.7ms   39.7ms   1.73x
dr1tot_c.sas7bdat               12881     9643   160    0   15.9ms    8.8ms   1.82x
demoadv.sas7bdat                 5809    10122    72    0    6.8ms    4.2ms   1.62x
ct_19931231.sas7bdat            12856   325689     9    3   23.8ms   23.5ms   1.01x  (mixed/narrow floats)
demo_c.sas7bdat                  2513    10122    31    0    3.0ms    1.9ms   1.60x
demo_b.sas7bdat                  2097    11039    24    0    2.5ms    1.6ms   1.60x
calcmilk.sas7bdat                 809    10122    10    0    1.4ms    0.8ms   1.72x
```

The win scales with ``nrows × n_full_precision_float_cols``. Files with mostly short-width float columns see no change. Small (<100 KB) files show occasional 5–20 µs regressions on sub-millisecond reads — likely the cost of the extra ``if lngt == 8`` branch when the fast path never triggers. These are at the noise floor of files dominated by I/O and DataFrame construction, not the inner loop.

### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({'a': [1, 2, 3], 'b': [1, 4, 9], 'c': [1, 8, 27]})

# Scenario 1
print(df.query('b <= a <= c'))
# Returns the first row (Expected)

# Scenario 2
print(df.query('b + 1 <= a <= c'))
# Returns an empty dataframe (Expected)

# Scenario 3
print(df.query('b in (a, c)'))
# Returns an empty dataframe (Shouldn't this also return the first row)

df = pd.DataFrame({'a': ['a', 'a', 'b'], 'b': ['a', 'b', 'c'], 'c': ['b', 'b', 'c']})

# Scenario 4
print(df.query('b in (a, c)'))
# ArrowInvalid error
```

### Issue Description

My gripe is obviously with scenarios 3 and 4. I think the outcome should be consistent and independent of the datatypes of the columns. 

### Expected Behavior

Both the scenarios should either:
- return a filtered dataframe by using a dynamic expression which evaluates column tokens on both the left and the right hand sides (the closest example would be scenarios 1 and 2, although they have 3 operands)
- or throw the same error

Can't paste as I've tested the sample code in a different machine, but I've upgraded pandas to 3.0.2 before doing so.

title: PERF: read_csv parse_dates directly to datetime64 in C parser
body:
## Summary

For columns named in `parse_dates`, the C tokenizer now parses each ISO8601 field from its `const char*` buffer straight into a `datetime64` output, skipping the intermediate `ndarray[object]` of Python strings that `date_converter` would otherwise feed to `to_datetime`.

The new Cython helper `_datetime_box_utf8` in `pandas/_libs/parsers.pyx` handles:
- Naive and tz-aware inputs (uniform offset, including `Z` → UTC)
- Mixed resolutions within a column (single recursive reparse at the widest unit, matching `array_strptime`'s `creso_ever_changed` pattern)
- NaT / na_values / empty fields

The fastpath is semantics-preserving by construction:
- With `date_format=None`, every value must share the layout of the first parsed value (same length, digits/non-digits in the same positions, identical separators), mirroring `to_datetime`'s infer-format-from-first-element behavior. Mixed ISO layouts parse per-row only with `date_format="ISO8601"`, where that is already the documented contract.
- Any case the fastpath can't safely own (non-ISO input, layout mismatch, differing tz offsets, mixed aware+naive, all-NA column, explicit non-ISO `date_format`, `dayfirst=True`, int64 overflow when shifting a fixed offset to UTC) falls back to the existing `_string_box_utf8` + `to_datetime` pipeline.
- In `low_memory=True` (default) chunked reads, the conversion decision must be all-or-nothing for the whole column, not per chunk. Each successfully converted chunk therefore also keeps a raw-byte receipt (a compact arena of the column's words plus offsets, far smaller than the equivalent Python str objects); per-read state carries the format template and tz-awareness across chunks. If any chunk falls back, the earlier chunks' object-string arrays are rebuilt from their receipts, so the result is identical to a non-chunked read. Receipts are dropped when the read completes successfully.

No downstream changes: `date_converter` already passes through arrays with `dtype.kind in "Mm"`. Naive fastpath output is a `DatetimeArray` rather than a raw `ndarray` — transparent to users (same `.dtype`), but it keeps mixed-unit chunks on the ExtensionArray concat path, where raw-ndarray `concat_compat` would silently demote `M8[us]`+`M8[ns]` to object.

## Benchmarks (500k rows, default `low_memory=True`)

| case | main | this PR |
|------|-----:|------:|
| ISO naive `%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S` | 103 ms | **62 ms** |
| ISO tz-aware `...+05:00` | 1000 ms | **73 ms** |
| ISO `Z` → UTC | 476 ms | **65 ms** |
| mixed ISO layouts, `date_format=None` | 76 ms (`str`) | 80 ms (`str`, falls back) |
| mixed ISO layouts, `date_format="ISO8601"` | 103 ms | **59 ms** |
| non-ISO `%m/%d/%Y %H:%M:%S` | 107 ms | 114 ms (falls back) |

Fallback cases pay a small penalty for the attempted fastpath (and, in chunked reads, for rebuilding strings from receipts when a late chunk bails); that is the price of exact slow-path semantics in the cases that previously could diverge.

## Behavior notes

No user-visible behavior changes. Parity with the slow path (python engine / pre-PR C engine) is verified value-for-value and dtype-for-dtype across naive/tz/`Z`/NaT/all-NA/mixed-layout/non-ISO inputs, both `low_memory` modes, multi-chunk reads, and `dtype_backend="numpy_nullable"`/`"pyarrow"`, including:
- mixed ISO layouts with `date_format=None` still fall back to strings
- all-NA columns still come out `datetime64[s]`
- near-bounds tz offsets still raise `OverflowError` instead of wrapping
- a non-ISO value in a late `low_memory` chunk leaves the whole column as the raw strings

## Test plan

- [x] New tests: engine-parity matrix (13 payloads × both `low_memory` modes), `ISO8601` mixed-layout and resolution-bump cases, overflow regression, and four multi-chunk `low_memory` tests (non-ISO fallback, layout-mismatch fallback, all-ISO success, cross-chunk resolution bump)
- [x] All 4442 `pandas/tests/io/parser/` tests pass
- [x] All 1585 `pandas/tests/tools/test_to_datetime.py` + `pandas/tests/tslibs/` tests pass
- [x] `mypy` and `pyright` clean
- [x] pre-commit clean

title: PERF: read_csv faster for integer and string columns
body:
## Summary

Reuse the token lengths the C tokenizer already records in `word_starts` to eliminate redundant `strlen` calls on the hot path, in three spots:

- `str_to_int64` / `str_to_uint64` now receive the token length from the caller (derived from `word_starts`) and pass it to `std::from_chars` as the end pointer, so there is no `strlen` on any path — with or without a thousands separator. Previously the length was recomputed via `strlen` for every numeric token.
- `_string_box_utf8` (the object-dtype / non-pyarrow string path) derives the token length from adjacent `word_starts` entries (via a new `COLITER_NEXT_WITH_IDX` macro) on the `kh_strbox` dedup-miss path. It now also calls `kh_put_strbox` directly — using `ret == 0` to detect an already-present key, dropping the separate `kh_get` lookup — and `PyUnicode_DecodeUTF8` to skip the encoding-name lookup.
- `parser_consume_rows` uses `word_starts[word_deletions]` (the start of the first surviving word) to find the end of the last deleted word, replacing a per-chunk `strlen`.

No new data structures, no `word_lens` array, no changes to the tokenizer inner-loop writes. The length is *derived* from `word_starts`, not stored.

## Numbers

Freshly measured against current `main`, which now includes GH-64515 (SIMD tokenizer), GH-65347 (`from_chars` integer parsing), and GH-65283 (C→pyarrow string output). Base = this branch with the change reverted; patched = this branch — so both wheels include all three of those and differ *only* by this PR. Built clean into isolated venvs; byte-identical parse output on every fixture. M2 MacBook, ABBA-paired (base/patched swapped each round to cancel thermal drift), best-of-3 per cell, 12 rounds; paired t across the 12 rounds (|t|>2.2 → p<0.05 at 11 df).

**Integers** (2M rows × 8 integer columns, default read) — the headline. `from_chars` needs the token length unconditionally (explicit `end` pointer); this PR supplies it from `word_starts` instead of letting `from_chars` recover it with an internal `strlen` — an O(token-length) scan replaced by an O(1) lookup. The speedup scales inversely with integer width (narrower files spend proportionally more time in per-field parsing, so removing the scan helps them most); all rows faster in 12/12 rounds:

| scenario | best Δ | median Δ | paired t |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `int_narrow_8col` (1–4 digit) | −13.3% | −12.9% | −197 |
| `int_8col` (~10 digit) | −10.0% | −9.4% | −104 |
| `int_wide_8col` (18–19 digit) | −4.4% | −3.4% | −20.5 |
| `uint_8col` (~20 digit) | −3.7% | −3.5% | −44.8 |
| `chunked_int_8col_50k` | −8.9% | −7.7% | −23.5 |

A byte-identical `num_float_8col` control (this PR does not touch float parsing) reads +0.4%, quantifying ~0.4% of build-layout bias against the patched wheel — so the real speedups are marginally *larger* than the figures above.

**Strings.** The `_string_box_utf8` refinement speeds up `dtype=object` reads — and *all* string reads when pyarrow is not installed — by roughly **15–20%** on high-cardinality columns (e.g. `str_medium_8col` −15.2%, `str_long_8col` −20.0% median, 12/12 rounds); low-cardinality and 1–2-char columns are within the ~0.4% noise floor. Note the scope: default `str`-dtype reads with pyarrow installed route through the C→pyarrow path added in GH-65283, which this PR leaves byte-for-byte unchanged (0%). Float parsing is likewise untouched.

## Behavior note

Fields containing an embedded NUL byte change behavior on the object-dtype string path: previously the C engine truncated every such value at the NUL (`x\0y` -> `"x"`, consistently). Now the first occurrence of a token decodes to its full length, but the interning table still keys on the C string, so a later token with the same pre-NUL prefix (`x\0z`) gets the first occurrence's value. Both behaviors are wrong for this (pathological) input; there is no cheap fix without reintroducing the scan this PR removes. Integer parsing is unaffected (`from_chars` stops at the NUL regardless of the supplied length).

## Test plan

- [x] `pytest pandas/tests/io/parser/` — 4485 passed, 174 skipped, 192 xfailed
- [x] `pre-commit run` clean on changed files
- [ ] CI

## Problem

`DataFrame.query()` raised a `KeyError` when a column was named `inf` or `Inf` and used in a chained comparison:

```python
df = pd.DataFrame({'inf': [0.1, 0.5, 0.9]})
df.query('0.25 < inf < 0.75')  # KeyError: False
```

## Root cause

`Term.__init__` sets `is_local=True` when the name appears in `DEFAULT_GLOBALS` (which includes `'inf'` → `np.inf`). `Term._resolve_name()` only overrode this flag for names whose scope value is a `type` (e.g. `datetime`, `list`). For non-type globals like `np.inf` (a float), the override never fired, so the resolver fetched `np.inf` from scope instead of the column. The chained comparison `0.25 < np.inf < 0.75` evaluated to a Python `bool` (`False`), which then caused `df.loc[False]` → `KeyError`.

## Fix

In `_resolve_name()`, add an `elif` branch: when the name is not an `@`-prefixed local variable and exists as a column in the DataFrame resolvers, set `is_local=False` so the column takes priority over the `DEFAULT_GLOBALS` value.

title: PERF: faster integer column parsing in read_csv C engine
body:
## Summary

Swap ``str_to_int64`` / ``str_to_uint64`` in the C parser from libc ``strtoll`` / ``strtoull`` to ``std::from_chars`` via a thin ``extern "C"`` wrapper. ``std::from_chars`` is locale-independent and avoids the per-call ``errno``-TLS access, mirroring the ``fast_float`` adoption for float parsing in #64432.

Additional hot-path cleanup:
- ``copy_string_without_char`` now returns the number of bytes written, removing a redundant ``strlen()`` in the thousands-separator path.
- ``parser.thousands`` is hoisted to a local in ``_try_int64_nogil`` and ``_try_uint64_nogil`` to keep the hot loop cleaner.

## Benchmarks

Measured end-to-end ``read_csv`` wall-clock on macOS / Apple clang 15 / M-series, 200-iteration percentiles (p50):

| workload                           | baseline | new     | Δ       |
|------------------------------------|---------:|--------:|--------:|
| int64 wide range                   | 54.54 ms | 50.87 ms | **−6.7%** |
| uint64                             | 66.01 ms | 60.52 ms | **−8.3%** |
| int64 18-digit                     | 65.25 ms | 61.33 ms | **−6.0%** |
| int64 thousands=,                  | 69.48 ms | 67.21 ms | −3.3% |
| asv ``read_uint64``                | 0.869 ms | 0.806 ms | **−7.2%** |
| int64 all-negative                 | 13.24 ms | 12.58 ms | **−5.0%** |
| uint64 overflow→retry path         | 20.57 ms | 19.68 ms | −4.3% |

I expect larger wins on Linux/glibc where ``strtoll`` has more per-call locale overhead.

I also specifically bench-tested a handful of adversarial cases (``+``-prefixed values, leading zeros, leading whitespace, trailing-junk overflow e.g. ``18446744073709551616.0``, mixed signed/unsigned columns); none regressed.

## Follow-up opportunity

A subsequent PR that threads token lengths through from the tokenizer (eliminating the per-call ``strlen(p)``) could compound on top of this change — ``std::from_chars`` already takes ``[start, end)`` so that refactor becomes a drop-in.

## Test plan

- [x] Full ``pandas/tests/io/parser/`` suite: 4406 passed, 174 skipped, 230 xfailed
- [x] mypy clean
- [x] pre-commit clean
- [ ] Linux/glibc CI timings

import pandas as pd

data = [1, 2, 3, None, None, 6, 7]

When interpolating a Series backed by a pyarrow dtype such as int64[pyarrow], `method="linear"` with `limit_direction="forward"` leaves missing values unchanged, while the equivalent series with a numpy backend interpolates as expected. import pandas as pd

title: BUG: Fix AttributeError in concat when result is Series
body:
## Fix pandas-dev/pandas#65333

**Bug**: `Series.combine_first` fails when `other.Series.name` is a Timestamp that sorts before `self.Series.name`.

**Error**:
```
AttributeError: 'Series' object has no attribute 'columns'
```

**Root Cause**: In `concat.py:489`, when `orig_axis == 0` and result is a Series (not DataFrame), the code tries to access `result.columns` which doesn't exist on Series objects.

**Fix**: Add `hasattr` check to fallback to `result.index` for Series objects.

```python
# Before
orig = result.index if orig_axis == 1 else result.columns

# After
orig = result.index if orig_axis == 1 else (
    result.columns if hasattr(result, "columns") else result.index
)
```

**Testing**:
```python
s1 = pd.Series([0], name=pd.to_datetime('2026'))
s3 = pd.Series([1,3], name=pd.to_datetime('2025'))
# Previously failed with AttributeError, now works
result = s1.combine_first(s3)  # ✅ Success
```

---
Closes #65333

## Description

When concatenating Series with `Timestamp` names that are not in chronological order, `Series.combine_first` crashes with `AttributeError: 'Series' object has no attribute 'columns'`.

### Root cause

In `pandas/core/reshape/concat.py`, when `sort` remains `lib.no_default` (because the Series names form non-monotonic `DatetimeIndex` objects), the deprecation warning logic unconditionally accesses `result.columns`. But when concatenating Series along axis=0, the result is a Series, which has no `.columns` attribute.

### Fix

Skip the deprecation warning check when the result is a Series by adding `if not isinstance(result, ABCSeries)`. Column axis sorting is not applicable to 1D objects.

### Reproducer

```python
import pandas as pd

s1 = pd.Series([0], name=pd.to_datetime('2026'))
s3 = pd.Series([1, 3], name=pd.to_datetime('2025'))
s1.combine_first(s3)  # raises AttributeError
```
